result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called major.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.57
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line called major.

**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the fourth binomial AD [D2.1], and let AD be divided into its terms at E, AE being the greater term. Since AD is a binomial, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; and since AD is a fourth binomial, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, and the greater term AE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB set out [D10.2.4].

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10]. Since ED is made up of the equal segments EF, FD, the square on ED is equal to the squares on EF, FD together with twice the rectangle EF, FD [2.4], that is, to four times the square on EF. Hence the square on EF is the fourth part of the square on ED.

**Step 3.** Apply to AE a parallelogram equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; let it be the rectangle contained by AG, GE, so that rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF). (This is possible: AE, being the greater term, exceeds ED, so EF, the half of ED, is less than the half of AE, and the square on EF is less than the square on the half of AE.)

**Step 4.** AE, ED are two unequal straight lines, AE the greater; the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE (Step 1); and to AE there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, ED (Step 2), and deficient by a square figure (Step 3). Therefore it divides AE into parts AG, GE which are incommensurable in length [10.18].

**Step 5.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB [1.31], meeting BC at H, K, L. Then AH, GK, EL, FC are the rectangles contained by AB and AG, GE, EF, FD respectively, AK is the rectangle contained by AB, AE [D2.1], and the whole area AC is made up of AH, GK, EL, FC.

**Step 6.** Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC stand on the equal bases EF, FD and are in the same parallels AD, BC; therefore EL = FC [1.36].

**Step 7.** AK is contained by AB and AE, which are rational straight lines commensurable in length (Step 1). Therefore AK is rational [10.19]. And AK is the sum of AH and GK.

**Step 8.** AE, ED are commensurable in square only, so AE is incommensurable in length with ED; but AE is commensurable in length with AB; therefore ED is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13]. Again, EF measures ED, ED being twice EF, so EF is commensurable in length with ED [D10.1.1]; and ED is incommensurable in length with AB; therefore EF is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13].

**Step 9.** The square on ED is four times the square on EF (Step 2), so the square on EF has to the square on ED the ratio which a number has to a number, and is commensurable with it [10.6]. ED is rational, so the square on ED is commensurable with the square on AB [D10.1.3, D10.1.2]. Therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on AB [10.12], that is, EF is commensurable in square with AB and is rational [D10.1.3]. Thus AB, EF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Step 8), and the rectangle contained by them, EL, is medial [10.21].

**Step 10.** AH and GK have the same height AB, so AH : GK = AG : GE [6.1]. But AG is incommensurable in length with GE (Step 4); therefore AH is incommensurable with GK [10.11].

**Step 11.** Likewise the square on AG and the rectangle AG, GE have the same height AG, so sq(AG) : rect(AG, GE) = AG : GE [6.1]; and rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF) (Step 3), so AG : GE = sq(AG) : sq(EF) [5.7]. Hence, by Step 10, AH : GK = sq(AG) : sq(EF) [5.11].

**Step 12.** Construct a square equal to AH and let SN be its side, and construct a square equal to GK [2.14]; produce SN to Q [P2] and cut off NQ equal to the side of the latter square [1.3]. Then sq(SN) = AH and sq(NQ) = GK, so sq(SN) : sq(NQ) = AH : GK [5.7] = sq(AG) : sq(EF) [5.11]. The squares are similar figures similarly described on SN, NQ, AG, EF; therefore SN : NQ = AG : EF [6.22].

**Step 13.** The square on SN and the rectangle SN, NQ have the same height SN, so sq(SN) : rect(SN, NQ) = SN : NQ [6.1]; and AH, EL have the same height AB, so AH : EL = AG : EF [6.1]. Since SN : NQ = AG : EF (Step 12), sq(SN) : rect(SN, NQ) = AH : EL [5.11]. But sq(SN) = AH, so AH : rect(SN, NQ) = AH : EL [5.7]; therefore rect(SN, NQ) = EL [5.9], and hence also rect(SN, NQ) = FC (Step 6).

**Step 14.** The straight line SQ is divided at N, so the square on SQ is equal to the squares on SN, NQ together with twice the rectangle SN, NQ [2.4]; and these are equal respectively to AH, GK, EL, FC, so that the square on SQ is equal to AH + GK + EL + FC [CN2], which is the whole area AC (Step 5). Therefore SQ is the "side" of AC, namely the straight line on which is described a square equal to the area AC [D10.1.4].

**Step 15.** Now the squares on SN, NQ are AH, GK, which are incommensurable with one another (Step 10); therefore SN, NQ are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2]. The sum of the squares on SN, NQ is AH + GK, that is AK, which is rational (Step 7). And the rectangle contained by SN, NQ is EL, which is medial (Step 9).

**Step 16.** Therefore SN, NQ are two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial; hence the whole SQ made up of them is irrational and is the straight line called major [10.39]. Thus the "side" of the area AC, contained by the rational straight line AB and the fourth binomial AD, is the irrational straight line called major. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fifth binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the fifth binomial AD, divided into its terms at E, so that AE is the greater term. Since AD is a binomial divided into its terms, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; and since AD is a fifth binomial, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, while the lesser term ED is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB [D10.2.4, D10.2.5]. It is required to prove that the "side" of AC is the side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10]. Since ED is bisected at F, the square on ED is four times the square on EF [2.4], so the square on EF is the fourth part of the square on ED. Apply to AE a parallelogram equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure [6.28] (this is possible, since EF, being half of ED, is less than half of AE), and let it be the rectangle contained by AG, GE; thus rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF). Now AE, ED are two unequal straight lines, the square on the greater AE exceeds the square on the less ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE, and to AE has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on ED and deficient by a square figure; therefore it divides AE into parts AG, GE which are incommensurable in length [10.18].

**Step 3.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB, meeting BC at H, K, L [1.31]. Then AC is divided into the rectangles AH, GK, EL, FC, contained by AB together with AG, GE, EF, FD respectively; AK is the rectangle contained by AB, AE, and EC is the rectangle contained by AB, ED. Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC stand on equal bases and lie in the same parallels AD, BC; therefore EL = FC [1.36].

**Step 4.** Construct a square equal to AH and let MN be one of its sides; construct a square equal to GK [2.14]; produce MN to O [P2] and cut off NO equal to a side of the second square [1.3]. On MO describe the square SQ [1.46]. Since MO is cut at N, the square on MO is equal to the squares on MN, NO together with twice the rectangle contained by MN, NO [2.4]; accordingly SQ is made up of the square SN on MN, the square NQ on NO, and two rectangles MR, OP, each contained by straight lines equal to MN, NO, so that MR = OP and SQ = SN + NQ + MR + OP. Moreover SN = AH and NQ = GK.

**Step 5.** Since rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF), the three straight lines AG, EF, GE are proportional: AG : EF = EF : GE [6.17]. But the rectangles AH, EL, GK are under the same height AB, so AH : EL = AG : EF and EL : GK = EF : GE [6.1]. Therefore AH : EL = EL : GK [5.11]; that is, EL is a mean proportional between AH and GK.

**Step 6.** Again, SN and MR are under the same height MN with bases MN, NO, and MR and NQ are under the same height NO with bases MN, NO; therefore SN : MR = MN : NO and MR : NQ = MN : NO [6.1], whence SN : MR = MR : NQ [5.11]. Since SN = AH and NQ = GK, AH : MR = SN : MR and MR : NQ = MR : GK [5.7]; therefore AH : MR = MR : GK [5.11]; that is, MR is also a mean proportional between AH and GK.

**Step 7.** EL = MR. For suppose EL > MR. Then AH has to the less, MR, a greater ratio than to the greater, EL [5.8]. But AH : MR = MR : GK and AH : EL = EL : GK, so MR has to GK a greater ratio than EL has to GK [5.13]; therefore MR > EL [5.10], which contradicts the supposition. In the same way EL is not less than MR. Therefore EL = MR; and since FC = EL and OP = MR, also FC = OP [CN1].

**Step 8.** Therefore SQ = SN + NQ + MR + OP = AH + GK + EL + FC = AC [CN2]. Thus the square on MO is equal to the area AC, and MO is the "side" of AC [D10.1.4].

**Step 9.** Since the rectangles AH, GK are under the same height AB, AH : GK = AG : GE [6.1]. But AG is incommensurable in length with GE (Step 2); therefore AH is incommensurable with GK [10.11]. Now AH is the square on MN and GK is the square on NO; hence the square on MN is incommensurable with the square on NO, and MN, NO are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 10.** The sum of the squares on MN, NO is SN + NQ = AH + GK = AK [CN2], the rectangle contained by AB, AE. Now ED is commensurable in length with AB, while ED is incommensurable in length with AE (Step 1); therefore AE is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13]. But AB and AE are both rational, so each is commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.3], and hence the squares on AB, AE are commensurable with one another [10.12]; thus AB, AE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [D10.1.2]. Therefore the rectangle AK contained by them is medial [10.21]; that is, the sum of the squares on MN, NO is medial.

**Step 11.** The rectangle contained by MN, NO is MR, which is equal to EL (Step 7). Since AB, ED are rational straight lines commensurable in length (Step 1), the rectangle EC contained by them is rational [10.19]. But EC = EL + FC = twice EL, so EL measures EC and is commensurable with it [D10.1.1]; and EC, being rational, is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.4]; therefore EL is commensurable with that square [10.12] and is rational [D10.1.4]. Hence the rectangle contained by MN, NO is rational.

**Step 12.** Therefore MN, NO are two straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 9) which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 10) but the rectangle contained by them rational (Step 11); so the whole MO, made up of them, is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area [10.40]. But MO is the "side" of AC (Step 8). Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fifth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area. Q.E.D.

Path note: the square on MO is decomposed at once by 2.4 into the squares on MN, NO and the two equal rectangles MN·NO; the alternative of constructing the two squares SN, NQ separately and placing them about a common diameter (which would require 6.26 and 1.43 to identify the complements) reaches the same figure by a longer route.

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the sixth binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of the sum of two medial areas.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the sixth binomial AD, divided into its terms at E, so that AE is the greater term. Since AD is a binomial, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; and since AD is a sixth binomial, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, and neither AE nor ED is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB set out [D10.2.6]. I say that the "side" of AC is the irrational straight line called the side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10], so that EF = FD and the square on EF is the fourth part of the square on ED. To AE apply a parallelogram equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; let it be the rectangle contained by AG, GE, so that rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF). (The application is possible, since EF, being half of ED, is less than half of AE, ED being less than AE.)

**Step 3.** Since the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, and to AE there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on ED and deficient by a square figure, AG is incommensurable in length with GE [10.18].

**Step 4.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB [1.31], meeting BC at H, K, L. Then AH, GK, EL, FC are the rectangles contained by AB and AG, GE, EF, FD respectively; AK is the rectangle contained by AB, AE; and EC is the rectangle contained by AB, ED.

**Step 5.** Since AG is incommensurable in length with GE, and AG : GE = AH : GK, the rectangles AH, GK being under the same height AB [6.1], AH is incommensurable with GK [10.11].

**Step 6.** AB is the rational straight line set out and AE is rational; hence AE is commensurable with AB either in length or in square only [D10.1.3]. But AE is incommensurable in length with AB; therefore AB, AE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and the rectangle AK contained by them is medial [10.21]. For the same reason, ED being rational and incommensurable in length with AB, the rectangle EC contained by AB, ED is medial [10.21].

**Step 7.** Since AE, ED are commensurable in square only, AE is incommensurable in length with ED. And AE : ED = AK : EC, the rectangles AK, EC being under the same height AB [6.1]; therefore AK is incommensurable with EC [10.11].

**Step 8.** Since EF = FD, the rectangles EL, FC, being on the equal bases EF, FD and in the same parallels AD, BC, are equal [1.36]; hence EC, which is made up of EL and FC, is double EL. Therefore EL measures EC, so that EL is commensurable with EC [D10.1.1]. But EC is medial [Step 6]; therefore EL, being commensurable with a medial area, is itself medial [10.23]. Further, since AK is incommensurable with EC [Step 7] and EC is commensurable with EL, AK is incommensurable with EL [10.13].

**Step 9.** Let MN be the side of the square equal to AH, and NO the side of the square equal to GK [2.14], and let MN, NO be placed in a straight line, so that MO is the whole. Then sq(MN) = AH and sq(NO) = GK. Since AH is incommensurable with GK [Step 5], sq(MN) is incommensurable with sq(NO); therefore MN, NO are straight lines incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 10.** Since sq(MN) = AH and sq(NO) = GK, sq(MN) : sq(NO) = AH : GK = AG : GE [6.1]. Again, AG : GE = sq(AG) : rect(AG, GE), the square and the rectangle being under the same height AG [6.1]; and rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF) [Step 2]. Therefore sq(MN) : sq(NO) = sq(AG) : sq(EF) [5.11]. But these are similar figures similarly described on MN, NO and on AG, EF; therefore MN : NO = AG : EF [6.22].

**Step 11.** Now sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = MN : NO, the square and the rectangle being under the same height MN [6.1]; and AG : EF = AH : EL, the rectangles AH, EL being under the same height AB [6.1]. Therefore, by Step 10, sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = AH : EL [5.11]. But sq(MN) = AH; therefore rect(MN, NO) = EL [5.9].

**Step 12.** Since the straight line MO is cut at N, sq(MO) = sq(MN) + sq(NO) + 2·rect(MN, NO) [2.4]. But sq(MN) = AH, sq(NO) = GK, and 2·rect(MN, NO) = 2·EL = EL + FC [Steps 8, 11]. Therefore sq(MO) = AH + GK + EL + FC, that is, sq(MO) is equal to the whole AC [CN2]. Hence MO is the "side" of the area AC.

**Step 13.** Now MN, NO are incommensurable in square [Step 9]. The sum of the squares on MN, NO is AH + GK, that is, the rectangle AK, which is medial [Step 6]. The rectangle contained by MN, NO is EL, which is medial [Steps 8, 11]. And this rectangle EL is incommensurable with the sum of the squares AK [Step 8]. Therefore MN, NO are two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial and the rectangle contained by them medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them; therefore the whole MO is irrational, namely the straight line called the side of the sum of two medial areas [10.41].

**Step 14.** But MO is the "side" of AC [Step 12]. Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the sixth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of the sum of two medial areas. Q.E.D.

Path note: the identification rect(MN, NO) = EL is obtained from the proportion MN : NO = AG : EF via 6.22, chosen over a mean-proportional argument because it avoids an otherwise unproved uniqueness claim for mean proportionals between areas.

result.statement: The square on the binomial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the first binomial.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.60
**Statement:** The square on the binomial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the first binomial.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a binomial straight line divided into its terms at C; then AC, CB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]. Since AC, CB are incommensurable in length they are unequal, for equal straight lines are commensurable, each being a measure of the other [D10.1.1]; let AC be the greater term. Let DE be a rational straight line, and let the rectangle DEFG, equal to the square on AB, be applied to DE, producing DG as its breadth. Throughout, "rational" is understood with respect to the assigned rational straight line, which I call R [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]. I say that DG is a first binomial straight line.

**Step 2.** To DE let there be applied the rectangle DH equal to the square on AC, and next to it along DG the rectangle KL equal to the square on CB, so that K, M lie on DG, H, L lie on EF, and each of DH, KL and the remaining rectangle MF has a side (DE, KH, ML respectively) equal to DE. Now the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4]. Since DEFG equals the square on AB, DH the square on AC, and KL the square on CB, the remainder MF equals twice the rectangle AC, CB [CN3].

**Step 3.** Bisect MG at N [1.10], and through N draw NO parallel to ML, meeting LF at O [1.31]. The parallelograms MO, NF stand on the equal bases MN, NG and are in the same parallels DG, EF; therefore MO = NF [1.36]. Together they make up MF, which is twice the rectangle AC, CB; hence each of MO, NF is equal to the rectangle AC, CB.

**Step 4.** Since AC, CB are rational, each is commensurable in square with R [D10.1.3]; so the squares on AC, CB are commensurable with the square on R and are rational areas [D10.1.4]. Since AC, CB are commensurable in square, the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB [D10.1.2]. Therefore their sum, the rectangle DL (= DH + KL), is commensurable with the square on AC [10.15], and hence with the square on R [10.12]; so DL is a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** DL, a rational area, is applied to the rational straight line DE, producing DM as breadth; therefore DM is rational and commensurable in length with DE [10.20].

**Step 6.** The rectangle AC, CB, being contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only, is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21]. MF is twice the rectangle AC, CB, so it is measured by that rectangle and is commensurable with it [D10.1.1]; and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]. Therefore MF is a medial area.

**Step 7.** MF, a medial area, is applied to ML, which is equal to the rational straight line DE, producing MG as breadth; therefore MG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE [10.22].

**Step 8.** DM is commensurable in length with DE (Step 5), and DE is incommensurable in length with MG (Step 7); therefore DM is incommensurable in length with MG [10.13]. But DM, MG are both rational, so each is commensurable in square with R [D10.1.3]; hence the squares on DM, MG are commensurable with one another [10.12], that is, DM, MG are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Thus DM, MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and their sum DG is a binomial straight line with terms DM, MG [10.36].

**Step 9.** The square on AC and the rectangle AC, CB are parallelograms under the same height AC on the bases AC, CB; and the rectangle AC, CB and the square on CB are parallelograms under the same height CB on the bases AC, CB. Hence the square on AC is to the rectangle AC, CB as AC is to CB, and the rectangle AC, CB is to the square on CB as AC is to CB [6.1]; therefore the square on AC is to the rectangle AC, CB as the rectangle AC, CB is to the square on CB [5.11]. Since DH, MO, NF, KL are equal respectively to the square on AC, the rectangle AC, CB, the rectangle AC, CB, and the square on CB, it follows that DH is to MO as NF is to KL [5.7].

**Step 10.** DH, MO are parallelograms under the same height (between the parallels DG, EF) on the bases DK, MN, and NF, KL are parallelograms under the same height on the bases NG, KM; therefore DH is to MO as DK is to MN, and NF is to KL as NG is to KM [6.1]. Hence, by Step 9, DK is to MN as NG is to KM [5.11]; and since NG = MN, DK is to MN as MN is to KM [5.7]. Therefore the rectangle DK, KM is equal to the square on MN [6.17].

**Step 11.** The square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB (Step 4), so DH is commensurable with KL; and DH is to KL as DK is to KM [6.1]; therefore DK is commensurable in length with KM [10.11].

**Step 12.** From CA cut off CX equal to CB [1.3]; X lies between A and C, since AC is greater than CB. Since the straight line AC is cut at X, the square on AC together with the square on XC is equal to twice the rectangle AC, XC together with the square on AX [2.7]; that is, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AX. Therefore the squares on AC, CB together are greater than twice the rectangle AC, CB [CN5]; that is, DL is greater than MF.

**Step 13.** I say that DM is greater than MG. If DM were equal to MG, then DL, MF, being parallelograms on equal bases and in the same parallels DG, EF, would be equal [1.36], contrary to Step 12. If DM were less than MG, cut off MP equal to DM from MG [1.3] and through P draw PQ parallel to ML, meeting LF at Q [1.31]; then the parallelogram MQ, on the base MP equal to DM and in the same parallels, is equal to DL [1.36]; but MQ is a part of MF, so DL would be less than MF [CN5], again contrary to Step 12. Therefore DM is greater than MG.

**Step 14.** Since MG is bisected at N, the square on MG is equal to the squares on MN, NG together with twice the rectangle MN, NG, that is, to four times the square on MN [2.4]. So the square on MN is the fourth part of the square on MG, and by Step 10 the rectangle DK, KM is equal to the fourth part of the square on MG.

**Step 15.** DM, MG are two unequal straight lines of which DM is the greater (Step 13). To DM there has been applied the parallelogram contained by DK, KM, deficient by the square on KM, which is equal to the fourth part of the square on MG (Step 14), and it divides DM into the parts DK, KM which are commensurable in length (Step 11). Therefore the square on DM is greater than the square on MG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with DM [10.17].

**Step 16.** DG is a binomial straight line divided into its terms DM, MG (Step 8); the square on the greater term DM exceeds the square on the lesser term MG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with DM (Step 15); and the greater term DM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE set out (Step 5). Therefore DG is a first binomial straight line [D10.2.1]. Hence the square on a binomial straight line, applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth the first binomial. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the inequality of Step 12 (Heath's lemma preceding X.60) is proved inline from 2.7 since no separate lemma is available; the passage from DL > MF to DM > MG (Step 13) is made by 1.36 rather than by a proportion between areas and lines, because 5.14 cannot be applied to magnitudes of different kinds.

**USED:** 10.36, D10.1.1, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4, D10.2.1, 2.4, 2.7, CN3, CN5, 1.3, 1.10, 1.31, 1.36, 5.7, 5.11, 6.1, 6.17, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.15, 10.17, 10.20, 10.21, 10.22, 10.23

result.statement: The square on the first bimedial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the second binomial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a first bimedial straight line, and let C be the point at which it is divided into the two medial straight lines of which it is composed; then AC, CB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle [10.37]. AC and CB are unequal, since equal straight lines measure one another and would therefore be commensurable in length [D10.1.1]; let AC be the greater. Let DE be a rational straight line, and to DE let there be applied, in a right angle, the rectangle DF equal to the square on AB, producing DG as its breadth [1.44, 1.45]. I say that DG is a second binomial straight line.

**Step 2.** Since AB is divided at C, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4]. To DE apply the rectangle DH equal to the square on AC, producing DK as breadth; and to KH, which is equal to DE [1.34], apply the rectangle KL equal to the square on CB, producing KM as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. Then DH, KL together, that is the rectangle DL, are equal to the squares on AC, CB [CN2]; and since the whole DF is equal to the square on AB, the remaining rectangle MF, contained by ML and MG, is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB [CN3]. Here ML, like KH, is equal to DE [1.34].

**Step 3.** Bisect MG at N [1.10], and through N draw NO parallel to ML [1.31]. The parallelograms MO, NF are on the equal bases MN, NG and in the same parallels DG, EF; therefore MO is equal to NF [1.36]. Since together they make up MF, each of them is half of MF; that is, each of MO, NF is equal to the rectangle AC, CB. Thus the four rectangles DH, KL, MO, NF stand on the bases DK, KM, MN, NG respectively and are all of the same height, each having a side equal to DE [1.34].

**Step 4.** [DM is rational and incommensurable in length with DE.] Since AC is medial, the square on AC is a medial area, being equal to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.21]; similarly the square on CB is medial. Since AC, CB are commensurable in square, the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB [D10.1.2]; therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is commensurable with the square on AC [10.15], and, being commensurable with a medial area, it is itself medial [10.23, Porism]. But DL is equal to the squares on AC, CB (Step 2); therefore DL is a medial area, and it is applied to the rational straight line DE producing DM as breadth. Therefore DM is rational and incommensurable in length with DE [10.22].

**Step 5.** [MG is rational and commensurable in length with DE.] The rectangle AC, CB is rational, that is, commensurable with the square on the rational straight line DE [D10.1.4]. MF is twice the rectangle AC, CB, so that the rectangle AC, CB measures MF and the two are commensurable [D10.1.1]; hence MF is commensurable with the square on DE [10.12], and so MF is a rational area [D10.1.4]. Now MF is applied to the rational straight line ML, which is equal to DE, producing MG as breadth; therefore MG is rational and commensurable in length with ML, that is, with DE [10.20].

**Step 6.** [DG is a binomial.] MG is commensurable in length with DE, and DE is incommensurable in length with DM; therefore MG is incommensurable in length with DM [10.13]. But DM, MG are both rational, so that each is commensurable in square with DE [D10.1.3]; hence the squares on DM, MG are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Therefore DM, MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and their sum DG is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms DM, MG at M [10.36].

**Step 7.** [DM is the greater term.] Since AC is greater than CB, cut off from AC the part CP equal to CB [1.3]. AC being cut at P, the squares on AC, CP together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CP together with the square on AP [2.7]; that is, the squares on AC, CB are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AP, and so are greater than twice the rectangle AC, CB [CN5]. Therefore DL is greater than MF. Now DL, MF are rectangles of the same height DE on the bases DM, MG. If DM were equal to MG, DL would be equal to MF [1.36]; if DM were less than MG, then, a part of MG being cut off equal to DM [1.3], DL would be equal to the rectangle on that part [1.36] and so less than MF [CN5]. Neither is the case; therefore DM is greater than MG.

**Step 8.** [DK, KM are commensurable in length.] Since the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB (Step 4), DH is commensurable with KL. DH, KL being of the same height, DH is to KL as DK is to KM [6.1]; therefore DK is commensurable in length with KM [10.11].

**Step 9.** [The rectangle DK, KM is equal to the square on MN.] The square on AC and the rectangle AC, CB are parallelograms of the same height AC on the bases AC, CB; therefore the square on AC is to the rectangle AC, CB as AC is to CB [6.1]. Again, the rectangle AC, CB and the square on CB are of the same height CB on the bases AC, CB; therefore the rectangle AC, CB is to the square on CB as AC is to CB [6.1]. Hence the square on AC is to the rectangle AC, CB as the rectangle AC, CB is to the square on CB [5.11]. Since DH, MO, KL are equal respectively to the square on AC, the rectangle AC, CB and the square on CB, it follows that DH is to MO as MO is to KL [5.7]. But, the rectangles being of the same height, DH is to MO as DK is to MN, and MO is to KL as MN is to KM [6.1]. Therefore DK is to MN as MN is to KM [5.11], and the rectangle DK, KM is equal to the square on MN [6.17].

**Step 10.** [The square on DM exceeds the square on MG by the square on a straight line commensurable with DM.] Since MG is bisected at N, the square on MG is equal to the squares on MN, NG together with twice the rectangle MN, NG [2.4], that is, to four times the square on MN; so the square on MN, and therefore the rectangle DK, KM, is the fourth part of the square on MG. Now DM, MG are two unequal straight lines of which DM is the greater (Step 7), and to DM there has been applied the rectangle DK, KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, MG, and deficient by the square figure on KM; and it divides DM at K into the parts DK, KM, which are commensurable in length (Step 8). Therefore the square on DM is greater than the square on MG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with DM [10.17].

**Step 11.** [Conclusion.] DG is a binomial straight line with terms DM, MG (Step 6), of which DM is the greater (Step 7); the square on the greater term DM exceeds the square on the lesser term MG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with DM (Step 10); and the lesser term MG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE set out (Step 5). Therefore DG is a second binomial straight line [D10.2.2]. Thus the square on the first bimedial straight line AB, applied to the rational straight line DE, produces as breadth the second binomial DG. Q.E.D.

Path note: the rationality of DM (Step 4) could equally be obtained by applying 10.22 to DH and KL separately and combining with Step 8 and 10.15; the route through the medial area DL is taken as the more direct.

result.statement: The square on the second bimedial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the third binomial.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.62
**Statement:** The square on the second bimedial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the third binomial.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a second bimedial straight line, divided into its medials at C, AC being the greater. Then, by the definition of a second bimedial (10.38), AC and CB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle. Let DE be a rational straight line, and to DE let there be applied, in a right angle, the rectangle DF equal to the square on AB (1.44, 1.45), producing DG as breadth. It is to be proved that DG is a third binomial straight line.

**Step 2.** To DE apply the rectangle DL equal to the square on AC, producing DH as breadth, and to HL apply the rectangle HM equal to the square on CB, producing HK as breadth (1.44, 1.45); let the remaining part of DF be the rectangle KF, with breadth KG. Since HL and KM are opposite sides of rectangles, each of them equals DE (1.34), so that the rectangles DL, HM, KF stand on the breadths DH, HK, KG under the same height DE. Now the square on AB equals the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB (2.4). Taking away DL and HM, which equal the squares on AC, CB, the remainder KF equals twice the rectangle AC·CB (CN3).

**Step 3.** Since AC is medial, its square DL, applied to the rational straight line DE, produces as breadth DH rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22). Similarly, since CB is medial, HK is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 4.** Since AC, CB are commensurable in square, the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB (D10.1.2); that is, DL is commensurable with HM. But DL : HM = DH : HK, these rectangles having the same height DE (6.1). Hence DH is commensurable in length with HK (10.11). Therefore the whole DK is commensurable with DH (10.15). Hence the square on DK is commensurable with the square on DH, which is commensurable with the square on DE (DH being rational); so the square on DK is commensurable with the square on DE (10.12), and DK is rational (D10.1.3). Moreover, since DH is incommensurable in length with DE and DK is commensurable with DH, DK is incommensurable in length with DE (10.13).

**Step 5.** The rectangle AC·CB is medial by hypothesis. KF is twice this rectangle and therefore commensurable with it, having to it the ratio 2 : 1 which a number has to a number (10.6); hence KF is a medial area (10.23). Since KF, a medial area, is applied to the rational straight line KM, which equals DE, it produces as breadth KG rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 6.** Since AC, CB are commensurable in square only, AC is incommensurable in length with CB (D10.1.2). Now AC : CB = (square on AC) : (rectangle AC·CB), the square on AC and the rectangle AC·CB having the same height AC (6.1). Hence the square on AC is incommensurable with the rectangle AC·CB (10.11). But the squares on AC, CB together are commensurable with the square on AC (10.15), and twice the rectangle AC·CB is commensurable with the rectangle AC·CB (10.6). Therefore the squares on AC, CB together are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC·CB (10.13, applied twice); that is, the rectangle DM, which is DL together with HM, is incommensurable with KF. But DM : KF = DK : KG (6.1). Hence DK is incommensurable in length with KG (10.11).

**Step 7.** DK and KG are both rational (Steps 4, 5), each being commensurable in square with DE; hence they are commensurable in square with one another (10.12). Being also incommensurable in length (Step 6), DK, KG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore DG is a binomial straight line (10.36), its terms being DK and KG.

**Step 8.** Since AC is greater than CB, the squares on AC, CB together equal twice the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on the excess of AC over CB (2.7); hence the squares on AC, CB together are greater than twice the rectangle AC·CB (CN5), that is, DM is greater than KF. Since DM : KF = DK : KG (6.1), DK is greater than KG. Thus DK is the greater term and KG the lesser term of the binomial DG.

**Step 9.** Bisect KG at N (1.10), and through N draw NO parallel to KM, meeting MF at O (1.31). The rectangles KO, NF stand on the equal bases KN, NG and lie in the same parallels KG, MF; therefore they are equal (1.36). Together they make up KF, which is twice the rectangle AC·CB; therefore KO equals the rectangle AC·CB.

**Step 10.** Since AC : CB = (square on AC) : (rectangle AC·CB) and also AC : CB = (rectangle AC·CB) : (square on CB) (6.1), it follows that (square on AC) : (rectangle AC·CB) = (rectangle AC·CB) : (square on CB) (5.11); that is, DL : KO = KO : HM. But DL : KO = DH : KN and KO : HM = KN : HK, all these rectangles having the same height DE (6.1). Therefore DH : KN = KN : HK (5.11), so that the rectangle DH·HK equals the square on KN (6.17).

**Step 11.** Since KG is bisected at N, the square on KG equals the squares on KN, NG together with twice the rectangle KN·NG (2.4), that is, four times the square on KN; hence the square on KN is the fourth part of the square on KG. Thus the rectangle DH·HK, which equals the square on KN (Step 10), is the fourth part of the square on the lesser straight line KG.

**Step 12.** Accordingly, to the greater DK of the two unequal straight lines DK, KG there has been applied a parallelogram, namely the rectangle DH·HK, equal to the fourth part of the square on the lesser KG and deficient by a square figure (the square on HK), and it divides DK into the parts DH, HK, which are commensurable in length (Step 4). Therefore the square on DK is greater than the square on KG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with DK (10.17).

**Step 13.** Therefore DG is a binomial straight line (Step 7) whose terms DK, KG are both incommensurable in length with the rational straight line DE set out (Steps 4, 5), and the square on the greater term DK is greater than the square on the lesser term KG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with DK (Step 12). Hence DG is a third binomial straight line (D10.2.3). Since DF, which equals the square on AB, was applied to the rational straight line DE producing DG as breadth, the square on the second bimedial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the third binomial. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 1.10, 1.31, 1.34, 1.36, 1.44, 1.45, 2.4, 2.7, 5.11, 6.1, 6.17, 10.6, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.15, 10.17, 10.22, 10.23, 10.36, 10.38, CN3, CN5, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.2.3

result.statement: The square on the major straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fourth binomial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a major straight line. By 10.39, AB is the sum of two straight lines AC, CB (meeting at C) which are incommensurable in square, such that the sum of the squares on AC, CB is rational while the rectangle AC·CB is medial. Since AC, CB are incommensurable in square they are unequal; let AC be the greater. Let DE be a rational straight line, and to DE apply the rectangle DEFG equal to the square on AB, producing DG as breadth (1.44). It is to be shown that DG is a fourth binomial.

**Step 2.** Along DG apply to DE the rectangle DH equal to the square on AC, producing DK as breadth, and next to it the rectangle KL equal to the square on CB, producing KM as breadth (1.44); H, L lie on EF. Then DL = DH + KL = AC² + CB² (CN2). By 2.4 the square on AB equals the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB; since DF = AB² and DL = AC² + CB², the remainder MF = 2·AC·CB (CN3). Bisect MG at N (1.10) and draw NO parallel to ML, with O on LF (1.31). The rectangles MO, NF stand on the equal bases MN, NG in the same parallels, so MO = NF (1.36); hence each is half of MF, that is, each is equal to the rectangle AC·CB.

**Step 3.** Since AC² + CB² is rational, DL is a rational area applied to the rational straight line DE; therefore its breadth DM is rational and commensurable in length with DE (10.20).

**Step 4.** The rectangle AC·CB is medial. The areas 2·AC·CB and AC·CB are both measured by AC·CB, so they are commensurable (D10.1.1); and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23, Porism). Hence MF = 2·AC·CB is a medial area, i.e. it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, and it is applied to the rational straight line DE; therefore its breadth MG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 5.** DM is commensurable in length with DE while MG is incommensurable in length with DE; therefore DM is incommensurable in length with MG (10.13). Moreover DM and MG are both rational, so the square on each is commensurable with the square on DE (D10.1.3), whence the squares on DM, MG are commensurable with one another (10.12). Thus DM, MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and DG is a binomial straight line divided into its terms at M (10.36).

**Step 6.** DM is the greater term. From CA cut off CP equal to CB (1.3), so that AC is cut at P. By 2.7, AC² + PC² = 2·AC·PC + AP², that is, AC² + CB² = 2·AC·CB + AP²; hence AC² + CB² > 2·AC·CB (CN5), which means DL > MF. Since DL and MF are rectangles of the same height DE, they are to one another as their bases DM, MG (6.1); therefore DM > MG.

**Step 7.** Since AC, CB are incommensurable in square, the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on CB (D10.1.2); that is, DH is incommensurable with KL. But DH : KL = DK : KM, these rectangles having the same height DE (6.1); therefore DK is incommensurable in length with KM (10.11).

**Step 8.** The square on AC and the rectangle AC·CB have the same height AC, so AC² : AC·CB = AC : CB (6.1); likewise the rectangle AC·CB and the square on CB have the same height CB, so AC·CB : CB² = AC : CB (6.1). Hence AC² : AC·CB = AC·CB : CB² (5.11), that is, DH : MO = MO : KL. Again, DH : MO = DK : MN and MO : KL = MN : KM, since these rectangles have the same height DE (6.1). Therefore DK : MN = MN : KM (5.11), and so the rectangle DK·KM is equal to the square on MN (6.17).

**Step 9.** Since MN = NG, by 2.4 the square on MG equals MN² + NG² + 2·MN·NG = 4·MN²; so the square on MN is the fourth part of the square on MG. Thus DM, MG are two unequal straight lines with DM the greater, and to DM there has been applied the parallelogram DK·KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, MG, and deficient by the square figure on KM, and it divides DM into the parts DK, KM which are incommensurable in length. Therefore the square on DM is greater than the square on MG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DM (10.18).

**Step 10.** DG is therefore a binomial straight line whose greater term DM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE set out, and the square on the greater term DM exceeds the square on the lesser term MG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DM. Hence DG is a fourth binomial (D10.2.4). Therefore the square on the major straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fourth binomial. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on the side of a rational plus a medial area applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fifth binomial.
result.proof:
**Statement.** The square on the side of a rational plus a medial area applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fifth binomial.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of a rational plus a medial area, divided into its straight lines at C. By the definition of such a straight line (10.40), AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, and the rectangle AC·CB is rational. Since AC, CB are incommensurable in square they are unequal; let AC be the greater. Let DE be a rational straight line, and to DE apply the rectangle DF equal to the square on AB (1.44), DE and DG being its adjacent sides, so that DG is the breadth produced. I say that DG is a fifth binomial.

**Step 2.** To DE apply the rectangle DH equal to the square on AC, and to KH (the side of DH opposite DE) apply the rectangle KL equal to the square on CB (1.44), so that D, K, M lie in order on DG and E, H, L on the opposite side EF. Then DL = DH + KL = AC² + CB² (CN2). By 2.4, AB² = AC² + CB² + 2·AC·CB. Since DF = AB², the remaining rectangle MF, whose breadth is MG, equals DF − DL = 2·AC·CB (CN3).

**Step 3.** DL equals the sum of the squares on AC, CB, which is medial; thus DL is a medial area applied to the rational straight line DE. Therefore its breadth DM is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 4.** MF is double the rectangle AC·CB, which is rational. Having to that rectangle the ratio of 2 to 1, MF is commensurable with it (10.6); hence MF is commensurable with the rational square with which that rectangle is commensurable (10.12), and so MF is a rational area (D10.1.4). MF being a rational area applied to the rational straight line DE, its breadth MG is rational and commensurable in length with DE (10.20).

**Step 5.** MG is commensurable in length with DE, and DE is incommensurable in length with DM; therefore MG is incommensurable in length with DM (10.13). Moreover DM and MG are both rational, that is, each is commensurable in square with DE (D10.1.3); so the squares on DM, MG are each commensurable with the square on DE and hence with one another (10.12). Thus DM, MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and their sum DG is a binomial straight line whose terms are DM, MG (10.36).

**Step 6.** Next, DM is greater than MG. Since AC > CB, cut off CP from CA equal to CB (1.3). AC is then cut at P, so AC² + CP² = 2·AC·CP + AP² (2.7); and since CP = CB this gives AC² + CB² = 2·AC·CB + AP². Hence AC² + CB² > 2·AC·CB (CN5), that is, DL > MF. Now DL and MF are rectangles of the same height DE on the bases DM, MG. If DM were equal to MG, DL and MF would be equal (1.36); if DM were less than MG, then cutting off from MG a part equal to DM (1.3), the rectangle on that part would equal DL (1.36) and would be a part of MF, so DL would be less than MF (CN5). Either case contradicts DL > MF; therefore DM > MG.

**Step 7.** Bisect MG at N (1.10) and through N draw NO parallel to GF, meeting LF at O (1.31). The rectangles MO, NF stand on the equal bases MN, NG between the same parallels MG, LF, so MO = NF (1.36). Together they make up MF, which is twice the rectangle AC·CB; therefore each of MO, NF is equal to the rectangle AC·CB.

**Step 8.** The square on AC and the rectangle AC·CB are under the same height AC, so AC² : AC·CB = AC : CB; and the rectangle AC·CB and the square on CB are under the same height CB, so AC·CB : CB² = AC : CB (6.1). Therefore AC² : AC·CB = AC·CB : CB² (5.11). Since DH = AC², MO = AC·CB and KL = CB², it follows that DH : MO = MO : KL. But DH, MO, KL are all under the same height DE, so DH : MO = DK : MN and MO : KL = MN : KM (6.1). Hence DK : MN = MN : KM (5.11), and therefore the rectangle DK·KM is equal to the square on MN (6.17).

**Step 9.** Since AC, CB are incommensurable in square, the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on CB (D10.1.2); that is, DH is incommensurable with KL. But DH : KL = DK : KM (6.1). Therefore DK is incommensurable in length with KM (10.11).

**Step 10.** Since MG is bisected at N, MG² = MN² + NG² + 2·MN·NG = 4·MN² (2.4), so the square on MN is the fourth part of the square on MG; hence the rectangle DK·KM is equal to the fourth part of the square on MG. Thus DM, MG are two unequal straight lines of which DM is the greater (Step 6); to DM there has been applied the parallelogram DK·KM, deficient by the square on KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less MG; and it divides DM into the parts DK, KM, which are incommensurable in length (Step 9). Therefore the square on DM is greater than the square on MG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DM (10.18).

**Step 11.** DG is therefore a binomial straight line (Step 5) whose greater term DM has its square exceeding the square on the lesser term MG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DM (Step 10), while the lesser term MG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE set out (Step 4). Hence DG is a fifth binomial (D10.2.4, D10.2.5). Therefore the square on the side of a rational plus a medial area, applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth the fifth binomial. Q.E.D.

*Path note.* The inequality AC² + CB² > 2·AC·CB (Step 6) was obtained by cutting off CP = CB and applying 2.7, rather than by bisecting AB and combining 2.5 with 2.9; the former route is the more direct.

**USED:** 1.3, 1.10, 1.31, 1.36, 1.44, 2.4, 2.7, 5.11, 6.1, 6.17, 10.6, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.18, 10.20, 10.22, 10.36, 10.40, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4, D10.2.4, D10.2.5, CN2, CN3, CN5

result.statement: The square on the side of the sum of two medial areas applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the sixth binomial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of the sum of two medial areas, divided into its terms at C, and let AC be the greater term. By 10.41, AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, and the rectangle AC·CB is medial and incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB.

**Step 2.** Let DE be the rational straight line set out. To DE apply the rectangle DF equal to the square on AB, producing DG as breadth (1.44). It is to be shown that DG is a sixth binomial.

**Step 3.** To DE apply the rectangle DH equal to the square on AC, producing DK as breadth; and to KH, which is equal to DE as the opposite side of the rectangle DH (1.34), apply the rectangle KL equal to the square on CB, producing KM as breadth (1.44). Since the square on AB equals the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB (2.4), and DH, KL are the squares on AC, CB, the remainder MF equals twice the rectangle AC·CB (CN3).

**Step 4.** Bisect MG at N (1.10) and through N draw NO parallel to ML (1.31). The rectangles MO, NF stand on the equal bases MN, NG and lie in the same parallels, so they are equal (1.36); together they make up MF, which is twice the rectangle AC·CB, so each of MO, NF equals the rectangle AC·CB. Also ML equals DE, being the side of the rectangle DL opposite to DE (1.34).

**Step 5.** The rectangle DL, made up of DH and KL, equals the sum of the squares on AC, CB, which is medial (Step 1). DL is applied to the rational straight line DE and produces DM as breadth. Therefore DM is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 6.** MF is double MO, so MO measures both MO and MF, and MF is commensurable with MO (D10.1.1). MO is the rectangle AC·CB, which is medial (Steps 1, 4). An area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23, Porism); hence MF is medial. MF is applied to ML, which is rational and equal to DE, producing MG as breadth. Therefore MG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 7.** The rectangle AC·CB, that is MO, is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB, that is DL (Step 1). Since MF is commensurable with MO and MO is incommensurable with DL, MF is incommensurable with DL (10.13). DL and MF are rectangles under the same height DE with bases DM, MG, so DL : MF = DM : MG (6.1). Hence DM is incommensurable in length with MG (10.11).

**Step 8.** DM and MG are each rational and incommensurable in length with DE (Steps 5, 6); a rational straight line is commensurable with DE either in length or in square only (D10.1.3), so each of DM, MG is commensurable in square with DE, that is, the square on DM and the square on MG are each commensurable with the square on DE. Therefore the squares on DM, MG are commensurable with one another (10.12), so DM, MG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). Together with Step 7, DM and MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore DG, the sum of DM and MG, is a binomial straight line (10.36) whose terms are DM and MG.

**Step 9.** Neither term of the binomial DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE, since DM is incommensurable in length with DE (Step 5) and MG is incommensurable in length with DE (Step 6). It remains to determine which term is the greater and to show that the square on the greater exceeds the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater.

**Step 10.** Since AC is greater than CB, the squares on AC, CB together equal twice the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on the excess of AC over CB (2.7); hence the squares on AC, CB together exceed twice the rectangle AC·CB (CN5), that is, DL is greater than MF. DL and MF are rectangles under the same height DE, and are to one another as their bases DM, MG (6.1); so the greater rectangle DL has the greater base, and DM is greater than MG.

**Step 11.** The square on AC and the rectangle AC·CB are parallelograms under the same height AC with bases AC, CB, so the square on AC is to the rectangle AC·CB as AC is to CB (6.1); likewise the rectangle AC·CB and the square on CB are under the same height CB, so the rectangle AC·CB is to the square on CB as AC is to CB (6.1). Hence the square on AC is to the rectangle AC·CB as the rectangle AC·CB is to the square on CB (5.11), that is, DH : MO = MO : KL. But DH, MO, KL are rectangles under the same height DE, so DH : MO = DK : MN and MO : KL = MN : KM (6.1). Therefore DK : MN = MN : KM (5.11), and since the three straight lines DK, MN, KM are proportional, the rectangle DK·KM equals the square on MN (6.17).

**Step 12.** Since MG is bisected at N, the square on MG equals the squares on MN, NG together with twice the rectangle MN·NG (2.4); as MN equals NG, this is four times the square on MN. Hence the square on MN, and therefore the rectangle DK·KM, is the fourth part of the square on MG. Thus to the greater straight line DM there has been applied the parallelogram DK·KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less MG and deficient by the square figure on KM, and it divides DM at K into the parts DK, KM.

**Step 13.** Since AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on CB (D10.1.2), that is, DH is incommensurable with KL. DH and KL are rectangles under the same height DE, so DH : KL = DK : KM (6.1); therefore DK is incommensurable in length with KM (10.11).

**Step 14.** DM and MG are two unequal straight lines with DM the greater (Step 10); to DM has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on MG and deficient by a square figure (Step 12), and it divides DM into parts DK, KM which are incommensurable (Step 13). Therefore the square on DM is greater than the square on MG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DM (10.18).

**Step 15.** DG is a binomial straight line with greater term DM and lesser term MG (Steps 8, 10); the square on the greater term exceeds the square on the lesser by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater (Step 14); and neither term is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE set out (Step 9). Therefore, by the definition of the sixth binomial (D10.2.4, D10.2.6), DG is a sixth binomial. Hence the square on the side of the sum of two medial areas, applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth the sixth binomial. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A straight line commensurable in length with a binomial straight line is itself also binomial and the same in order.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a binomial straight line and let CD be commensurable in length with AB; let ρ be the rational straight line set out, with respect to which the orders of binomial straight lines are reckoned. Since AB is binomial, it is divided into its terms at a point E, so that AE, EB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (10.36); let AE be the greater term, so that AE > EB.

**Step 2.** Take F on CD so that AB : CD = AE : CF (6.12). Since AB > AE, also CD > CF (5.14); hence F falls between C and D, and FD is the remainder of CD when CF is taken from it.

**Step 3.** Since the whole AB is to the whole CD as the part AE taken away is to the part CF taken away, the remainder EB is to the remainder FD as AB is to CD (5.19).

**Step 4.** AB is commensurable in length with CD, and AB : CD = AE : CF; therefore AE is commensurable in length with CF (10.11). Again AB : CD = EB : FD; therefore EB is commensurable in length with FD (10.11).

**Step 5.** Since AE : CF = AB : CD and EB : FD = AB : CD, AE : CF = EB : FD (5.11). In this proportion AE > EB, so CF > FD (5.14). Alternately, AE : EB = CF : FD (5.16).

**Step 6.** AE is rational, i.e. commensurable with ρ either in length and in square or in square only; in either case the square on AE is commensurable with the square on ρ (D10.1.3, D10.1.2). Since CF is commensurable in length with AE, the squares on CF, AE have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), so the square on CF is commensurable with the square on AE (10.6). Hence the square on CF is commensurable with the square on ρ (10.12); that is, CF is commensurable in square with ρ (D10.1.2), and so CF is rational (D10.1.3). By the same reasoning, since FD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EB, the square on FD is commensurable with the square on ρ, and FD is rational.

**Step 7.** The squares on CF and on FD are each commensurable with the square on ρ (Step 6); therefore they are commensurable with one another (10.12), that is, CF and FD are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 8.** AE and EB, being commensurable in square only, are incommensurable in length. Since AE : EB = CF : FD (Step 5), CF is incommensurable in length with FD (10.11). Together with Step 7, CF and FD are commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** Thus CD is composed of two rational straight lines CF, FD commensurable in square only; therefore CD is binomial (10.36), divided into its terms at F, with CF the greater term (Step 5).

**Step 10.** I say next that CD is of the same order as AB. The square on AE exceeds the square on EB by the square on a straight line which is either commensurable or incommensurable in length with AE. Since AE : EB = CF : FD, if the square on AE exceeds the square on EB by the square on a straight line commensurable with AE, then the square on CF exceeds the square on FD by the square on a straight line commensurable with CF; and if the square on AE exceeds the square on EB by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE, then the square on CF exceeds the square on FD by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CF (10.14).

**Step 11.** Moreover, AE is commensurable in length with CF and EB with FD (Step 4). Hence, if AE is commensurable in length with ρ, CF is also commensurable in length with ρ (10.12); if EB is commensurable in length with ρ, FD is also (10.12); and if neither AE nor EB is commensurable in length with ρ, then, AE being incommensurable with ρ and commensurable with CF, CF is incommensurable with ρ, and likewise FD is incommensurable with ρ (10.13).

**Step 12.** First let the square on AE exceed the square on EB by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, so that the square on CF exceeds the square on FD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CF (Step 10). (a) If the greater term AE is commensurable in length with ρ, then the greater term CF is also (Step 11), and AB, CD are each a first binomial (D10.2.1). (b) If the lesser term EB is commensurable in length with ρ, then the lesser term FD is also, and AB, CD are each a second binomial (D10.2.2). (c) If neither AE nor EB is commensurable in length with ρ, then neither CF nor FD is, and AB, CD are each a third binomial (D10.2.3).

**Step 13.** Next let the square on AE exceed the square on EB by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, so that the square on CF exceeds the square on FD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with CF (Step 10). (a) If AE is commensurable in length with ρ, so is CF, and AB, CD are each a fourth binomial (D10.2.4). (b) If EB is commensurable in length with ρ, so is FD, and AB, CD are each a fifth binomial (D10.2.5). (c) If neither AE nor EB is commensurable in length with ρ, neither CF nor FD is, and AB, CD are each a sixth binomial (D10.2.6).

**Step 14.** Therefore, in every case, CD is binomial and of the same order as AB. Hence a straight line commensurable in length with a binomial straight line is itself also binomial and the same in order. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A straight line commensurable in length with a bimedial straight line is itself also bimedial and the same in order.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a bimedial straight line, and let CD be commensurable in length with AB. Since AB is bimedial, it is the sum of two medial straight lines commensurable in square only; let AB be divided at E into its terms AE, EB, so that AE, EB are medial and commensurable in square only, while the rectangle AE·EB is either rational (AB being a first bimedial, 10.37) or medial (AB being a second bimedial, 10.38).

**Step 2.** Cut CD at F similarly to AB cut at E [6.10], so that CF : FD = AE : EB. (Path note: the division is made directly by 6.10 rather than through a fourth proportional, as this is the more direct route.)

**Step 3.** Alternately, CF : AE = FD : EB [5.16]. Hence, as one antecedent is to one consequent, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents [5.12]: CD : AB = CF : AE = FD : EB.

**Step 4.** Since CD is commensurable in length with AB, and CD : AB = CF : AE = FD : EB, therefore CF is commensurable in length with AE, and FD is commensurable in length with EB [10.11].

**Step 5.** AE and EB are medial; therefore CF and FD, being commensurable with them, are also medial [10.23].

**Step 6.** Since AE, EB are commensurable in square only, AE is incommensurable in length with EB. And since AE : EB = CF : FD, therefore CF is incommensurable in length with FD [10.11].

**Step 7.** Since AE : EB = CF : FD, the squares described on them, being similar figures similarly described, are proportional: sq(AE) : sq(EB) = sq(CF) : sq(FD) [6.22]. But the square on AE is commensurable with the square on EB; therefore the square on CF is commensurable with the square on FD [10.11]. Hence CF, FD are commensurable in square only [D10.1.2].

**Step 8.** Thus CD is the sum of two medial straight lines CF, FD commensurable in square only; therefore CD is bimedial [10.37, 10.38]. It remains to show that it is of the same order as AB.

**Step 9.** The rectangles AE·EB and CF·EB stand under the same height EB, so rect(AE,EB) : rect(CF,EB) = AE : CF [6.1]; since AE is commensurable with CF, rect(AE,EB) is commensurable with rect(CF,EB) [10.11]. Likewise rect(CF,EB) : rect(CF,FD) = EB : FD [6.1]; since EB is commensurable with FD, rect(CF,EB) is commensurable with rect(CF,FD) [10.11]. Therefore rect(AE,EB) is commensurable with rect(CF,FD) [10.12].

**Step 10.** If AB is a first bimedial, rect(AE,EB) is rational [10.37], that is, commensurable with the rational square set out [D10.1.4]; then rect(CF,FD), being commensurable with rect(AE,EB), is commensurable with that rational square [10.12], and so is itself rational [D10.1.4]. Therefore CF, FD are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a rational rectangle, and CD is a first bimedial [10.37].

**Step 11.** If AB is a second bimedial, rect(AE,EB) is medial [10.38]; then rect(CF,FD), being commensurable with a medial area, is medial [10.23, Porism]. Therefore CF, FD are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle, and CD is a second bimedial [10.38].

**Step 12.** Therefore a straight line CD commensurable in length with a bimedial straight line AB is itself bimedial and the same in order. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A straight line commensurable with a major straight line is itself also major.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.68
**Statement:** A straight line commensurable with a major straight line is itself also major.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a major straight line, and let CD be a straight line commensurable in length with AB. Since AB is major, it is the sum of two straight lines AE, EB which are incommensurable in square and which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial [10.39]; let E be the point at which AB is so divided.

**Step 2.** To the three straight lines AB, CD, AE find a fourth proportional X [6.12], so that as AB is to CD, so is AE to X. Since AB is greater than AE, CD is greater than X [5.14]. From CD cut off CF equal to X [1.3]; then F lies between C and D, FD is the remainder, and as AB is to CD, so is AE to CF.

**Step 3.** Since the whole AB is to the whole CD as the part AE is to the part CF, the remainder EB is to the remainder FD as the whole AB is to the whole CD [5.19].

**Step 4.** As AB is to CD, so is AE to CF, and AB is commensurable with CD; therefore AE is commensurable with CF [10.11]. Likewise, as AB is to CD, so is EB to FD; therefore EB is commensurable with FD [10.11].

**Step 5.** The ratios AE : CF and EB : FD are each the same as AB : CD; therefore as AE is to CF, so is EB to FD [5.11]. Alternately, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD [5.16].

**Step 6.** Squares are similar figures similarly described on their sides; hence, since as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD, the square on AE is to the square on EB as the square on CF is to the square on FD [6.22]. AE, EB are incommensurable in square, that is, the square on AE is incommensurable with the square on EB [D10.1.2]; therefore the square on CF is incommensurable with the square on FD [10.11], so that CF, FD are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 7.** AE is commensurable in length with CF; therefore the square on AE has to the square on CF the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9], so the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF [10.6]. In the same way, since EB is commensurable in length with FD, the square on EB is commensurable with the square on FD [10.9, 10.6].

**Step 8.** Since as AE is to CF, so is EB to FD, the square on AE is to the square on CF as the square on EB is to the square on FD [6.22]. Therefore, as one antecedent is to one consequent, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents: the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the sum of the squares on CF, FD as the square on AE is to the square on CF [5.12]. The square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF; therefore the sum of the squares on AE, EB is commensurable with the sum of the squares on CF, FD [10.11].

**Step 9.** The sum of the squares on AE, EB is rational, that is, commensurable with the rational square set out [D10.1.4]. The sum of the squares on CF, FD and the rational square set out are each commensurable with the sum of the squares on AE, EB; therefore they are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Hence the sum of the squares on CF, FD is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** The rectangle AE, EB and the square on EB are parallelograms under the same height EB with bases AE, EB; therefore the rectangle AE, EB is to the square on EB as AE is to EB [6.1]. Likewise the rectangle CF, FD is to the square on FD as CF is to FD [6.1]. But as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD (Step 5); therefore the rectangle AE, EB is to the square on EB as the rectangle CF, FD is to the square on FD [5.11]. Alternately, the rectangle AE, EB is to the rectangle CF, FD as the square on EB is to the square on FD [5.16].

**Step 11.** The square on EB is commensurable with the square on FD (Step 7); therefore the rectangle AE, EB is commensurable with the rectangle CF, FD [10.11]. But the rectangle AE, EB is medial, and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]; therefore the rectangle CF, FD is medial.

**Step 12.** Thus CF, FD are straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 6) which make the sum of the squares on them rational (Step 9) but the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 11). Therefore the whole CD, which is the sum of CF and FD, is irrational and is the straight line called major [10.39]. Hence a straight line commensurable with a major straight line is itself also major. Q.E.D.

Path note: the point F was fixed by a fourth proportional [6.12] with the remainders handled by [5.19], rather than by cutting CD similarly to AB [6.10], because this route yields the three needed proportions AB : CD = AE : CF = EB : FD at once.

**USED:** 10.39, 6.12, 5.14, 1.3, 5.19, 10.11, 5.11, 5.16, 6.22, D10.1.2, 10.9, 10.6, 5.12, 10.12, D10.1.4, 6.1, 10.23

result.statement: A straight line commensurable with the side of a rational plus a medial area is itself also the side of a rational plus a medial area.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of a rational plus a medial area, and let CD be a straight line commensurable in length with AB. It is to be proved that CD is also the side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 2.** Since AB is the side of a rational plus a medial area, it is composed of two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial but the rectangle contained by them rational [10.40]. Let AB be divided into these straight lines at E; then AE, EB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AE, EB is medial, and the rectangle AE, EB is rational.

**Step 3.** Let CD be cut at F similarly to AB cut at E [6.10], so that, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD.

**Step 4.** Since AE : EB = CF : FD, alternately AE : CF = EB : FD [5.16]. Hence, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents [5.12]; that is, as AE is to CF, so is AB (= AE + EB) to CD (= CF + FD), and so also is EB to FD.

**Step 5.** Now AB is commensurable with CD, and AB : CD = AE : CF; therefore AE is commensurable with CF [10.11]. Likewise, since AB : CD = EB : FD, EB is commensurable with FD [10.11].

**Step 6.** Since AE : EB = CF : FD, the squares on them, being similar figures similarly described on proportional straight lines, are also proportional: the square on AE is to the square on EB as the square on CF is to the square on FD [6.22]. But AE, EB are incommensurable in square, that is, the square on AE is incommensurable with the square on EB [D10.1.2]; therefore the square on CF is incommensurable with the square on FD [10.11]; that is, CF, FD are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 7.** Since AE is commensurable in length with CF (Step 5), the square on AE has to the square on CF the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF [10.6].

**Step 8.** Since AE : CF = EB : FD (Step 4), the square on AE is to the square on CF as the square on EB is to the square on FD [6.22]. Therefore, as one antecedent is to one consequent, so is the sum of the antecedents to the sum of the consequents [5.12]: the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the sum of the squares on CF, FD as the square on AE is to the square on CF. But the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF (Step 7); therefore the sum of the squares on AE, EB is commensurable with the sum of the squares on CF, FD [10.11]. And the sum of the squares on AE, EB is medial (Step 2); therefore the sum of the squares on CF, FD, being commensurable with a medial area, is also medial [10.23, Porism].

**Step 9.** Again, since AE : EB = CF : FD (Step 3): the square on AE and the rectangle AE, EB are parallelograms under the same height AE, so the square on AE is to the rectangle AE, EB as the base AE is to the base EB [6.1]; similarly the square on CF is to the rectangle CF, FD as CF is to FD [6.1]. Therefore the square on AE is to the rectangle AE, EB as the square on CF is to the rectangle CF, FD [5.11]. Alternately, the square on AE is to the square on CF as the rectangle AE, EB is to the rectangle CF, FD [5.16]. But the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF (Step 7); therefore the rectangle AE, EB is commensurable with the rectangle CF, FD [10.11].

**Step 10.** Now the rectangle AE, EB is rational (Step 2), that is, it is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]. The rectangle CF, FD is commensurable with the rectangle AE, EB; therefore it is also commensurable with the square on the rational straight line [10.12], and hence the rectangle CF, FD is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 11.** Therefore CF, FD are straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 6) which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 8) but the rectangle contained by them rational (Step 10). Therefore the whole CD, which is composed of CF, FD, is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area [10.40]. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A straight line commensurable with the side of the sum of two medial areas is the side of the sum of two medial areas.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of the sum of two medial areas, and let CD be a straight line commensurable with AB. Since AB is the side of the sum of two medial areas, it is by 10.41 the sum of two straight lines AE, EB incommensurable in square, such that the sum of the squares on AE, EB is medial, the rectangle AE·EB is medial, and the rectangle AE·EB is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AE, EB. Let AB be so divided at E. We must show that CD is also the side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 2.** To the three straight lines AB, CD, AE find a fourth proportional CF, so that AB : CD = AE : CF [6.12]. Since AB > AE and AB : CD = AE : CF, it follows that CD > CF [5.14]; so F falls on CD between C and D, and FD is the remainder.

**Step 3.** Since the whole AB is to the whole CD as the part AE subtracted is to the part CF subtracted, the remainder EB is to the remainder FD as AB is to CD [5.19]. Hence AB : CD = AE : CF = EB : FD.

**Step 4.** Now AB is commensurable with CD; therefore, since AB : CD = AE : CF and AB : CD = EB : FD, AE is commensurable in length with CF, and EB with FD [10.11].

**Step 5.** Since AE : CF = EB : FD, alternately AE : EB = CF : FD [5.16]. The squares on AE, EB, CF, FD are similar figures similarly described on these four proportional straight lines; therefore the square on AE is to the square on EB as the square on CF is to the square on FD [6.22]. But AE, EB are incommensurable in square, that is, the square on AE is incommensurable with the square on EB [D10.1.2]; therefore the square on CF is incommensurable with the square on FD [10.11]; that is, CF, FD are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 6.** Since AE is commensurable in length with CF, the square on AE has to the square on CF the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF [10.6].

**Step 7.** Since AE : CF = EB : FD, likewise the square on AE is to the square on CF as the square on EB is to the square on FD [6.22]. Therefore, as one antecedent is to one consequent, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents: the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the sum of the squares on CF, FD as the square on AE is to the square on CF [5.12]. But the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF (Step 6); therefore the sum of the squares on AE, EB is commensurable with the sum of the squares on CF, FD [10.11]. And the sum of the squares on AE, EB is medial (Step 1); therefore the sum of the squares on CF, FD, being an area commensurable with a medial area, is medial [10.23, Porism].

**Step 8.** The square on AE and the rectangle AE·EB are parallelograms under the same height AE, standing on the bases AE and EB; therefore the square on AE is to the rectangle AE·EB as AE is to EB [6.1]. Likewise the square on CF is to the rectangle CF·FD as CF is to FD [6.1]. But AE : EB = CF : FD (Step 5); therefore the square on AE is to the rectangle AE·EB as the square on CF is to the rectangle CF·FD [5.11]. Alternately, the square on AE is to the square on CF as the rectangle AE·EB is to the rectangle CF·FD [5.16]. Since the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF (Step 6), the rectangle AE·EB is commensurable with the rectangle CF·FD [10.11]. And the rectangle AE·EB is medial (Step 1); therefore the rectangle CF·FD, being an area commensurable with a medial area, is medial [10.23, Porism].

**Step 9.** By Steps 7 and 8, the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the sum of the squares on CF, FD as the square on AE is to the square on CF, and the rectangle AE·EB is to the rectangle CF·FD in this same ratio; therefore the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the sum of the squares on CF, FD as the rectangle AE·EB is to the rectangle CF·FD [5.11]. Alternately, the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the rectangle AE·EB as the sum of the squares on CF, FD is to the rectangle CF·FD [5.16]. But the sum of the squares on AE, EB is incommensurable with the rectangle AE·EB (Step 1); therefore the sum of the squares on CF, FD is incommensurable with the rectangle CF·FD [10.11].

**Step 10.** Therefore CF, FD are two straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 5) which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 7) and the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 8) and moreover incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them (Step 9). Therefore CD, the sum of CF and FD, is the side of the sum of two medial areas [10.41].

Therefore a straight line commensurable with the side of the sum of two medial areas is itself the side of the sum of two medial areas. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a rational and a medial area be added together, four irrational straight lines arise, namely a binomial or a first bimedial or a major or a side of a rational plus a medial area.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the rational area and CD the medial area. Set out a rational straight line EF and take it as the assigned rational straight line, so that the square on EF is the rational square: areas commensurable with it are rational and areas incommensurable with it are irrational [D10.1.3, D10.1.4].
