To EF apply, in a right angle, the rectangle EG equal to AB, producing EH as breadth [1.44, applied successively to the triangles into which AB is divided, in the manner of 1.45]. EG is the rectangle contained by EF, EH, and its side HG opposite to EF is equal to EF [1.34].

**Step 2.** Produce EH to K [P2]. Since the angle EHG is right, the angles EHG, GHK which HG makes with the straight line EK are together equal to two right angles, so the angle GHK is right [1.13]. To HG apply, in the right angle GHK, the rectangle HI equal to CD, producing HK as breadth [1.44, 1.45]; HK lies along EH produced, so EK is one straight line and the rectangle EI contained by EF, EK is made up of EG and HI. Therefore EI is equal to AB together with CD [CN2], and the "side" of EI, namely the straight line the square on which is equal to EI [D10.1.4], is the straight line whose square equals the sum of the rational and the medial area.

**Step 3.** EG is equal to the rational area AB, so EG is rational; and it is applied to the rational straight line EF. Therefore its breadth EH is rational and commensurable in length with EF [10.20].

**Step 4.** CD is a medial area, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, the side of a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.21]. Hence HI is equal to the square on a medial straight line, and it is applied to HG; HG is equal to EF and is therefore commensurable with EF and rational [D10.1.1, D10.1.3]. Therefore the breadth HK is rational and incommensurable in length with HG [10.22], and hence incommensurable in length with EF, since HG is equal to EF and a common measure of HK, EF would be a common measure of HK, HG [D10.1.1].

**Step 5.** AB is rational, so AB is commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.4]. CD is medial, hence irrational [10.21], that is, incommensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.4]. Since AB is commensurable with the square on EF, and the square on EF is incommensurable with CD, AB is incommensurable with CD [10.13]. As EG is equal to AB and HI to CD, any common measure of EG, HI would be a common measure of AB, CD; therefore EG is incommensurable with HI [D10.1.1].

**Step 6.** The rectangles EG, HI stand on the bases EH, HK and have the same height, EF being equal to HG; therefore EG : HI = EH : HK [6.1]. Since EG is incommensurable with HI, EH is incommensurable in length with HK [10.11].

**Step 7.** EH and HK are rational [Steps 3, 4], so each of them is commensurable in square with EF [D10.1.3]; thus the squares on EH and on HK are each commensurable with the square on EF, and therefore are commensurable with one another [10.12], so that EH, HK are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. But they are incommensurable in length [Step 6]. Therefore EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and EK, their sum, is a binomial straight line whose terms are EH, HK [10.36].

**Step 8.** Since AB is incommensurable with CD, AB is not equal to CD, for equal magnitudes are measured by one and the same measure [D10.1.1]. Therefore either AB is greater than CD, or AB is less than CD.

**Step 9.** Case I: let AB be greater than CD. Then EG is greater than HI. Since EG : HI = EH : HK [Step 6], and EG exceeds HI, taking each of the four magnitudes once as its own equimultiple shows that EH exceeds HK [D5.5]. Thus EH is the greater term of the binomial EK, and EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out [Step 3]. The square on EH exceeds the square on HK by the square on some straight line, and this straight line is either commensurable or incommensurable in length with EH.

**Step 10.** Case I(a): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EH. Since the greater term EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out, EK is a first binomial [D10.2.1]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the first binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called binomial [10.54].

**Step 11.** Case I(b): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EH. Since the greater term EH is commensurable in length with EF, EK is a fourth binomial [D10.2.4]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the fourth binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called major [10.57].

**Step 12.** Case II: let AB be less than CD. Then HI is greater than EG, and since EG : HI = EH : HK [Step 6], HK exceeds EH [D5.5]. Thus HK is the greater term and EH the lesser term of the binomial EK, and the lesser term EH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out [Step 3]. The square on HK exceeds the square on EH by the square on some straight line, either commensurable or incommensurable in length with HK.

**Step 13.** Case II(a): let the square on HK be greater than the square on EH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with HK. Since the lesser term EH is commensurable in length with EF, EK is a second binomial [D10.2.2]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the second binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called first bimedial [10.55].

**Step 14.** Case II(b): let the square on HK be greater than the square on EH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with HK. Since the lesser term EH is commensurable in length with EF, EK is a fifth binomial [D10.2.5]. The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the fifth binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area [10.58].

**Step 15.** The cases of Steps 9 and 12, each with its two sub-cases, exhaust all possibilities [Step 8]. Therefore the straight line the square on which is equal to the sum AB + CD of a rational and a medial area is, according to the case, a binomial, a major, a first bimedial, or a side of a rational plus a medial area; so when a rational and a medial area are added together, these four irrational straight lines arise. Q.E.D.

Path note: the proof applies both areas to one rational straight line and classifies the binomial breadth EK by the definitions D10.2; the passage from the order of the binomial to the side of the area uses 10.54, 10.55, 10.57, 10.58 directly. The third and sixth binomials (10.56, 10.59) cannot occur, because the term EH is always commensurable in length with EF.

result.statement: If two medial areas incommensurable with one another be added together, the remaining two irrational straight lines arise, namely either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB, CD be two medial areas incommensurable with one another (each equal to the square on a medial straight line), and let AD be the area made up of both. It is required to prove that the straight line which produces AD, that is, the side of the square equal to AD [D10.1.4], is either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line EF [D10.1.3]. To EF apply the rectangle EG equal to AB, producing EH as breadth; and to HG, the side of EG opposite to EF, apply the rectangle HI equal to CD, producing HK as breadth [1.44]. Since HG is opposite to EF in the parallelogram EG, HG = EF [1.34]; and EH, HK lie in one straight line EK, so that the whole EI is the rectangle contained by EF and EK.

**Step 3.** Since AB is a medial area and EG = AB, EG is the square on a medial straight line applied to the rational straight line EF; therefore its breadth EH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Likewise HI = CD is a medial area applied to HG, which is rational, being equal to EF; therefore HK is rational and incommensurable in length with HG, that is, with EF [10.22].

**Step 4.** The rectangles EG and HI are under the same height EF (= HG) and stand on the bases EH, HK; therefore EG : HI = EH : HK [6.1]. But EG = AB and HI = CD, and AB is incommensurable with CD; therefore EG is incommensurable with HI, and hence EH is incommensurable in length with HK [10.11].

**Step 5.** EH is rational and not commensurable in length with EF; therefore it is commensurable in square with EF [D10.1.3], so that the square on EH is commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]. In the same way the square on HK is commensurable with the square on EF. Therefore the square on EH is commensurable with the square on HK [10.12], that is, EH and HK are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Since by Step 4 they are incommensurable in length, EH, HK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 6.** Therefore EK, the sum of EH and HK, is a binomial straight line [10.36], divided into its terms EH, HK at the point H.

**Step 7.** EH and HK are unequal: equal straight lines measure one another and are therefore commensurable [D10.1.1], whereas EH, HK are incommensurable. Let EH be the greater term. The square on EH exceeds the square on HK by the square on some straight line, and this straight line is either commensurable or incommensurable in length with EH; so two cases arise.

**Step 8.** Case (i): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EH. By Step 3 neither term EH nor HK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EF set out. Therefore EK is a third binomial [D10.2.3].

**Step 9.** The area EI is contained by the rational straight line EF and the third binomial EK; therefore the side of EI, the straight line whose square is equal to EI, is a second bimedial [10.56].

**Step 10.** Case (ii): let the square on EH be greater than the square on HK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with EH. Again neither term is commensurable in length with EF; therefore EK is a sixth binomial [D10.2.6].

**Step 11.** The area EI is then contained by the rational straight line EF and the sixth binomial EK; therefore the side of EI is the side of the sum of two medial areas [10.59].

**Step 12.** But EG = AB and HI = CD; adding these equals, EI = EG + HI = AB + CD = AD [CN2]. Therefore the straight line whose square is equal to AD is the very side of EI found in Step 9 or Step 11.

**Step 13.** Hence, when two medial areas incommensurable with one another are added together, the straight line which produces the sum is, according as the square on the greater term of EK exceeds the square on the lesser by the square on a straight line commensurable or incommensurable in length with the greater, either a second bimedial or a side of the sum of two medial areas. These are the two irrational straight lines not obtained from the sum of a rational and a medial area. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If from a rational straight line there be subtracted a rational straight line commensurable with the whole in square only, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called   an apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ρ be the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3). Let AB be a rational straight line, and from AB let there be subtracted the straight line BC, rational and commensurable in square only with AB, so that AC is the remainder. I say that AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since BC is commensurable in square only with AB, the squares on AB and BC are measured by a common area, so sq(AB) is commensurable with sq(BC) (D10.1.2, D10.1.1); but the straight lines AB, BC themselves have no common measure, that is, AB is incommensurable in length with BC (D10.1.1).

**Step 3.** The square on AB and the rectangle contained by AB, BC are parallelograms under the same height AB, standing on the bases AB and BC respectively. Therefore, as AB is to BC, so is sq(AB) to rect(AB, BC) (6.1).

**Step 4.** In this proportion the first term AB is incommensurable with the second term BC (Step 2). Therefore the third term sq(AB) is incommensurable with the fourth term rect(AB, BC) (10.11).

**Step 5.** Since sq(AB) and sq(BC) are commensurable (Step 2), when they are added together the whole, sq(AB) + sq(BC), is commensurable with each of them, in particular with sq(AB) (10.15).

**Step 6.** Now sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(AB) (Step 5), and sq(AB) is incommensurable with rect(AB, BC) (Step 4). Therefore sq(AB) + sq(BC) is incommensurable with rect(AB, BC) (10.13).

**Step 7.** The rectangle rect(AB, BC) measures both itself and twice itself, so rect(AB, BC) and 2·rect(AB, BC) are measured by the same measure and are commensurable (D10.1.1). Since 2·rect(AB, BC) is commensurable with rect(AB, BC), and rect(AB, BC) is incommensurable with sq(AB) + sq(BC) (Step 6), 2·rect(AB, BC) is incommensurable with sq(AB) + sq(BC) (10.13).

**Step 8.** The straight line AB is cut at C. Therefore the square on the whole AB together with the square on the segment BC is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC together with the square on the remaining segment AC (2.7); that is, sq(AB) + sq(BC) = 2·rect(AB, BC) + sq(AC).

**Step 9.** Thus the whole sq(AB) + sq(BC) is made up of the two magnitudes 2·rect(AB, BC) and sq(AC), and the whole is incommensurable with one of them, namely 2·rect(AB, BC) (Step 7). Therefore the two magnitudes 2·rect(AB, BC) and sq(AC) are incommensurable with one another (10.16).

**Step 10.** Again, since the two incommensurable magnitudes 2·rect(AB, BC) and sq(AC) are added together to make sq(AB) + sq(BC), the whole is incommensurable with each of them; in particular sq(AB) + sq(BC) is incommensurable with sq(AC) (10.16).

**Step 11.** Next, sq(AB) + sq(BC) is rational. For AB is rational, so AB is commensurable with ρ either in length and in square or in square only; in either case AB is commensurable in square with ρ (D10.1.3), so sq(AB) is commensurable with sq(ρ) (D10.1.2). Since sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(AB) (Step 5) and sq(AB) is commensurable with sq(ρ), sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(ρ) (10.12); and sq(ρ) is the rational area, so sq(AB) + sq(BC) is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 12.** Now sq(AB) + sq(BC) is commensurable with sq(ρ) (Step 11) and incommensurable with sq(AC) (Step 10). Therefore sq(ρ) is incommensurable with sq(AC) (10.13). Hence sq(AC) is irrational (D10.1.4), and AC, the straight line on which this irrational square is described, is irrational (D10.1.4).

**Step 13.** Therefore, if from a rational straight line there be subtracted a rational straight line commensurable with the whole in square only, the remainder AC is irrational; and let it be called an apotome. Q.E.D.

**USED:** D10.1.1, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4, 2.7, 6.1, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.15, 10.16

Path note: in Step 7 the commensurability of 2·rect(AB, BC) with rect(AB, BC) is taken directly from the definition of commensurable magnitudes (D10.1.1), since the rectangle is a common measure of both; the alternative route via the ratio 2:1 and 10.6 was not needed.

result.statement: If from a medial straight line there be subtracted a medial straight line which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle, the remainder is irrational. And let it be called a first apotome of a medial straight line.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If from a medial straight line there be subtracted a medial straight line which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle, the remainder is irrational. And let it be called a first apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a medial straight line, and from AB let there be subtracted the straight line BC, so that C lies on AB between A and B, where BC is medial, BC is commensurable with AB in square only, and the rectangle contained by AB, BC is rational. I say that the remainder AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since AB is medial, the square on AB is equal to a rectangle contained by two rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and such an area is irrational [10.21]; this area is what is called a medial area. Thus the square on AB is a medial area, and it is irrational, that is, incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]. In the same way the square on BC is a medial area.

**Step 3.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square, the squares on AB, BC are measured by the same area, that is, they are commensurable with one another [D10.1.2]. Therefore, the two commensurable magnitudes, the square on AB and the square on BC, being added together, the whole, namely the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is commensurable with the square on AB [10.15].

**Step 4.** But the square on AB is a medial area (Step 2); and an area commensurable with a medial area is itself medial [10.23]. Therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a medial area, and hence it is irrational [10.21], that is, incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** The rectangle AB, BC is rational by hypothesis, that is, it is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]. Now the rectangle AB, BC measures twice the rectangle AB, BC, so that the rectangle AB, BC and twice the rectangle AB, BC are measured by the same measure and are commensurable [D10.1.1]. Since twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC, and the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out, twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with that square [10.12]; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 6.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the square on the whole AB together with the square on the segment BC is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC together with the square on the remaining segment AC [2.7]. Thus the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a whole made up of two parts, namely twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC.

**Step 7.** I say that the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC. For, if it were commensurable with it, then, since twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out (Step 5), the sum of the squares on AB, BC would also be commensurable with that square [10.12], and so would be rational [D10.1.4]; but it is medial and irrational (Step 4), which is impossible. Therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC.

**Step 8.** Now the whole, the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is made up of twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC (Step 6), and the whole is incommensurable with one of them, twice the rectangle AB, BC (Step 7). But if the whole be incommensurable with one of the magnitudes added together, the original magnitudes are incommensurable [10.16]. Therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the square on AC.

**Step 9.** I say that the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out. For, if it were commensurable with it, then, since twice the rectangle AB, BC is also commensurable with that square (Step 5), the square on AC would be commensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC [10.12], contrary to Step 8. Therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out, and so the square on AC is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** Since the square on AC is an irrational area, the straight line AC, on which the square is described, is irrational [D10.1.4]. Therefore the remainder AC is irrational, which was to be proved. And let AC be called a first apotome of a medial straight line.

**USED:** 2.7, 10.12, 10.15, 10.16, 10.21, 10.23, D10.1.1, D10.1.2, D10.1.4

result.statement: If from a medial straight line there be subtracted a medial straight line which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called a second apotome of a medial straight line.
result.proof:
**Statement.** If from a medial straight line there be subtracted a medial straight line which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called a second apotome of a medial straight line.

**Setting out.** Let AB be a medial straight line, and from AB let there be subtracted the medial straight line BC, which is commensurable with the whole AB in square only and is such that the rectangle AB, BC contained by it with the whole is medial. I say that the remainder AC is irrational.

**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line DI be set out (D10.1.3). To DI let there be applied the rectangle DE equal to the squares on AB, BC, producing DG as breadth; and to DI let there be applied the rectangle DH equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC, producing DF as breadth, F being taken on the line DG (1.44).

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the squares on AB, BC together are equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC (2.7). Hence DE is equal to DH together with the square on AC. Therefore DE is greater than DH (CN5), so that DF is less than DG and F falls between D and G; and, subtracting DH from DE, the remainder FE is equal to the square on AC (CN3).

**Step 3.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square, the square on AB is commensurable with the square on BC (D10.1.2). Therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with the square on AB (10.15). But the square on AB is a medial area, being the square on the medial straight line AB; and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial (Porism to 10.23). Therefore DE, which is equal to the squares on AB, BC, is medial, that is, DE is equal to the square on a medial straight line.

**Step 4.** DE is the square on a medial straight line applied to the rational straight line DI, producing DG as breadth; therefore DG is rational and incommensurable in length with DI (10.22).

**Step 5.** The rectangle AB, BC is medial by hypothesis. Twice the rectangle AB, BC has to the rectangle AB, BC the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC (10.6). Hence twice the rectangle AB, BC, and therefore DH which is equal to it, is medial (Porism to 10.23). DH is thus the square on a medial straight line applied to the rational straight line DI, producing DF as breadth; therefore DF is rational and incommensurable in length with DI (10.22).

**Step 6.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, AB is incommensurable in length with BC. Now the square on AB and the rectangle AB, BC are parallelograms under the same height AB, standing on the bases AB and BC respectively; therefore, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the rectangle AB, BC (6.1). Since AB is incommensurable with BC, the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC (10.11).

**Step 7.** The sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with the square on AB (Step 3), and the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC (Step 6); therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC (10.13). Again, twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC (Step 5), and the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC (10.13). That is, DH is incommensurable with DE.

**Step 8.** DE and DH are parallelograms under the same height DI, standing on the bases DG and DF; therefore, as DE is to DH, so is DG to DF (6.1). Since DE is incommensurable with DH, DG is incommensurable in length with DF (10.11).

**Step 9.** DG is rational and incommensurable in length with DI (Step 4); hence DG is commensurable with DI in square only (D10.1.3), so that the square on DG is commensurable with the square on DI. Likewise DF is rational and incommensurable in length with DI (Step 5), so that the square on DF is commensurable with the square on DI. Therefore the square on DG is commensurable with the square on DF (10.12), that is, DG and DF are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). Together with Step 8, DG and DF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 10.** DF is less than DG (Step 2), and from the rational straight line DG there has been subtracted the rational straight line DF commensurable with DG in square only; therefore the remainder FG is an apotome, and it is irrational (10.73).

**Step 11.** The rectangle FE is contained by FG and FH, where FH is equal to the rational straight line DI; that is, FE is an area applied to the rational straight line DI with FG as breadth. If FE were a rational area, then, being applied to the rational straight line DI, it would produce as breadth a straight line rational and commensurable in length with DI (10.20); but its breadth FG is irrational (Step 10). Therefore FE is not rational; that is, FE is an irrational area (D10.1.4).

**Step 12.** But FE is equal to the square on AC (Step 2). Therefore AC is the straight line on which is described a square equal to an irrational area; hence AC is irrational (D10.1.4).

**Conclusion.** Therefore, if from a medial straight line AB there be subtracted a medial straight line BC commensurable with the whole in square only and containing with the whole a medial rectangle, the remainder AC is irrational; and let it be called a second apotome of a medial straight line. Q.E.D.

**Path note.** The proof follows the application-of-areas route used for the additive irrationals (compare 10.38): the square on the remainder is exhibited as a rectangle under the rational line DI with an apotome as breadth, and 10.20 (contrapositive) then forces the area, and hence its side, to be irrational. The medial character of DE and DH is obtained from the Porism to 10.23 (an area commensurable with a medial area is medial) rather than by re-deriving it from 2.14 and 10.21, which is why 10.23 appears and 10.21 does not.

**USED:** 1.44, 2.7, 6.1, 10.6, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.15, 10.20, 10.22, 10.23, 10.73, CN3, CN5, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4

result.statement: If from a straight line there be subtracted a straight line which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the squares on them added together rational, but the rectangle contained by them medial, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called minor.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line, and from AB let there be subtracted the straight line BC, so that C lies on AB and AC is the remainder; and let BC be incommensurable in square with the whole AB, let the sum of the squares on AB, BC be rational, and let the rectangle AB, BC be medial. I say that the remainder AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Let R denote the square on the assigned rational straight line. Since the sum of the squares on AB, BC is rational, it is commensurable with R [D10.1.4].

**Step 3.** Since the rectangle AB, BC is medial, it is irrational [10.21]; that is, it is incommensurable with R [D10.1.4].

**Step 4.** Now the sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with R, and R is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC; therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [10.13].

**Step 5.** The rectangle AB, BC measures both itself and twice the rectangle AB, BC; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [D10.1.1]. And since the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC, twice the rectangle AB, BC is also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC [10.13].

**Step 6.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the squares on AB, BC together are equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC [2.7]. Thus the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a whole composed of the two parts twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC.

**Step 7.** This whole, the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is incommensurable with one of its parts, twice the rectangle AB, BC [Step 5]; therefore the two parts, twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC, are incommensurable with one another [10.16].

**Step 8.** And since twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC are incommensurable magnitudes added together, the whole, the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is incommensurable with each of them, and in particular with the square on AC [10.16].

**Step 9.** But the sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with R [Step 2] and is incommensurable with the square on AC; therefore R is incommensurable with the square on AC [10.13].

**Step 10.** Therefore the square on AC is irrational, and hence its side AC is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 11.** Therefore, if from a straight line AB there be subtracted a straight line BC which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial, the remainder AC is irrational. Let it be called minor.

result.statement: If from a straight line there be subtracted a straight line which is incommensurable in square with the whole, and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational, the remainder is irrational: and let it be called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line, and from AB let there be subtracted the straight line BC, so that C lies on AB and AC is the remainder. Suppose that BC is incommensurable in square with the whole AB, that the sum of the squares on AB and BC is medial, and that twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational. We must show that the remainder AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the squares on AB and BC taken together are equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC [2.7]. Thus the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a whole composed of exactly two parts, namely twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC.

**Step 3.** Let a rational straight line be set out; its square is the rational area with reference to which areas are called rational or irrational [D10.1.4]. The sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, which is a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only; such an area is irrational [10.21], i.e. incommensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4]. On the other hand, twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational, so it is commensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4].

**Step 4.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rational square, while the rational square is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC [Step 3]; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AB, BC [10.13].

**Step 5.** The whole, namely the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is therefore incommensurable with one of its two parts, twice the rectangle AB, BC [Step 2, Step 4]. Hence the two parts are incommensurable with one another: the square on AC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC [10.16].

**Step 6.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rational square [Step 3], and it is incommensurable with the square on AC [Step 5]; therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the rational square [10.13]. Hence the square on AC is an irrational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** The square on AC is irrational, and AC is the side of that square; therefore the straight line AC is irrational [D10.1.4]. And let AC be called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole, since the square on AC added to the rational area twice the rectangle AB, BC makes up the medial whole, the sum of the squares on AB, BC [Step 2]. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If from a straight line there be subtracted a straight line which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial, twice the rectangle contained by them medial, and further the squares on them incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them, the remainder is irrational; and let it be called that which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line and let BC be subtracted from it (C lying on AB), so that AC is the remainder. By hypothesis, AB and BC are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a medial area, twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC is a medial area, and the squares on AB, BC together are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC. We must show that the remainder AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the squares on AB and BC together are equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC (2.7). Hence the square on AC is the excess of the squares on AB, BC over twice the rectangle AB, BC (CN3), and twice the rectangle AB, BC, being a part of the squares on AB, BC, is less than them (CN5).

**Step 3.** Let a rational straight line DI be set out (D10.1.3). To DI let there be applied, in a right angle, the rectangle DE equal to the squares on AB, BC, producing DG as breadth (1.44, 1.45); and to DI, on the same side, let there likewise be applied the rectangle DH equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC, producing DF as breadth. Since DH is less than DE (Step 2) and the two rectangles have the same height DI, DF is less than DG; for if DF were not less than DG, DE would be contained in DH, so that DH would be equal to or greater than DE (CN5), which is impossible. Thus F lies between D and G, DH is a part of DE, and the remaining rectangle FE, contained by FG and the height DI, is equal to the excess of DE over DH, that is, to the square on AC (CN3).

**Step 4.** The squares on AB, BC together form a medial area, that is, they are equal to the square on a medial straight line; and DE is equal to them. Therefore DE is the square on a medial straight line, and it is applied to the rational straight line DI, producing DG as breadth. Therefore DG is rational and incommensurable in length with DI (10.22).

**Step 5.** Again, twice the rectangle AB, BC is a medial area, and DH is equal to it; so DH is the square on a medial straight line applied to the rational straight line DI, producing DF as breadth. Therefore DF is also rational and incommensurable in length with DI (10.22).

**Step 6.** Since the squares on AB, BC are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC, and DE, DH are equal to these respectively, DE is incommensurable with DH. But DE and DH are rectangles under the same height DI; therefore, as DE is to DH, so is DG to DF (6.1). Consequently DG is incommensurable with DF (10.11); that is, DG and DF are incommensurable in length.

**Step 7.** DG is rational and incommensurable in length with DI, so DG is commensurable with DI in square only (D10.1.3), whence the square on DG is commensurable with the square on DI (D10.1.2). In the same way the square on DF is commensurable with the square on DI. Therefore the squares on DG and DF, being commensurable with the same square, are commensurable with one another (10.12), so that DG and DF are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). Combined with Step 6, DG and DF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 8.** Now FG is the remainder when DF is subtracted from DG. From the rational straight line DG there has been subtracted the rational straight line DF which is commensurable with the whole in square only; therefore the remainder FG is irrational, namely an apotome (10.73).

**Step 9.** The rectangle FE is contained by the rational straight line DI (as height) and the irrational straight line FG. I say that FE is irrational. For suppose FE were a rational area (D10.1.4). Then FE would be a rational area applied to the rational straight line DI, producing FG as breadth, and hence FG would be rational and commensurable in length with DI (10.20). But FG is irrational (Step 8), and a straight line cannot be both rational and irrational (D10.1.3). This is impossible; therefore FE is not rational, that is, FE is an irrational area (D10.1.4).

**Step 10.** But FE is equal to the square on AC (Step 3). Therefore the square on AC is an irrational area, and so its side AC, the straight line which produces it, is irrational (D10.1.4). Therefore the remainder AC is irrational, which was to be proved. And since the square on AC, added to the medial area DH (twice the rectangle AB, BC), makes up the medial whole DE (the squares on AB, BC), let AC be called that which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

result.statement: To an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be an apotome, and let BC be the annex to it: C lies on AB produced beyond B, AC is a rational straight line, CB is a rational straight line commensurable with AC in square only, and AB is the remainder when CB is subtracted from AC [10.73]. Let ρ denote the assigned rational straight line, so that every rational straight line is commensurable with ρ in length or in square only, and in either case its square is commensurable with the square on ρ [D10.1.3]; such areas are rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that a second rational straight line BD, different from BC, can be annexed to AB so as to be commensurable with the whole AD in square only. Since DB is rational, the square on DB is commensurable with the square on ρ; since AD is commensurable in square with DB, the square on AD is commensurable with the square on DB; hence the square on AD is commensurable with the square on ρ [10.12], so AD is rational [D10.1.3]. Thus AD, DB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and AB is the apotome obtained by subtracting DB from AD [10.73].

**Step 3.** The points C and D both lie on AB produced beyond B and are distinct, so one of BC, BD is the greater; let BD be the greater (if BC is the greater, interchange the letters C and D throughout). Then C lies between B and D, so that AC is a part of AD and BC a part of BD; therefore AD is greater than AC and DB is greater than CB [CN5]. Consequently the square on AC is a part of the square on AD and the square on CB a part of the square on DB, so the squares on AD, DB together exceed the squares on AC, CB together [CN5]. Let the excess be the area E, so that the squares on AD, DB together are equal to the squares on AC, CB together with E.

**Step 4.** The straight line AC is cut at B; therefore the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Likewise the straight line AD is cut at B; therefore the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB [2.7].

**Step 5.** Substituting the equalities of Step 4 into the equality of Step 3, twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB and with E [CN1]. Subtracting the square on AB from both, twice the rectangle AD, DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with E [CN3]. That is, twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by the area E.

**Step 6.** The area E is rational. For AD, DB, AC, CB are rational straight lines, so the squares on them are each commensurable with the square on ρ [D10.1.3] and are therefore rational [D10.1.4] and commensurable with one another [10.12]. The squares on AD, DB being commensurable, their sum is commensurable with the square on AD [10.15], hence with the square on ρ [10.12]; likewise the sum of the squares on AC, CB is commensurable with the square on ρ. These two sums, being each commensurable with the square on ρ, are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Now the greater sum (the squares on AD, DB) is composed of the lesser sum (the squares on AC, CB) and E, and the whole is commensurable with the part consisting of the lesser sum; therefore the lesser sum and E are commensurable [10.15]. Hence E is commensurable with the square on ρ [10.12], that is, E is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** Twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial. For AD, DB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so the rectangle AD, DB is medial [10.21]. Twice this rectangle has to the rectangle the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1, so it is commensurable with the rectangle [10.6]; and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]. Therefore twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial. In the same way, since AC, CB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle AC, CB is medial [10.21], and twice it, being commensurable with it [10.6], is medial [10.23, Porism].

**Step 8.** By Steps 5, 6 and 7, the medial area twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds the medial area twice the rectangle AC, CB by the rational area E. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area [10.26]. This is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false: no rational straight line other than BC can be annexed to the apotome AB so as to be commensurable with the whole in square only. Hence to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a first apotome of a medial straight line only one medial straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a first apotome of a medial straight line, and let BC be its annex, so that AC is the whole. By the definition of a first apotome of a medial straight line [10.74], AC and CB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only, and the rectangle contained by AC, CB is rational; B lies between A and C, and AB is the remainder when CB is subtracted from AC.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that another medial straight line DB, with D a point different from C, can also be annexed to AB, so that AD and DB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only and the rectangle contained by AD, DB is rational [10.74]. Since DB is subtracted from the whole AD to leave the remainder AB, the point B lies between A and D; thus C and D both lie on AB produced beyond B.

**Step 3.** Since D is different from C, the annexes BC and BD are unequal; let BD be the greater (the argument is identical if BC is the greater). Then C lies between B and D, so that AC is a part of AD and CB is a part of DB; hence AD is greater than AC and DB is greater than CB [CN5]. Consequently the square on AD is greater than the square on AC (the square on AC being a part of the square on AD when the two are placed with a common angle), and likewise the square on DB is greater than the square on CB [CN5]. Therefore the squares on AD, DB together exceed the squares on AC, CB together by some area; call this excess X, so that sq(AD) + sq(DB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + X.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Likewise, since the straight line AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB [2.7].

**Step 5.** By Step 3 and Step 4, the area twice rect(AD, DB) + sq(AB) and the area twice rect(AC, CB) + sq(AB) + X are each equal to the squares on AD, DB together; hence they are equal to one another [CN1]. Subtracting the square on AB from each [CN3], twice rect(AD, DB) = twice rect(AC, CB) + X. Thus twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by the very area X by which the squares on AD, DB exceed the squares on AC, CB.

**Step 6.** The area X is rational. Let r be the rational straight line set out; an area is rational when it is commensurable with the square on r [D10.1.4]. The rectangle AD, DB is rational (Step 2), so it is commensurable with sq(r). Twice the rectangle AD, DB has to the rectangle AD, DB the ratio 2 : 1, which a number has to a number, so twice rect(AD, DB) is commensurable with rect(AD, DB) [10.6]; therefore twice rect(AD, DB) is commensurable with sq(r) [10.12] and is rational [D10.1.4]. In the same way twice rect(AC, CB) is rational and commensurable with sq(r). Being both commensurable with sq(r), the areas twice rect(AD, DB) and twice rect(AC, CB) are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Now by Step 5 the whole twice rect(AD, DB) is made up of the two parts twice rect(AC, CB) and X, and the whole is commensurable with the part twice rect(AC, CB); therefore the two parts twice rect(AC, CB) and X are commensurable with one another [10.15]. Hence X is commensurable with sq(r) [10.12], that is, X is a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** The squares on AD, DB together form a medial area. Since AD is a medial straight line, the square on AD is equal to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only, that is, the square on AD is a medial area [10.21]. Since AD, DB are commensurable in square, the square on DB is commensurable with the square on AD [D10.1.2]; hence their sum sq(AD) + sq(DB) is commensurable with the square on AD [10.15]. But an area commensurable with a medial area is itself medial [10.23]. Therefore sq(AD) + sq(DB) is a medial area. In exactly the same way, since AC, CB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only, sq(AC) + sq(CB) is a medial area.

**Step 8.** By Steps 3, 6 and 7, the medial area sq(AD) + sq(DB) exceeds the medial area sq(AC) + sq(CB) by the rational area X. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area [10.26]. This is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore no medial straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB so as to be commensurable with the whole in square only and to contain with the whole a rational rectangle. Hence to a first apotome of a medial straight line only one medial straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a second apotome of a medial straight line only one medial straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a second apotome of a medial straight line, and let BC be the medial straight line annexed to it, so that AC, CB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle AC·CB [10.75]. I say that no medial straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB so as to be commensurable with the whole in square only and to contain with the whole a medial rectangle.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let another medial straight line BD, different from BC, be so annexed to AB, so that AD, DB are also medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle AD·DB. Since BD is different from BC, one of them is the greater; let BD be the greater (the argument is the same in the other case). Then C lies between B and D, so that AC is a part of AD and CB is a part of DB; hence AD is greater than AC and DB is greater than CB [CN5].

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line EF. To EF let there be applied the rectangle EL equal to the square on AB, producing EH as breadth [1.45]; and, in the same manner and so that EH and its continuation are in a straight line, let there be applied on the side of H remote from E the rectangle HG equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB, producing HM as breadth, and the rectangle HI equal to twice the rectangle AD·DB, producing HN as breadth [1.45]. Thus EG is a rectangle applied to EF with breadth EM, and EI is a rectangle applied to EF with breadth EN.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Now EG is made up of EL and HG, that is, of the square on AB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB [CN2]; therefore EG is equal to the squares on AC, CB [CN1]. In the same way, since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB are equal to twice the rectangle AD·DB together with the square on AB [2.7], and EI is made up of EL and HI [CN2]; therefore EI is equal to the squares on AD, DB [CN1].

**Step 5.** Since AC is medial, the square on AC is a medial area [10.21]; and since AC, CB are commensurable in square, the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB [D10.1.2]; hence the sum of the squares on AC, CB is commensurable with the square on AC [10.15], and is therefore itself a medial area [10.23, Porism]. Thus EG is a medial area applied to the rational straight line EF; therefore its breadth EM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. By the same reasoning the sum of the squares on AD, DB is a medial area [10.21, D10.1.2, 10.15, 10.23], and EI being that area applied to EF, its breadth EN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 6.** Again, the rectangle AC·CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC·CB has to the rectangle AC·CB the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1, so that the two are commensurable [10.6]; therefore twice the rectangle AC·CB is a medial area [10.23, Porism]. Thus HG is a medial area applied to the rational straight line EF, so that its breadth HM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Similarly twice the rectangle AD·DB is commensurable with the medial rectangle AD·DB [10.6] and is therefore medial [10.23], so that the breadth HN of HI is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 7.** Since AC, CB are commensurable in square only, AC is incommensurable in length with CB [D10.1.2]. Now the square on AC and the rectangle AC·CB are under the same height AC, so that the square on AC is to the rectangle AC·CB as AC is to CB [6.1]; therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the rectangle AC·CB [10.11]. But the sum of the squares on AC, CB is commensurable with the square on AC (Step 5); therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with the rectangle AC·CB [10.13]. And twice the rectangle AC·CB is commensurable with the rectangle AC·CB (Step 6); therefore twice the rectangle AC·CB is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB [10.13]; that is, HG is incommensurable with EG. In exactly the same way, AD being incommensurable in length with DB, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD·DB [6.1, 10.11, 10.13]; that is, HI is incommensurable with EI.

**Step 8.** Now EG and HG are rectangles under the same height EF; therefore EG is to HG as EM is to HM [6.1]. And EG is incommensurable with HG; therefore EM is incommensurable in length with HM [10.11]. Similarly EI is to HI as EN is to HN [6.1], and EI is incommensurable with HI; therefore EN is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11].

**Step 9.** Further, EM and HM are each rational and incommensurable in length with EF (Steps 5, 6); therefore each of them is commensurable in square with EF [D10.1.3], that is, the square on EM and the square on HM are each commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]; hence the square on EM is commensurable with the square on HM [10.12], so that EM, HM are commensurable in square. Combining this with Step 8, EM and HM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH, the remainder when HM is subtracted from EM, is an apotome, and HM is a rational straight line annexed to it which is commensurable with the whole EM in square only [10.73]. By the same argument EN and HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [D10.1.3, D10.1.2, 10.12], so that EH, the remainder when HN is subtracted from EN, is an apotome with HN annexed to it, HN being commensurable with the whole EN in square only [10.73].

**Step 10.** But HN is not the same straight line as HM. For since AC is a part of AD and CB is a part of DB (Step 2), the rectangle AC·CB is a part of the rectangle AD·DB, so that the rectangle AD·DB is greater than the rectangle AC·CB, and twice the rectangle AD·DB is greater than twice the rectangle AC·CB [CN5]; that is, HI is greater than HG. Now HI and HG are under the same height EF, so that HI is to HG as HN is to HM [6.1]; and HI is greater than HG; therefore HN is greater than HM [5.14]. Thus HM and HN are different straight lines.

**Step 11.** Therefore to the apotome EH there have been annexed two different rational straight lines, HM and HN, each of which is commensurable with the whole in square only. But to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only [10.79]: which is impossible. Therefore the supposition is false, and no medial straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB which is commensurable with the whole in square only and contains with the whole a medial rectangle.

Therefore to a second apotome of a medial straight line only one medial straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a minor straight line only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which makes, with the whole, the sum of the squares on them rational but twice the rectangle contained by them medial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a minor straight line. By 10.76, AB is the remainder obtained when from a straight line AC there is subtracted a straight line CB which is incommensurable in square with AC and which makes with AC the sum of the squares on AC, CB rational but twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB medial. Thus BC is an annex to AB: the point B lies between A and C, AC is the whole, CB is the annex, and AC, CB satisfy the stated conditions. [10.76]

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that a different straight line BD can also be so annexed to AB, so that D lies on AB produced beyond B, D is distinct from C, AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is rational, and twice the rectangle contained by AD, DB is medial.

**Step 3.** Since C and D both lie on AB produced beyond B and are distinct points, the straight lines AC, AD are unequal. Let AD be the greater; if AC is the greater, the same argument applies with the letters C and D interchanged, since the conditions imposed on AC, CB and on AD, DB are identical. Then C lies between B and D, so that AD is cut at C into the segments AC, CD, and DB is cut at C into the segments DC, CB.

**Step 4.** Since DB is cut at C, the rectangle contained by AD, DB is equal to the rectangles contained by AD, DC and by AD, CB [2.1]; therefore the rectangle AD, DB is greater than the rectangle AD, CB [CN5]. Again, since AD is cut at C, the rectangle contained by AD, CB is equal to the rectangles contained by AC, CB and by CD, CB [2.1]; therefore the rectangle AD, CB is greater than the rectangle AC, CB [CN5]. Hence the rectangle AD, DB is greater than the rectangle AC, CB, and consequently twice the rectangle AD, DB is greater than twice the rectangle AC, CB. Let R be the area by which twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB, so that twice the rectangle AD, DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with R.

**Step 5.** Since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Likewise, since AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Let X denote the sum of the squares on AD, DB, Y the sum of the squares on AC, CB, P twice the rectangle AD, DB, and Q twice the rectangle AC, CB; then X is equal to P together with the square on AB, and Y is equal to Q together with the square on AB.

**Step 6.** By Step 4, P is equal to Q together with R. Adding R to the equals Y and Q together with the square on AB [CN2], Y together with R is equal to Q, the square on AB and R together; and this is P together with the square on AB, which is X (Step 5). Therefore X is equal to Y together with R [CN1]; that is, the squares on AD, DB exceed the squares on AC, CB by the very same area R by which twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB.

**Step 7.** Now the sum X of the squares on AD, DB is rational (Step 2), and the sum Y of the squares on AC, CB is rational (Step 1); that is, each of X and Y is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]. Therefore X and Y, being commensurable with the same area, are commensurable with one another [10.12].

**Step 8.** Since the whole X is made up of the two parts Y and R (Step 6), and the whole X is commensurable with one of the parts, namely Y (Step 7), the two parts Y and R are commensurable with one another [10.15]. But Y is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out (Step 7); therefore R is also commensurable with that square [10.12], and so R is a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 9.** But twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial (Step 2) and twice the rectangle AC, CB is medial (Step 1), and by Step 4 the former exceeds the latter by the area R, which has been shown to be rational (Step 8). Thus a medial area would exceed a medial area by a rational area; which is impossible [10.26].

**Step 10.** Therefore no straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which makes with the whole the sum of the squares on them rational but twice the rectangle contained by them medial. Hence to a minor straight line only one such straight line can be annexed. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let BC be a straight line annexed to AB, so that AC is the whole straight line and CB the annex. By 10.77, AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that a second straight line BD, different from BC, can also be annexed to AB with the same properties: AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial, and twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational (10.77). Since BC and BD are unequal, let BD be the greater; then C lies between B and D, so AC is a part of AD and CB a part of DB, whence AD is greater than AC and DB greater than CB (CN5). Consequently the square on AD is greater than the square on AC and the square on DB is greater than the square on CB, the lesser square being a part of the greater (CN5); so the sum of the squares on AD, DB exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB by some area. Call this excess E.

**Step 3.** Since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB (2.7). Likewise, since AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB (2.7).

**Step 4.** By Step 2, the squares on AD, DB are equal to the squares on AC, CB together with E. Replacing each sum of squares by the equal area found in Step 3 (CN1), twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB and E. Subtracting the common square on AB from both (CN3), twice the rectangle AD, DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with E. Thus twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by the same area E by which the squares on AD, DB exceed the squares on AC, CB.

**Step 5.** E is a rational area. Let K be the square on the rational straight line set out. Twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational and is therefore commensurable with K, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational and is therefore commensurable with K (D10.1.4). Hence twice the rectangle AD, DB is commensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB (10.12). Now twice the rectangle AD, DB is the whole composed of the two parts twice the rectangle AC, CB and E, and this whole is commensurable with the part twice the rectangle AC, CB; therefore the parts are commensurable, that is, E is commensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB (10.15). Since twice the rectangle AC, CB is commensurable with K, E is also commensurable with K (10.12), and therefore E is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 6.** Therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB, which is a medial area, exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB, which is also a medial area, by the rational area E. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area (10.26). This is impossible.

**Step 7.** Hence no straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB so as to be incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and to make with the whole the sum of the squares on them medial but twice the rectangle contained by them rational. Therefore to a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one such straight line can be annexed. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, and let BC be the straight line annexed to it, so that AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, twice the rectangle AC, CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB [10.78]. I say that no other straight line can be annexed to AB satisfying the same conditions.

**Step 2.** For suppose, if possible, that BD, a straight line different from BC, is also annexed to AB, so that AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial, twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial, and the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD, DB.

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line EF [D10.1.3]. To EF apply a rectangle EG equal to the sum of the squares on AC, CB, producing EM as breadth [1.44, 1.45]; and from EG cut off, on the same side EF, a rectangle HG equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB, producing HM as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. Let EL be the remaining rectangle, with breadth EH.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB [2.7]. But EG is equal to the squares on AC, CB, and HG is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB; therefore EG is equal to HG together with the square on AB [CN1]. Taking away HG from both, the remainder EL is equal to the square on AB [CN3].

**Step 5.** Again, to EF apply a rectangle EI equal to the sum of the squares on AD, DB, producing EN as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. Since AB is less than AD, the square on AB, that is EL, is less than EI [CN5]; both being applied to EF from the point E, EL is a part of EI and H falls between E and N. Since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB [2.7]; that is, EI is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with EL [CN1]. Taking away EL from both, the remainder HI is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB [CN3], and its breadth is HN.

**Step 6.** The sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21]; and EG is equal to it. Thus EG, the square on a medial straight line, is applied to the rational straight line EF producing EM as breadth; therefore EM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Likewise twice the rectangle AC, CB is medial and HG is equal to it, so that HG is the square on a medial straight line applied to EF producing HM as breadth; therefore HM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 7.** Since the sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB, and EG, HG are equal to these respectively, EG is incommensurable with HG. Now EG and HG are rectangles of the same height EF standing on the bases EM, HM; therefore, as EG is to HG, so is EM to HM [6.1]. Since the first is incommensurable with the second, EM is incommensurable in length with HM [10.11].

**Step 8.** EM and HM are each rational and each incommensurable in length with EF; hence each is commensurable in square only with EF [D10.1.3], so that the squares on EM and on HM are each commensurable with the square on EF and therefore with one another [10.12]; that is, EM and HM are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Together with Step 7, EM and HM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH, the remainder when HM is subtracted from EM, is an apotome, and HM is its annex [10.73].

**Step 9.** In the same way, EI is equal to the sum of the squares on AD, DB, which is medial, and is applied to EF producing EN; therefore EN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. HI is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB, which is medial, and is applied to EF producing HN; therefore HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Since the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD, DB, EI is incommensurable with HI; and, as EI is to HI, so is EN to HN [6.1]; therefore EN is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11]. Moreover EN and HN, being rational and each commensurable in square only with EF, are commensurable in square with one another [D10.1.3, 10.12, D10.1.2]. Therefore EN, HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and EH, the remainder when HN is subtracted from EN, is an apotome with HN as its annex [10.73].

**Step 10.** The annexes HM and HN are different. For BD is not equal to BC; let BD be the greater (the other case is treated in the same way). Then AD is greater than AC and DB is greater than CB, so the sum of the squares on AD, DB is greater than the sum of the squares on AC, CB [CN5]; that is, EI is greater than EG. If EN were equal to EM, the rectangles EI and EG, applied to the same EF from the same point E, would coincide and be equal [CN4]; therefore EN is not equal to EM. And if HN were equal to HM, then, the common EH being added to each, EN would be equal to EM [CN2]; therefore HN is not equal to HM.

**Step 11.** Thus to the apotome EH two different rational straight lines, HM and HN, have been annexed, each commensurable in square only with the corresponding whole EM or EN. But to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only [10.79]. This is impossible; therefore no straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB satisfying the conditions of Step 2.

**Step 12.** Therefore to a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To find the first apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the rational straight line set out (D10.1.3), and let BG be a straight line commensurable in length with A. Then BG, being commensurable with the rational straight line A, is itself rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 2.** Let two square numbers DE, EF be taken, the point F lying between D and E so that DE is made up of DF and FE, and such that the difference DF is not a square number: namely, let DE be the number 9, which is 3 multiplied by 3, and EF the number 4, which is 2 multiplied by 2, so that both are square numbers (D7.18); then DF is the number 5, which is not square, since 2 by 2 makes 4 and 3 by 3 makes 9, and no number lies between 2 and 3, so that no number multiplied by itself makes 5. Also ED is greater than DF, since DF is a part of DE.

**Step 3.** ED has not to DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For if it had, then, since the first, ED, is a square number, the second, DF, would also be a square number (8.24); but DF is not square (Step 2).

**Step 4.** Using the numbers ED, DF and the straight line BG, let a straight line X be found, by the Porism to 10.6, such that, as the number ED is to the number DF, so is the square on BG to the square on X (10.6): a straight line Y is found such that BG is to Y as ED is to DF, and X is taken as a mean proportional between BG and Y, so that BG is to Y as the square on BG is to the square on X.

**Step 5.** Since, as ED is to DF, so is the square on BG to the square on X, take the doubles of ED and of the square on BG (equimultiples of the first and third) and the doubles of DF and of the square on X (equimultiples of the second and fourth). Since ED is greater than DF (Step 2), the double of ED exceeds the double of DF; therefore, by the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio, the double of the square on BG exceeds the double of the square on X (D5.5). Hence the square on BG is greater than the square on X, and therefore BG is greater than X; for if X were equal to or greater than BG, the square on X would be equal to or greater than the square on BG.

**Step 6.** From the greater straight line GB let GC be cut off equal to the less, X (1.3), so that C lies on BG between B and G, and BC is the remainder when GC is subtracted from BG. Since GC is equal to X, the square on GC is equal to the square on X; therefore, as the number ED is to the number DF, so is the square on BG to the square on GC, and BG is greater than GC.

**Step 7.** Since the square on BG has to the square on GC the ratio which the number ED has to the number DF, the square on BG is commensurable with the square on GC (10.6).

**Step 8.** Since BG is commensurable in length with A, the square on BG has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and therefore the ratio which a number has to a number; hence the square on BG is commensurable with the square on A (10.6). But the square on GC is commensurable with the square on BG (Step 7). Therefore the square on GC is commensurable with the square on A (10.12); that is, GC is commensurable in square with A (D10.1.2), and so GC is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 9.** Since ED has not to DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 3), and the square on BG has to the square on GC the same ratio as ED has to DF (Step 6), neither has the square on BG to the square on GC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BG is incommensurable in length with GC (10.9). Thus BG, GC are rational straight lines (Steps 1, 8) which are commensurable in square (Step 7, D10.1.2) but incommensurable in length, that is, commensurable in square only.

**Step 10.** Therefore, since from the rational straight line BG there has been subtracted the rational straight line GC, which is commensurable with the whole BG in square only (Step 6, Step 9), the remainder BC is an apotome (10.73), its whole being BG and its annex GC.

**Step 11.** Let BG be bisected at O (1.10), and with centre O and distance OB let the circle BKG be described (P3), of which BG is a diameter. Since GC is less than BG (Step 6), let there be fitted into the circle, from the point G, the straight line GK equal to GC (4.1), and let BK be joined (P1). The angle BKG, being an angle in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on BG is equal to the squares on GK, KB (1.47), that is, to the squares on GC, KB. Let H denote the straight line KB. Thus the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on H.

**Step 12.** Since, as ED is to DF, so is the square on BG to the square on GC (Step 6), and ED exceeds DF by FE (Step 2), while the square on BG exceeds the square on GC by the square on H (Step 11), therefore, convertendo, as DE is to EF, so is the square on BG to the square on H (5.19, Porism).

**Step 13.** But DE, EF are square numbers (Step 2); therefore DE has to EF the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence the square on BG also has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BG is commensurable in length with H (10.9).

**Step 14.** Therefore BC is an apotome (Step 10) whose whole is BG and whose annex is GC; the square on the whole BG is greater than the square on the annex GC by the square on H (Step 11), a straight line commensurable in length with the whole BG (Step 13); and the whole BG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 1). Therefore BC is a first apotome (D10.3.1). Thus the first apotome BC has been found. Q.E.F.

**Path note.** The square numbers were fixed explicitly (9, 4, difference 5) rather than by appeal to the unnumbered lemma after 10.28, and the straight line H whose square is the excess of the square on BG over the square on GC was constructed by the semicircle method (4.1, 3.31, 1.47) rather than by citing the unnumbered lemma after 10.13, since lemmas carry no proposition numbers; this matches the convention used for 10.29, 10.30 and 10.49 in this run.

**USED:** D10.1.3, D7.18, 8.24, 10.6, D5.5, 1.3, 10.9, 10.12, D10.1.2, 10.73, 1.10, P3, 4.1, P1, 3.31, 1.47, 5.19, D10.3.1

result.statement: To find the second apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the rational straight line set out, and let GC be a straight line commensurable in length with A. Then GC is rational [D10.1.3]. Further, since GC is commensurable in length with A, the square on GC has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore the square on GC is commensurable with the square on A [10.6], so that the square on GC is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 2.** Let two square numbers DE, EF be set out, DE being the greater, such that their difference FD (that is, DE less EF) is not a square number; for example, let DE be 9 (contained by 3 and 3) and EF be 4 (contained by 2 and 2), so that their difference FD is 5, which is not a square number [D7.18].

**Step 3.** Let it be contrived that, as the number FD is to the number DE, so is the square on CG to the square on GB [10.6, Por.], GB being drawn from G along the straight line GC in the direction of C. Then, inversely, as the square on GB is to the square on CG, so is the number DE to the number FD [5.7, Por.].

**Step 4.** Since the square on GB has to the square on CG the ratio which a number has to a number, the square on GB is commensurable with the square on CG [10.6]; hence GB and CG are commensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 5.** Since, as DE is to FD, so is the square on GB to the square on CG, then, by the definition of the same ratio, if equimultiples be taken of DE and of the square on GB, and equimultiples of FD and of the square on CG, the former alike exceed or alike fall short of the latter; taking each magnitude once, since DE exceeds FD, the square on GB exceeds the square on CG [D5.5]. Hence GB is greater than CG (for the square on the less of two straight lines is less than the square on the greater); therefore the point B falls beyond C, so that C lies between B and G and CG is a part of GB.

**Step 6.** Now the square on GB is commensurable with the square on CG, and the square on CG is commensurable with the square on A; therefore the square on GB is commensurable with the square on A [10.12]. Hence the square on GB is rational [D10.1.4], and GB, being commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2], is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 7.** But DE has not to FD the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For, if it had, then, since DE is square, FD would also be square [8.24]; but FD is not square. Therefore neither has the square on GB to the square on CG the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore GB is incommensurable in length with CG [10.9].

**Step 8.** Therefore GB, CG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. And from the rational straight line GB there has been subtracted the rational straight line CG commensurable with the whole in square only; therefore the remainder BC is an apotome [10.73], GB being the whole and CG the annex.

**Step 9.** I say next that BC is a second apotome. Let a square be constructed equal to the excess of the square on GB over the square on CG [2.14], and let H be its side; then the square on GB is greater than the square on CG by the square on H.

**Step 10.** Since, as the square on GB is to the square on CG, so is the number DE to the number FD, therefore, convertendo, as the square on GB is to the excess of the square on GB over the square on CG, that is, to the square on H, so is DE to the excess of DE over FD, that is, to EF [5.19, Por.].

**Step 11.** But DE and EF are both square numbers; therefore the square on GB has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore GB is commensurable in length with H [10.9].

**Step 12.** Therefore the square on the whole GB is greater than the square on the annex CG by the square on a straight line H commensurable in length with the whole GB; and the annex CG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out. Therefore the apotome BC is a second apotome [D10.3.2].

**Step 13.** Therefore the second apotome BC has been found. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find the third apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out [D10.1.3], and let three numbers E, BC, CD be set out which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but such that CB has to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; here D lies between B and C, so that BD is the excess of the number BC over the number CD. (Such numbers exist, e.g. E, BC, CD = 3, 8, 6, whence BD = 2 and CB : BD = 4 : 1.)

**Step 2.** By the porism to 10.6, let it be contrived that, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH [10.6].

**Step 3.** Since the square on A has to the square on FG the ratio which the number E has to the number BC, the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG [10.6].
