The square on A is rational [D10.1.4]; therefore the square on FG is rational [D10.1.4], and FG, being commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2], is rational [D10.1.3]. But E has not to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence the square on A has not to the square on FG the ratio of a square number to a square number, so that A and FG are incommensurable in length [10.9].

**Step 4.** Again, since the square on FG has to the square on GH the ratio which the number BC has to the number CD, the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6]. The square on FG is commensurable with the square on A (Step 3); therefore the square on GH is commensurable with the square on A [10.12], hence rational [D10.1.4], and GH is rational [D10.1.3]. But BC has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence FG and GH are incommensurable in length [10.9]. Therefore FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 5.** Since CD is a part of BC, BC is greater than CD [CN5]; and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH; therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on GH [5.14], so that FG is greater than GH. From the rational straight line FG let the rational straight line GH, commensurable with FG in square only, be subtracted; the remainder FH is an apotome [10.73], FG being its whole and GH its annex.

**Step 6.** Since, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH [5.22]. But E has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence the square on A has not to the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number, so that A and GH are incommensurable in length [10.9]. Thus neither the whole FG (Step 3) nor the annex GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out.

**Step 7.** On FG let the semicircle FLG be described; since GH is less than the diameter FG (Step 5), let FL equal to GH be fitted into it [4.1], and let LG be joined. The angle FLG, being in a semicircle, is right [3.31]; therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FL, LG [1.47], that is, to the squares on GH, LG. Let K be equal to LG; then the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 8.** Since, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, convertendo, as BC is to the excess BD, so is the square on FG to its excess over the square on GH, that is, as CB is to BD, so is the square on FG to the square on K [5.19].

**Step 9.** But CB has to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on FG has to the square on K the ratio which a square number has to a square number, so that FG and K are commensurable in length [10.9]. Hence the square on the whole FG is greater than the square on the annex GH by the square on a straight line K commensurable in length with the whole FG.

**Step 10.** Therefore FH is an apotome (Step 5) of which neither the whole FG nor the annex GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 6), while the square on the whole is greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable with the whole (Step 9). Therefore FH is a third apotome [D10.3.3]. Thus the third apotome FH has been found. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find the fourth apotome.
result.proof:
**Statement:** To find the fourth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out, and let BG be a straight line commensurable in length with A. Then BG is rational (D10.1.3). Moreover, since BG, A are commensurable in length, the square on BG has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), so the square on BG is commensurable with the square on A (10.6); hence the square on BG is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 2.** Let two numbers DF, FE be set out such that the whole DE has to neither of the numbers DF, FE the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Since DE is the whole and EF, DF are parts of it, DE is greater than each of EF, DF (CN5).

**Step 3.** By the Porism to 10.6, let a straight line be found such that, as the number DE is to the number EF, so is the square on BG to the square on that line; and let a straight line equal to it be cut off from GB, beginning at G, as GC (1.3). Thus, as DE is to EF, so is the square on BG to the square on GC. Since DE exceeds EF, the definition of sameness of ratio (D5.5), taking each of the four terms once, shows that the square on BG exceeds the square on GC. Hence GC is less than BG: for if GC were equal to BG the squares would be equal, and if GC were greater the square on BG would be a part of the square on GC and so less than it (CN5). Therefore C falls between B and G, and BC is the remainder when GC is subtracted from BG.

**Step 4.** Since, as DE is to EF, so is the square on BG to the square on GC, and DE, EF are numbers, the square on BG has to the square on GC the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore the square on BG is commensurable with the square on GC (10.6). But the square on BG is commensurable with the square on A (Step 1); hence the square on GC is also commensurable with the square on A (10.12). Therefore the square on GC is rational (D10.1.4), and GC, being commensurable in square with A (D10.1.2), is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 5.** The ratio of the square on BG to the square on GC is the same as the ratio of DE to EF, and DE has not to EF the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on BG to the square on GC such a ratio. Consequently BG is incommensurable in length with GC (10.9). But the squares on BG, GC are commensurable (Step 4), so BG, GC are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). Thus BG, GC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 6.** Since from the rational straight line BG there is subtracted the rational straight line GC, which is commensurable with the whole BG in square only, the remainder BC is an apotome (10.73); its whole is BG and its annex is GC.

**Step 7.** BG, GC being unequal, BG the greater, let H be the straight line such that the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on H (Lemma to 10.13); that is, the square on BG is equal to the squares on GC, H together.

**Step 8.** Now, as DE is to EF, so is the square on BG to the square on GC, where DE exceeds EF by DF and the square on BG exceeds the square on GC by the square on H. Therefore, convertendo (D5.16; Porism to 5.19), as DE is to DF, so is the square on BG to the square on H.

**Step 9.** DE has not to DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence neither has the square on BG to the square on H such a ratio. Therefore BG is incommensurable in length with H (10.9).

**Step 10.** Accordingly BC is an apotome (Step 6) such that the square on the whole BG is greater than the square on the annex GC by the square on H, a straight line incommensurable in length with the whole BG (Steps 7, 9); and the whole BG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 1). Therefore BC is a fourth apotome (D10.3.4). Q.E.F.

Path note: the ratio of squares in Step 3 is obtained directly from the Porism to 10.6 (rather than assembling it from 6.12, 6.13 and the Porism to 6.19), and the line H in Step 7 from the Lemma to 10.13 (rather than re-deriving it from 4.1, 3.31, 1.47); both are the most direct available tools.

**USED:** D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4, D10.3.4, D5.5, D5.16, CN5, 1.3, 5.19, 10.6, 10.9, 10.12, 10.13, 10.73

result.statement: To find the fifth apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the rational straight line set out, and let CG be a straight line commensurable in length with A (for instance, equal to A). Then CG is rational [D10.1.3]. Moreover, since CG, A are commensurable in length, the square on CG has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9], so that the square on CG is commensurable with the square on A [10.6]; that is, the square on CG is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 2.** Set out two numbers DF, FE such that the whole DE has neither to DF nor to FE the ratio which a square number has to a square number (for instance DF = 1, FE = 2, so that DE = 3). Then FE has not to ED the ratio which a square number has to a square number either; for otherwise ED would have to FE the inverse ratio, which would again be a ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 3.** By the Porism to 10.6, from the straight line CG and the numbers FE, ED construct a straight line GB such that, as FE is to ED, so is the square on CG to the square on GB [10.6]; let GB lie in a straight line with GC, on the side of C.

**Step 4.** Since FE is less than ED, and as FE is to ED so is the square on CG to the square on GB, the square on CG is less than the square on GB [D5.5, taking each of the four magnitudes once]; hence CG is less than GB, so that C falls between B and G, and BC is what remains when GC is subtracted from BG.

**Step 5.** Since the square on CG has to the square on GB the ratio FE : ED, which is the ratio of a number to a number, the square on CG is commensurable with the square on GB [10.6]. But the square on CG is commensurable with the square on A (Step 1); therefore the square on GB is also commensurable with the square on A [10.12], that is, the square on GB is rational [D10.1.4]. Hence GB is commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2] and is therefore rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 6.** Since FE has not to ED the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 2), neither has the square on CG to the square on GB that ratio; therefore CG is incommensurable in length with GB [10.9]. On the other hand the squares on BG, GC are commensurable (Step 5), so that BG, GC are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Therefore BG, GC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 7.** Therefore, GC being subtracted from the rational straight line BG, the remainder BC is an apotome [10.73], its whole being BG and its annex GC.

**Step 8.** It remains to show that BC is a fifth apotome. Describe a circle having BG as diameter, and into it fit the straight line BK equal to GC, which is possible since GC is less than BG [4.1]; join KG. The angle BKG, being in a semicircle, is right [3.31]; therefore the square on BG is equal to the squares on BK, KG, that is, to the squares on GC, KG [1.47]. Let H denote KG; then the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on H.

**Step 9.** Since as FE is to ED so is the square on CG to the square on BG (Step 3), inversely, as ED is to FE so is the square on BG to the square on CG [5.7, Porism]. Therefore, convertendo, as ED is to the excess DF by which ED exceeds FE, so is the square on BG to the excess by which the square on BG exceeds the square on CG; that is, as ED is to DF, so is the square on BG to the square on H [5.19, Porism].

**Step 10.** But ED has not to DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 2); therefore neither has the square on BG to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BG is incommensurable in length with H [10.9].

**Step 11.** Thus BC is an apotome (Step 7) such that the square on its whole BG is greater than the square on its annex GC by the square on a straight line H incommensurable in length with the whole BG (Steps 8, 10), while the annex GC is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 1). Therefore BC is a fifth apotome [D10.3.5]; and it has been found. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find the sixth apotome.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.90
**Statement:** To find the sixth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out, and let three numbers E, BC, CD be set out such that no two of them have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; let D lie on BC, so that BD is the excess of BC over CD, and let CB also not have to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number. (Such numbers exist: for instance E = 2, BC = 6, CD = 3, whence BD = 3; the ratios 2 : 6 = 1 : 3, 6 : 3 = 2 : 1, 2 : 3 and CB : BD = 6 : 3 = 2 : 1 are none of them ratios of a square number to a square number.) Since CD is a part of BC, BC is greater than CD [CN5].

**Step 2.** By the Porism to 10.6, contrive a straight line FG such that, as the number E is to the number BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG; and again contrive a straight line GH, laid along GF from G, such that, as the number BC is to the number CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH [10.6].

**Step 3.** Since the square on A has to the square on FG the ratio which the number E has to the number BC, the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG [10.6]. Therefore FG is commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2], and A being rational, FG is rational [D10.1.3]. Further, since E has not to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, the square on A has not to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number (the two ratios being the same); therefore A is incommensurable in length with FG [10.9].

**Step 4.** Since the square on FG has to the square on GH the ratio which the number BC has to the number CD, the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6]; therefore FG and GH are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. And since BC has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on FG to the square on GH; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH [10.9].

**Step 5.** Since, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH [5.22]. Hence the square on A is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6], so GH is commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2] and is therefore rational [D10.1.3]. And since E has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on A to the square on GH; therefore A is incommensurable in length with GH [10.9].

**Step 6.** Since BC is greater than CD (Step 1), and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, it follows from the definition of the same ratio, taking each of the four magnitudes once, that the square on FG is greater than the square on GH [D5.5]. Hence FG is greater than GH (for the square on a lesser line is a part of the square on a greater, and so less than it), so that H falls between F and G, and FH is the remainder when GH is subtracted from FG.

**Step 7.** Now FG and GH are rational (Steps 3, 5), commensurable in square (Step 4) but incommensurable in length (Step 4), that is, commensurable in square only; and GH, the less, has been subtracted from FG, the greater. Therefore the remainder FH is an apotome [10.73], FG being the whole and GH the annex.

**Step 8.** Since the square on FG is greater than the square on GH (Step 6), let K be the side of a square equal to the excess of the square on FG over the square on GH [2.14], so that the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on K. Since, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, convertendo, as CB is to BD, so is the square on FG to the excess of the square on FG over the square on GH, that is, to the square on K [5.19]. But CB has not to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on K, and so FG is incommensurable in length with K [10.9].

**Step 9.** Therefore the square on the whole FG is greater than the square on the annex GH by the square on a straight line K incommensurable in length with the whole FG (Step 8); and neither the whole FG nor the annex GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Steps 3, 5). Therefore the apotome FH is a sixth apotome [D10.3.6]. Thus the sixth apotome FH has been found. Q.E.F.

**USED:** CN5, D5.5, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.3.6, 2.14, 5.19, 5.22, 10.6, 10.9, 10.73

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a first apotome, the âsideâ of the area is an apotome.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.91
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a first apotome, the "side" of the area is an apotome.

Notation: "rect. X, Y" denotes the rectangle contained by X and Y; "sq. X" denotes the square on X.

**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the first apotome AD, AC being the rational straight line set out with respect to which AD is a first apotome. Let DG be the annex of AD: that is, let G lie on AD produced beyond D, so that AD is the remainder when DG is subtracted from AG, where AG and DG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.73]; in particular DG is less than AG, and DG is incommensurable in length with AG. Since AD is a first apotome, the whole AG is commensurable in length with AC, and sq. AG is greater than sq. DG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG [D10.3.1]. It is to be proved that the straight line whose square is equal to AB is an apotome.

**Step 2.** Bisect DG at E [1.10]. Since DG is cut at E, sq. DG = sq. DE + sq. EG + 2 rect. DE, EG [2.4]; and DE = EG, so that sq. DE = sq. EG and rect. DE, EG = sq. EG. Hence sq. DG is four times sq. EG, i.e. sq. EG is the fourth part of sq. DG.

**Step 3.** Since DG is less than AG, the half EG of DG is less than the half of AG, so that sq. EG is not greater than the square on the half of AG. Therefore to AG there can be applied a parallelogram equal to sq. EG and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; let it be applied, and let it be rect. AF, FG with F on AG, so that rect. AF, FG = sq. EG and AG is cut at F into the segments AF, FG.

**Step 4.** AG, DG are two unequal straight lines of which AG is the greater; sq. AG exceeds sq. DG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG (Step 1); and to AG there has been applied the parallelogram rect. AF, FG, equal to the fourth part of sq. DG (Steps 2 and 3) and deficient by a square figure. Therefore AF, FG are commensurable in length [10.17].

**Step 5.** Since AF, FG are commensurable, the whole AG is commensurable in length with each of AF, FG [10.15]. But AG is commensurable in length with AC (Step 1); therefore each of AF, FG is commensurable in length with AC [10.12], and, AC being the rational straight line set out, each of AF, FG is rational [D10.1.3]. Therefore rect. AC, AF and rect. AC, FG, each being contained by rational straight lines commensurable in length, are rational [10.19], that is, each of them is commensurable with sq. AC [D10.1.4].

**Step 6.** DG is incommensurable in length with AG (Step 1), and AG is commensurable in length with AC; therefore DG is incommensurable in length with AC [10.13]. Now EG measures DG, DG being double of EG; hence EG, DG are commensurable [D10.1.1], and therefore EG is incommensurable in length with AC [10.13]. Again, DG is rational, hence commensurable with AC either in length or in square only [D10.1.3]; and DG is incommensurable in length with AC; therefore DG is commensurable in square with AC, i.e. sq. DG is commensurable with sq. AC [D10.1.2]. But sq. EG measures sq. DG (Step 2), so that sq. EG is commensurable with sq. DG [D10.1.1]; therefore sq. EG is commensurable with sq. AC [10.12], i.e. EG is commensurable in square with AC [D10.1.2] and is rational [D10.1.3]. Thus AC, EG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore rect. AC, EG is irrational [10.21], i.e. it is incommensurable with sq. AC [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** Since AG is cut at F, rect. AC, AG = rect. AC, AF + rect. AC, FG [2.1]. Since AG is cut at D, rect. AC, AG = rect. AC, AD + rect. AC, DG = AB + rect. AC, DG [2.1]. Since DG is cut at E, rect. AC, DG = rect. AC, DE + rect. AC, EG [2.1], and rect. AC, DE = rect. AC, EG because DE = EG; hence rect. AC, DG is double of rect. AC, EG. Therefore AB together with twice rect. AC, EG is equal to rect. AC, AF together with rect. AC, FG [CN1].

**Step 8.** Let LP be the side of a square equal to rect. AC, AF [2.14], so that sq. LP = rect. AC, AF; and let Q be a fourth proportional to the three straight lines AF, EG, LP, so that AF : EG = LP : Q [6.12].

**Step 9.** sq. LP and rect. LP, Q are parallelograms under the same height LP; hence sq. LP : rect. LP, Q = LP : Q [6.1]. Likewise rect. AC, AF and rect. AC, EG are under the same height AC, so that rect. AC, AF : rect. AC, EG = AF : EG [6.1]. Since LP : Q = AF : EG (Step 8), sq. LP : rect. LP, Q = rect. AC, AF : rect. AC, EG [5.11]. But sq. LP = rect. AC, AF, so that sq. LP : rect. LP, Q = rect. AC, AF : rect. LP, Q [5.7]; hence rect. AC, AF has the same ratio to rect. LP, Q as it has to rect. AC, EG [5.11], and therefore rect. LP, Q = rect. AC, EG [5.9].

**Step 10.** Since rect. AF, FG = sq. EG (Step 3), the three straight lines AF, EG, FG are proportional: AF : EG = EG : FG [6.17]. Also rect. AC, EG : rect. AC, FG = EG : FG [6.1] (same height AC), and rect. LP, Q : sq. Q = LP : Q [6.1] (same height Q). Since LP : Q = AF : EG = EG : FG, it follows that rect. LP, Q : sq. Q = rect. AC, EG : rect. AC, FG [5.11]. But rect. LP, Q = rect. AC, EG (Step 9), so that rect. LP, Q : sq. Q = rect. AC, EG : sq. Q [5.7]; hence rect. AC, EG has the same ratio to sq. Q as it has to rect. AC, FG [5.11], and therefore sq. Q = rect. AC, FG [5.9].

**Step 11.** sq. LP = rect. AC, AF and sq. Q = rect. AC, FG are rational, i.e. each is commensurable with sq. AC (Step 5). Hence each of LP, Q is commensurable in square with AC [D10.1.2] and is therefore rational [D10.1.3]; and sq. LP, sq. Q, being each commensurable with sq. AC, are commensurable with one another [10.12], so that LP, Q are commensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 12.** rect. LP, Q = rect. AC, EG is incommensurable with sq. AC (Step 6), while sq. Q = rect. AC, FG is commensurable with sq. AC (Step 5); therefore sq. Q is incommensurable with rect. LP, Q [10.13]. But rect. LP, Q : sq. Q = LP : Q (Step 10); therefore LP is incommensurable in length with Q [10.11]. Thus LP, Q are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Step 11).

**Step 13.** Since LP, Q are incommensurable in length, they are unequal (equal straight lines being commensurable [D10.1.1]). Let U denote the greater and V the less of LP, Q. Then U, V are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 11, 12); sq. U and sq. V are, in one order or the other, rect. AC, AF and rect. AC, FG (Steps 8, 10), so that sq. U + sq. V = rect. AC, AF + rect. AC, FG [CN2]; and rect. U, V = rect. LP, Q = rect. AC, EG (Step 9). From U cut off a straight line equal to V [1.3], and let W be the remainder, so that U is cut into the segments V and W. Since the rational straight line V, commensurable in square only with U, has been subtracted from the rational straight line U, the remainder W is an apotome [10.73].

**Step 14.** Since U is cut into V, W, sq. U + sq. V = 2 rect. U, V + sq. W [2.7]. Substituting the equals of Step 13, rect. AC, AF + rect. AC, FG = 2 rect. AC, EG + sq. W [CN1, CN2]. But rect. AC, AF + rect. AC, FG = AB + 2 rect. AC, EG (Step 7); therefore AB + 2 rect. AC, EG = 2 rect. AC, EG + sq. W [CN1], and, taking away 2 rect. AC, EG from each, AB = sq. W [CN3].

**Step 15.** Therefore the square on W is equal to the area AB, so that W is the "side" of AB [D10.1.4]; and W is an apotome (Step 13). Hence, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a first apotome, the "side" of the area is an apotome. Q.E.D.

Path note: the identity sq. U + sq. V = 2 rect. U, V + sq. W is taken directly from 2.7 rather than from squares about a common diameter with their complements (6.26, 1.43), and the equalities rect. LP, Q = rect. AC, EG and sq. Q = rect. AC, FG are obtained by constructing Q as a fourth proportional (6.12) and applying 5.9, rather than by constructing both squares and proving the uniqueness of a mean proportional; these are the more direct routes.

**USED:** D10.1.1, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4, D10.3.1, CN1, CN2, CN3, 1.3, 1.10, 2.1, 2.4, 2.7, 2.14, 5.7, 5.9, 5.11, 6.1, 6.12, 6.17, 6.28, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.15, 10.17, 10.19, 10.21, 10.73

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a second apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a first apotome of a medial straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the second apotome AD, so that AB is the rectangle AC, AD. I say that the "side" of AB, that is, the straight line on which is described a square equal to AB [D10.1.4], is a first apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 2.** Let DG be the annex to the apotome AD, so that AD is what remains when DG is subtracted from AG. Then AG, DG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.73], AG being the whole and DG the annex; and since AD is a second apotome, the annex DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on the whole AG is greater than the square on the annex DG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG [D10.3.2]. Also the whole AG is greater than its part DG [CN5].

**Step 3.** Since AG, DG are commensurable in square only, AG is incommensurable in length with DG; but DG is commensurable in length with AC; therefore AG is incommensurable in length with AC [10.13].

**Step 4.** Let DG be bisected at E [1.10]. Since DG is double of EG, the square on EG is the fourth part of the square on DG. To AG let there be applied a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; this is possible, since AG is greater than DG, so that the half of AG is greater than EG and the square on the half of AG is greater than the square on EG. Let the parallelogram be the rectangle AF, FG, F being a point on AG; then the rectangle AF, FG is equal to the square on EG.

**Step 5.** Since the square on the greater AG exceeds the square on the less DG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG, and to AG there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square figure, which divides AG at F, therefore AF, FG are commensurable in length [10.17].

**Step 6.** Therefore the whole AG is commensurable in length with each of AF, FG [10.15]. Now AG is rational, that is, commensurable with the assigned rational straight line; therefore each of AF, FG is also commensurable with the assigned rational straight line [10.12], and so is rational [D10.1.3]. And AG is incommensurable in length with AC (Step 3); therefore each of AF, FG is incommensurable in length with AC [10.13].

**Step 7.** Therefore AC, AF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (they are commensurable in square, being both rational, but incommensurable in length), and likewise AC, FG; hence each of the rectangles AC, AF and AC, FG is medial [10.21].

**Step 8.** Since DG is double of EG, DG is measured by EG, so that DG is commensurable in length with EG [D10.1.1]. But DG is commensurable in length with AC; therefore EG is commensurable in length with AC [10.12], and EG is rational [D10.1.3]. Therefore the rectangle AC, EG, being contained by rational straight lines commensurable in length, is rational [10.19].

**Step 9.** Since the rectangle AF, FG is equal to the square on EG, as AF is to EG, so is EG to FG [6.17]. But the rectangles AC, AF and AC, EG are under the same height AC; therefore, as AF is to EG, so is the rectangle AC, AF to the rectangle AC, EG [6.1]; and likewise, as EG is to FG, so is the rectangle AC, EG to the rectangle AC, FG [6.1]. Therefore, as the rectangle AC, AF is to the rectangle AC, EG, so is the rectangle AC, EG to the rectangle AC, FG [5.11].

**Step 10.** Let LP be the side of a square equal to the rectangle AC, AF [2.14], so that the square on LP is equal to the rectangle AC, AF; and since this rectangle is medial, LP is a medial straight line [10.21]. To the three straight lines LP, AC, EG let a fourth proportional PX be found, so that, as LP is to AC, so is EG to PX [6.12]. Then the rectangle contained by the extremes LP, PX is equal to the rectangle contained by the means AC, EG [6.16]; therefore the rectangle LP, PX is rational (Step 8).

**Step 11.** The square on LP and the rectangle LP, PX are under the same height LP; therefore, as LP is to PX, so is the square on LP to the rectangle LP, PX [6.1]. Again, the rectangle LP, PX and the square on PX are under the same height PX; therefore, as LP is to PX, so is the rectangle LP, PX to the square on PX [6.1]. Therefore, as the square on LP is to the rectangle LP, PX, so is the rectangle LP, PX to the square on PX [5.11].

**Step 12.** But the square on LP is equal to the rectangle AC, AF, and the rectangle LP, PX is equal to the rectangle AC, EG; hence, by Step 9, as the square on LP is to the rectangle LP, PX, so is the rectangle LP, PX to the rectangle AC, FG. Therefore the rectangle LP, PX has the same ratio to the square on PX that it has to the rectangle AC, FG [5.11]; therefore the square on PX is equal to the rectangle AC, FG [5.9]. And since the rectangle AC, FG is medial, PX is a medial straight line [10.21].

**Step 13.** Since the square on LP is equal to the rectangle AC, AF and the square on PX to the rectangle AC, FG, and these rectangles are under the same height AC, as the square on LP is to the square on PX, so is AF to FG [6.1]. But AF is commensurable in length with FG (Step 5); therefore the square on LP is commensurable with the square on PX [10.11], that is, LP, PX are commensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 14.** The rectangle LP, PX is rational, that is, commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.4]; but the square on PX, being equal to the medial rectangle AC, FG, is irrational [10.21], that is, incommensurable with that square [D10.1.4]. Therefore the rectangle LP, PX is incommensurable with the square on PX [10.13]. But, as the rectangle LP, PX is to the square on PX, so is LP to PX (Step 11); therefore LP is incommensurable in length with PX [10.11]. Hence LP, PX are medial straight lines commensurable in square only, and the rectangle LP, PX contained by them is rational.

**Step 15.** Since LP, PX are incommensurable in length, they are unequal. Let LP be the greater (if PX were the greater, the same construction and argument would apply with LP, PX interchanged, everything proved of them in Steps 10-14 being symmetrical); and from PL let PN be cut off equal to PX [1.3]. Then the rectangle LP, PN is equal to the rectangle LP, PX, that is, to the rectangle AC, EG; and the square on PN is equal to the square on PX, that is, to the rectangle AC, FG.

**Step 16.** Since the straight line LP is cut at N, the squares on LP, PN together are equal to twice the rectangle LP, PN together with the square on LN [2.7]. Now the squares on LP, PN are equal to the rectangles AC, AF and AC, FG together [CN2], and these, since AG is cut at F, are together equal to the rectangle AC, AG [2.1]. Therefore the rectangle AC, AG is equal to twice the rectangle AC, EG together with the square on LN [CN1].

**Step 17.** Again, since AG is cut at D, the rectangle AC, AG is equal to the rectangles AC, AD and AC, DG together [2.1], that is, to the area AB together with the rectangle AC, DG; and since DG is cut at E into the equal segments DE, EG, the rectangle AC, DG is equal to the rectangles AC, DE and AC, EG together [2.1], that is, to twice the rectangle AC, EG. Therefore the rectangle AC, AG is equal to the area AB together with twice the rectangle AC, EG.

**Step 18.** Therefore the square on LN together with twice the rectangle AC, EG is equal to the area AB together with twice the rectangle AC, EG [CN1]; and, twice the rectangle AC, EG being subtracted from each, the square on LN is equal to the area AB [CN3]. Therefore LN is the "side" of the area AB [D10.1.4].

**Step 19.** But LN is the remainder when from the medial straight line LP there is subtracted the medial straight line PN, which, being equal to PX, is commensurable with the whole LP in square only and contains with LP a rational rectangle (Steps 14, 15). Therefore LN is a first apotome of a medial straight line [10.74].

**Step 20.** Therefore the "side" of the area AB, which is contained by the rational straight line AC and the second apotome AD, is a first apotome of a medial straight line. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a third apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a second apotome of a medial straight line.
result.proof:
**Statement.** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a third apotome, the "side" of the area is a second apotome of a medial straight line.

Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the third apotome AD, the angle at A being right, so that AB is the rectangle contained by AC, AD. I say that the "side" of AB, that is, the straight line the square on which is equal to AB, is a second apotome of a medial straight line. (Below, sq(XY) denotes the square on XY and rect(XY, ZW) the rectangle contained by XY, ZW.)

**Step 1.** Let DG be the annex to AD, so that D lies between A and G and AD is the remainder when GD is subtracted from the whole AG. Since AD is an apotome, AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.73]. Since AD is a third apotome, neither AG nor GD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG [D10.3.3].

**Step 2.** Bisect DG at E [1.10]; then DE = EG and the square on EG is the fourth part of the square on DG. Since GD is a part of AG, AG is greater than GD [CN5]; hence EG, the half of DG, is less than the half of AG, and the square on EG is not greater than the square on the half of AG. Apply to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure [6.28], and let it be the rectangle contained by AF, FG, with F on AG; thus rect(AF, FG) = sq(EG). The segments AF, FG are unequal: for if AF were equal to FG, then rect(AF, FG) would be the square on AF, so that AF would equal EG and AG, being double of AF, would equal DG, whereas AG is greater than GD. Let AF be the greater segment. Now the square on AG exceeds the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG, and to the greater line AG there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less GD and deficient by a square; therefore AF and FG are commensurable in length [10.17].

**Step 3.** Through E, F, G draw EH, FI, GK parallel to AC [1.31], meeting CB produced [P2] in H, I, K. Then AK is the rectangle contained by AC, AG, and AB, DK, DH, EK, AI, FK are the rectangles contained by AC and AD, DG, DE, EG, AF, FG respectively; moreover AK is the sum of AB and DK, AK is the sum of AI and FK, and DK is the sum of DH and EK. Since DE = EG, the parallelograms DH and EK, being on equal bases and in the same parallels, are equal [1.36]; therefore DK is double of EK.

**Step 4.** Since AF and FG are commensurable in length, the whole AG is commensurable in length with each of AF, FG [10.15]. But AG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC; therefore each of AF, FG, being commensurable with the rational straight line AG, is rational [D10.1.3], and each of AF, FG is incommensurable in length with AC [10.13]. Thus AC, AF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and likewise AC, FG; therefore each of the rectangles AI, FK is medial [10.21].

**Step 5.** Since DE = EG, DG is commensurable in length with each of DE, EG [10.15]. But GD is rational and incommensurable in length with AC; therefore EG is rational [D10.1.3] and incommensurable in length with AC [10.13]. Thus AC, EG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore the rectangle EK is medial [10.21].

**Step 6.** Since AG, GD are commensurable in square only, AG is incommensurable in length with GD; and GD is commensurable in length with EG (Step 5); therefore AG is incommensurable in length with EG [10.13]. And AF is commensurable in length with AG (Step 4); therefore AF is incommensurable in length with EG [10.13].

**Step 7.** Construct a square equal to AI and let LP be its side; construct also a square equal to FK [2.14]. Since AF is greater than FG, the rectangle AI, which is under the same height AC as FK but on the greater base, is greater than FK; hence the side of the square equal to FK is less than LP. Cut off from LP a straight line PN equal to that side [1.3]. Then sq(LP) = AI, sq(PN) = FK, and N lies on LP, so that LN is the remainder when PN is subtracted from LP.

**Step 8.** The rectangles AI, FK are under the same height AC; therefore AI : FK = AF : FG [6.1], that is, sq(LP) : sq(PN) = AF : FG. Again, the square on AF and the rectangle AF, FG are under the same height AF; therefore sq(AF) : rect(AF, FG) = AF : FG [6.1]; and rect(AF, FG) = sq(EG), so that AF : FG = sq(AF) : sq(EG). Therefore sq(LP) : sq(PN) = sq(AF) : sq(EG) [5.11]. Since the squares are similar figures similarly described on the four straight lines LP, PN, AF, EG, it follows that LP : PN = AF : EG [6.22].

**Step 9.** The square on LP and the rectangle LP, PN are under the same height LP; therefore sq(LP) : rect(LP, PN) = LP : PN [6.1], and LP : PN = AF : EG (Step 8). Also AI and EK are under the same height AC, so that AI : EK = AF : EG [6.1]. Therefore sq(LP) : rect(LP, PN) = AI : EK [5.11]. But sq(LP) = AI; therefore AI has the same ratio to each of rect(LP, PN) and EK, and so rect(LP, PN) = EK [5.9].

**Step 10.** Since the straight line LP is cut at N, sq(LP) + sq(PN) = 2·rect(LP, PN) + sq(LN) [2.7]. Now sq(LP) + sq(PN) = AI + FK = AK, and 2·rect(LP, PN) = 2·EK = DK (Steps 3, 9). Therefore AK = DK + sq(LN). But AK = AB + DK. Therefore AB + DK = DK + sq(LN) [CN1], and, subtracting DK from each, AB = sq(LN) [CN3]. Hence LN is the "side" of the area AB.

**Step 11.** LP is the side of the square equal to AI, which is a rectangle contained by the rational straight lines AC, AF commensurable in square only; therefore LP is medial [10.21]. Likewise PN, the side of the square equal to FK, a rectangle contained by the rational straight lines AC, FG commensurable in square only, is medial [10.21].

**Step 12.** Since AF, FG are commensurable in length and AI : FK = AF : FG (Step 8), AI is commensurable with FK [10.11]; that is, the square on LP is commensurable with the square on PN; therefore LP, PN are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. But LP : PN = AF : EG (Step 8), and AF is incommensurable in length with EG (Step 6); therefore LP is incommensurable in length with PN [10.11]. Hence LP, PN are medial straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 13.** The rectangle contained by LP, PN is equal to EK (Step 9), and EK is medial (Step 5); therefore the medial straight lines LP, PN contain a medial rectangle.

**Step 14.** Thus from the medial straight line LP there has been subtracted the medial straight line PN, which is commensurable with the whole LP in square only and which contains with LP a medial rectangle; therefore the remainder LN is a second apotome of a medial straight line [10.75]. And LN is the "side" of the area AB (Step 10). Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a third apotome, the "side" of the area is a second apotome of a medial straight line. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 10.73, D10.3.3, 1.10, CN5, 6.28, 10.17, 1.31, P2, 1.36, 10.15, D10.1.3, 10.13, 10.21, 2.14, 1.3, 6.1, 5.11, 6.22, 5.9, 2.7, CN1, CN3, 10.11, D10.1.2, 10.75

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is minor.
result.proof:
**Statement.** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome, the "side" of the area is minor.

**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the fourth apotome AD, the angle at A being right and B the vertex opposite A. Let DG be the annex to AD, so that G lies on AD produced and AD is the remainder when DG is subtracted from AG. Since AD is an apotome, AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.73]; and since AD is a fourth apotome, the whole AG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on AG is greater than the square on the annex DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG [D10.3.4].

**Step 2.** DG, being a part of AG, is less than AG [CN5]. Bisect DG at E [1.10], so that the square on EG is the fourth part of the square on DG. To AG apply a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; this is possible because EG, the half of DG, is less than the half of AG. Let the applied parallelogram be the rectangle contained by AF, FG, with F on AG; thus rect(AF, FG) = sq(EG). Since the square on AG exceeds the square on DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AG, and a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square has been applied to AG, it divides AG into parts incommensurable in length: AF is incommensurable in length with FG [10.18]. AF and FG are therefore unequal; let the lettering be such that AF is the greater.

**Step 3.** Through E, F, G draw EH, FI, GK parallel to AC [1.31], and produce CB [P2] to meet them at H, I, K. The figures AK, AB, DK, AI, FK, EK, DH are then rectangles, each contained by a straight line equal to AC [1.34] and by AG, AD, DG, AF, FG, EG, DE respectively. Since AG is cut at D, AG is cut at F, and DG is cut at E, we have AK = AB + DK, AK = AI + FK, and DK = DH + EK [2.1]; and because DE = EG, the rectangle DH is equal to the rectangle EK, so that DK = 2·EK.

**Step 4.** AG is rational and commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC; therefore the rectangle AK contained by them is rational [10.19].

**Step 5.** AG is commensurable in length with AC (Step 1) but incommensurable in length with DG, since AG, GD are commensurable in square only (Step 1); therefore AC is incommensurable in length with DG [10.13]. Now DG is rational, that is, commensurable with the rational straight line AC set out either in length or in square only [D10.1.3]; being incommensurable in length with AC, it is commensurable in square only with AC. Thus AC, DG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and the rectangle DK contained by them is medial, that is, equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21].

**Step 6.** The rectangles AI, FK have equal heights (lines equal to AC) and bases AF, FG; therefore AI : FK = AF : FG [6.1]. Since AF is incommensurable in length with FG, AI is incommensurable with FK [10.11].

**Step 7.** Construct a square LM equal to the rectangle AI [2.14], and let LP be one of its sides, P being a vertex. Since AF > FG, the rectangle FK, contained by FG and a line equal to AC, is equal to a part of the rectangle AI, contained by AF and a line equal to AC; hence FK < AI [CN5]. Construct also a straight line whose square is equal to FK [2.14]; this line is less than LP, for otherwise its square would not be less than the square on LP, i.e. FK would not be less than AI. Cut off from PL a part PN equal to this line [1.3], so that N lies between P and L. Thus sq(LP) = AI, sq(PN) = FK, and LN is the excess of LP over PN.

**Step 8.** I say that rect(LP, PN) = EK. The square on AF and the rectangle contained by AF, FG have the same height AF; therefore sq(AF) : rect(AF, FG) = AF : FG [6.1], that is, sq(AF) : sq(EG) = AF : FG, because rect(AF, FG) = sq(EG) (Step 2). Also sq(LP) : sq(PN) = AI : FK = AF : FG (Steps 6, 7). Therefore sq(LP) : sq(PN) = sq(AF) : sq(EG) [5.11]. These are similar figures similarly described on the four straight lines LP, PN, AF, EG, all squares being similar [D6.1]; therefore LP : PN = AF : EG [6.22]. Again, since rect(AF, FG) = sq(EG), AF : EG = EG : FG [6.17]; and EG : FG = EK : FK, the rectangles EK, FK having the common height GK and bases EG, FG [6.1]. Hence LP : PN = EK : FK [5.11]. But rect(LP, PN) : sq(PN) = LP : PN, these two figures having the common height PN and bases LP, PN [6.1]; therefore rect(LP, PN) : sq(PN) = EK : FK [5.11]. And sq(PN) = FK; so rect(LP, PN) and EK have the same ratio to FK, whence rect(LP, PN) = EK [5.9].

**Step 9.** Since LP is cut at N, sq(LP) + sq(PN) = 2·rect(LP, PN) + sq(LN) [2.7]. Substituting from Steps 7 and 8, AI + FK = 2·EK + sq(LN), that is, by Step 3, AK = DK + sq(LN). But also AK = AB + DK (Step 3). Taking away the common DK, AB = sq(LN) [CN3]. Therefore LN is the "side" of the area AB [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** I say that LN is minor. (a) sq(LP) = AI and sq(PN) = FK are incommensurable with one another (Step 6); therefore LP, PN are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2]. (b) sq(LP) + sq(PN) = AI + FK = AK, which is rational (Step 4). (c) rect(LP, PN) = EK, and DK = 2·EK (Step 3), so EK measures DK and is commensurable with it [D10.1.1]; DK is medial (Step 5); therefore EK, being an area commensurable with a medial area, is medial [10.23]. Thus from the straight line LP there has been subtracted a straight line PN incommensurable in square with LP, such that the squares on LP, PN added together are rational while the rectangle contained by them is medial; therefore the remainder LN is the irrational straight line called minor [10.76].

**Step 11.** LN is the "side" of the area AB (Step 9) and LN is minor (Step 10). Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome, the "side" of the area is minor. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 10.73, D10.3.4, CN5, 1.10, 6.28, 10.18, 1.31, P2, 1.34, 2.1, 10.19, 10.13, D10.1.3, 10.21, 6.1, 10.11, 2.14, 1.3, D6.1, 6.22, 6.17, 5.11, 5.9, 2.7, CN3, D10.1.4, D10.1.2, D10.1.1, 10.23, 10.76

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fifth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
result.proof:
**Statement.** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fifth apotome, the "side" of the area is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.

Notation: sq(XY) denotes the square on XY, and rect(XY, ZW) the rectangle contained by XY, ZW.

**Step 1.** Let the area AB be the rectangle contained by the rational straight line AC and the fifth apotome AD, the angle at A being right, AC being the rational straight line set out with respect to which AD is a fifth apotome. Let DG be the annex to the apotome AD, so that AG is the whole straight line from which the annex DG is subtracted to leave AD; thus D lies between A and G. By the definition of an apotome [10.73], AG and DG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Since AD is a fifth apotome [D10.3.5], the annex DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on the whole AG is greater than the square on the annex DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG.

**Step 2.** Bisect DG at E [1.10]. Since DG is a part of AG, DG is less than AG [CN5]; hence EG, the half of DG, is less than the half of AG, and sq(EG) is less than the square on the half of AG. Therefore [6.28] a parallelogram equal to sq(EG) and deficient by a square figure can be applied to AG; let it be so applied, and let F be the point at which it cuts AG, so that the applied parallelogram is rect(AF, FG) and rect(AF, FG) = sq(EG). Since DG is double EG, sq(EG) is the fourth part of sq(DG).

**Step 3.** Thus AG, DG are two unequal straight lines, of which AG is the greater; the square on AG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AG [Step 1]; and to AG there has been applied a parallelogram, rect(AF, FG), equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, DG, and deficient by a square figure [Step 2]. Therefore [10.18] it divides AG into parts which are incommensurable: AF is incommensurable in length with FG.

**Step 4.** Through G, E, F draw GK, EH, FI parallel to AC [1.31], and produce CB [P2] to meet them at K, H, I. Then AK = rect(AC, AG), and AB, DK, DH, EK, AI, FK are respectively rect(AC, AD), rect(AC, DG), rect(AC, DE), rect(AC, EG), rect(AC, AF), rect(AC, FG); all of them lie between the same parallels AG, CK. The rectangle AK is composed of AB and DK, and also of AI and FK; the rectangle DK is composed of DH and EK. Since DE = EG [Step 2], the parallelograms DH, EK are on equal bases and in the same parallels, so DH = EK [1.36]; hence DK is double EK.

**Step 5.** AK is medial. AG is rational, so it is commensurable in square with the rational straight line AC set out [D10.1.3]. AG and DG, being commensurable in square only [Step 1], are incommensurable in length, while DG is commensurable in length with AC [Step 1]; since DG, AC are commensurable and DG is incommensurable with AG, AC is incommensurable in length with AG [10.13]. Hence AG, AC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and the rectangle AK contained by them is medial, that is, AK is equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21].

**Step 6.** DK is rational. DG and AC are rational straight lines commensurable in length [Step 1]; therefore the rectangle DK contained by them is rational [10.19].

**Step 7.** AI is incommensurable with FK. AI and FK are parallelograms under the same height, between the parallels AG, CK, with bases AF, FG; therefore AI : FK = AF : FG [6.1]. Since AF is incommensurable with FG [Step 3], AI is incommensurable with FK [10.11].

**Step 8.** Construct a square equal to AI [2.14] and let LP be its side, so that sq(LP) = AI; construct a square equal to FK [2.14]. The squares AI, FK are incommensurable [Step 7] and hence unequal, since equal magnitudes are measured by the same measure and so are commensurable [D10.1.1]; therefore the sides of these two squares are unequal. Let the greater be LP, the side of the square equal to AI (if the side of the square equal to FK is the greater, the argument below is the same with AF and FG interchanged throughout, all that has been proved so far being symmetric in AF and FG). From LP cut off PN equal to the side of the square equal to FK [1.3]; then sq(PN) = FK, and N lies on LP between L and P, so that LN is the remainder when PN is subtracted from LP.

**Step 9.** LP : PN = AF : EG. The square on AF and the rectangle rect(AF, FG) are parallelograms under the same height AF with bases AF, FG; hence AF : FG = sq(AF) : rect(AF, FG) [6.1], and since rect(AF, FG) = sq(EG) [Step 2], AF : FG = sq(AF) : sq(EG) [5.7]. Also AF : FG = AI : FK [Step 7], and AI = sq(LP), FK = sq(PN) [Step 8], so AF : FG = sq(LP) : sq(PN) [5.7]. Therefore sq(LP) : sq(PN) = sq(AF) : sq(EG) [5.11]. These are similar figures similarly described on the four straight lines LP, PN, AF, EG, and they are proportional; therefore the straight lines themselves are proportional: LP : PN = AF : EG [6.22].

**Step 10.** rect(LP, PN) = EK. The square on LP and the rectangle rect(LP, PN) are parallelograms under the same height LP with bases LP, PN; hence LP : PN = sq(LP) : rect(LP, PN) [6.1]. Again, AI and EK are parallelograms under the same height between the parallels AG, CK with bases AF, EG; hence AF : EG = AI : EK [6.1], and since AI = sq(LP), AF : EG = sq(LP) : EK [5.7]. By Step 9, LP : PN = AF : EG; therefore sq(LP) : rect(LP, PN) = sq(LP) : EK [5.11]. Magnitudes to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal; therefore rect(LP, PN) = EK [5.9].

**Step 11.** LN is the "side" of AB. The straight line LP is cut at N; therefore [2.7] sq(LP) + sq(PN) = 2·rect(LP, PN) + sq(LN). Now sq(LP) = AI and sq(PN) = FK [Step 8], so sq(LP) + sq(PN) = AI + FK = AK [CN2, Step 4]; and rect(LP, PN) = EK [Step 10], so 2·rect(LP, PN) = 2·EK = DK [CN2, Step 4]. Therefore AK = DK + sq(LN) [CN1]. But AK is composed of AB and DK [Step 4], so AB + DK = DK + sq(LN); subtracting DK from both, sq(LN) = AB [CN3]. Thus the square on LN is equal to the area AB, that is, LN is the "side" of AB [D10.1.4].

**Step 12.** LN produces with a rational area a medial whole. (i) sq(LP) = AI and sq(PN) = FK are incommensurable [Step 7]; hence LP, PN are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2]. (ii) sq(LP) + sq(PN) = AK [Step 11], which is medial [Step 5]; so the sum of the squares on LP, PN is medial. (iii) 2·rect(LP, PN) = DK [Step 11], which is rational [Step 6]; so twice the rectangle contained by LP, PN is rational. Thus from the straight line LP there has been subtracted the straight line PN, which is incommensurable in square with the whole LP and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial but twice the rectangle contained by them rational; therefore the remainder LN is the irrational straight line called that which produces with a rational area a medial whole [10.77]. And LN is the "side" of the area AB [Step 11]. Therefore the "side" of an area contained by a rational straight line and a fifth apotome is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. QED.

result.statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.96
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, the "side" of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a rational straight line, AD a sixth apotome, and let the area AC be the rectangle contained by AB, AD. Let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG is the whole from which the annex GD is subtracted; then, AD being an apotome, AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and GD is less than AG (10.73). Since AD is a sixth apotome, neither AG nor GD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB set out, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG (D10.3.6).

**Step 2.** Bisect DG at E (1.10). Since DG is less than AG, EG is less than the half of AG, so that the square on EG is less than the square on the half of AG; therefore to AG there can be applied a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure (6.28). Let it be applied, and let it be the rectangle contained by AF, FG, the defect being the square on FG; by the construction FG is less than the half of AG, so that AF is greater than FG. Also DE is equal to EG.

**Step 3.** Since DG is double of EG, the square on EG is the fourth part of the square on DG. Thus AG, DG are two unequal straight lines, and to the greater, AG, there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, DG, and deficient by a square figure; and the square on AG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AG (Step 1). Therefore the applied parallelogram divides AG into parts which are incommensurable (10.18): AF is incommensurable in length with FG.

**Step 4.** Let BC be produced (P2), and through E, F, G let EH, FI, GK be drawn parallel to AB (1.31), meeting BC produced in H, I, K. Then AK, AI, FK, DH, EK, DK and AC are rectangles of the same height AB standing on the bases AG, AF, FG, DE, EG, DG and AD respectively; AK is made up of AI and FK, and also of AC and DK; and DK is made up of DH and EK.

**Step 5.** AK and DK are medial. AG is rational (Step 1); hence AG is commensurable with the rational straight line AB either in length or in square only (D10.1.3). But AG is incommensurable in length with AB (Step 1). Therefore AB, AG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and the rectangle AK contained by them is medial (10.21). In the same way DG is rational and incommensurable in length with AB, so that AB, DG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and the rectangle DK contained by them is medial (10.21).

**Step 6.** AI is incommensurable with FK. The rectangles AI, FK have the same height; therefore, as AF is to FG, so is AI to FK (6.1). But AF is incommensurable with FG (Step 3); therefore AI is incommensurable with FK (10.11). Moreover, since AF is greater than FG, AI is greater than FK.

**Step 7.** AK is incommensurable with DK. As AG is to GD, so is AK to DK (6.1); and AG is incommensurable in length with GD, being commensurable with it in square only (Step 1); therefore AK is incommensurable with DK (10.11).

**Step 8.** Let the square LM be constructed equal to AI (2.14), P being one of its vertices, PL and PM the sides at P, and R the vertex opposite to P; and, since FK is less than AI (Step 6), let the square NO equal to FK (2.14) be taken away from LM so as to have with it the common angle LPM, N lying on PL, O on PM, and Q being the vertex of NO opposite to P. Since from the square LM the square NO, similar to it and having a common angle with it, has been taken away, LM and NO are about the same diameter (6.26); let PR be that diameter, so that Q lies on PR. Let NQ be produced to meet MR at S, and OQ produced to meet LR at T (P2). Then LM is divided into four parts: the square NO; the parallelograms NT (contained by NL, NQ) and OS (contained by OQ, QS), which are the complements about the diameter PR; and the parallelogram QR. In QR, QT is equal to NL and QS is equal to OM (1.34), while NL is the excess of PL over PN and OM is the excess of PM over PO, that is, of PL over PN, since PM = PL and PO = PN; hence QR, being right-angled with the adjacent sides QT, QS each equal to LN, is the square on LN. Further, the rectangle MN (that is, PNSM) is contained by PN, PM and is made up of NO and OS; the rectangle LO (that is, PLTO) is contained by PL, PO and is made up of NO and NT.

**Step 9.** EK is a mean proportional between AI and FK. The rectangle contained by AF, FG is equal to the square on EG (Step 2); therefore, as AF is to EG, so is EG to FG (6.17). But, the rectangles having the same height AB, as AF is to EG, so is AI to EK, and as EG is to FG, so is EK to FK (6.1). Therefore, as AI is to EK, so is EK to FK (5.11).

**Step 10.** MN is a mean proportional between LM and NO. LM and MN have the same height PM and stand on the bases PL, PN; therefore, as PL is to PN, so is LM to MN (6.1). Again, MN and NO have the same base PN and the heights PM, PO; therefore, as PM is to PO, so is MN to NO (6.1); and PM = PL, PO = PN, so that, as PL is to PN, so is MN to NO. Therefore, as LM is to MN, so is MN to NO (5.11).

**Step 11.** MN is equal to EK. Since LM is equal to AI and NO to FK, Step 9 gives: as LM is to EK, so is EK to NO. Suppose MN greater than EK. Then MN has to NO a greater ratio than EK has to NO, and LM has to EK a greater ratio than LM has to MN (5.8). But the ratio of LM to EK is the same as that of EK to NO, and the ratio of LM to MN is the same as that of MN to NO (Step 10); therefore EK has to NO a greater ratio than MN has to NO (5.13), which contradicts the former conclusion. In the same way MN cannot be less than EK. Therefore MN is equal to EK.

**Step 12.** DK is equal to NO, NO, OS, NT taken together. Since DE = EG (Step 2), the rectangles DH, EK, being on equal bases and in the same parallels, are equal (1.36). Hence DK, which is DH together with EK, is equal to EK taken twice, that is, to MN taken twice (Step 11, CN2). Now MN is NO together with OS (Step 8), and the complements OS, NT about the diameter PR are equal (1.43); therefore MN taken twice is equal to NO, NO, OS, NT taken together (CN2). Thus DK is equal to NO, NO, OS, NT taken together.

**Step 13.** LN is the "side" of AC. AK is AI together with FK, that is, LM together with NO (CN2); and LM is made up of NO, NT, OS, QR (Step 8); so AK is equal to NO, NO, NT, OS, QR taken together. But AK is also AC together with DK (Step 4). Taking away DK, which is equal to NO, NO, OS, NT taken together (Step 12), the remainder AC is equal to the remaining part QR (CN3), which is the square on LN (Step 8). Therefore the square on LN is equal to the area AC, that is, LN is the "side" of AC.

**Step 14.** The sum of the squares on LP, PN is medial. The squares on LP, PN are LM and NO, and LM together with NO is equal to AK (Step 13), which is medial (Step 5).

**Step 15.** Twice the rectangle contained by LP, PN is medial. MN is the rectangle contained by PN, PM, that is, by PN, PL, since PM = PL (Step 8); and DK is equal to twice MN (Step 12), DK being medial (Step 5). Therefore twice the rectangle LP, PN is medial.

**Step 16.** LP, PN are incommensurable in square. The square on LP is LM, equal to AI, and the square on PN is NO, equal to FK; and AI is incommensurable with FK (Step 6). Therefore the squares on LP, PN are incommensurable, that is, LP, PN are incommensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 17.** The sum of the squares on LP, PN is incommensurable with twice the rectangle LP, PN, for the former is AK and the latter is DK (Steps 14, 15), and AK is incommensurable with DK (Step 7).

**Step 18.** Now LN is the remainder when PN is subtracted from PL. From the straight line PL there has been subtracted the straight line PN which is incommensurable in square with the whole PL (Step 16), and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 14), twice the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 15), and the squares on them incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them (Step 17); therefore the remainder LN is the irrational straight line called that which produces with a medial area a medial whole (10.78). And LN is the "side" of the area AC (Step 13). Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, the "side" of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on an apotome applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a first apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be an apotome and CD a rational straight line. To CD apply the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB, producing CF as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. We must show that CF is a first apotome.

**Step 2.** Let BG be the annex to AB, so that AG is the whole straight line from which BG was subtracted to leave AB. Since AB is an apotome, AG and GB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.73].

**Step 3.** To CD apply the rectangle CH equal to the square on AG, producing CK as breadth, and adjoining it apply the rectangle KL equal to the square on GB, producing KM as breadth [1.44, 1.45], so that the whole CL is one rectangle applied to CD with breadth CM, and CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB together.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AG is cut at B, the squares on AG, GB together are equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Hence CL is equal to CE together with twice the rectangle AG, GB. Therefore CL is greater than CE [CN5], so that CF is less than CM and F falls between C and M; and, subtracting CE from CL, the remainder FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB [CN3].

**Step 5.** Bisect FM at N [1.10] and through N draw NO parallel to CD [1.31], meeting DL at O. The parallelograms FO and NL stand on the equal bases FN, NM and lie between the same parallels FM, EL; therefore FO is equal to NL [1.36]. Since FO and NL together make up FL, which is twice the rectangle AG, GB, each of FO, NL is equal to the rectangle AG, GB.

**Step 6.** Since AG and GB are rational, each is commensurable with the assigned rational straight line, so the squares on them are commensurable with the rational square and are rational areas [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]. Moreover, since AG, GB are commensurable in square, the squares on them are measured by the same area and so are commensurable with one another [D10.1.2, D10.1.1]. Hence the sum of the squares on AG, GB is commensurable with the square on AG [10.15], and therefore with the rational square [10.12]; that is, CL is a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** The rational area CL is applied to the rational straight line CD, producing CM as breadth; therefore CM is rational and commensurable in length with CD [10.20].

**Step 8.** Since AG, GB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle AG, GB is irrational and the side of the square equal to it is medial [10.21]; thus the rectangle AG, GB is a medial area, incommensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4]. Twice the rectangle AG, GB is measured by the rectangle AG, GB, so the two are commensurable [D10.1.1]; hence FL, being twice the rectangle AG, GB, is an area commensurable with a medial area and is therefore itself medial, that is, equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.23]. Further, FL, being commensurable with the rectangle AG, GB, which is incommensurable with the rational square, is itself incommensurable with the rational square [10.13].

**Step 9.** FL, equal to the square on a medial straight line, is applied to the rational straight line CD, producing FM as breadth; therefore FM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 10.** CL is commensurable with the rational square (Step 6), while FL is incommensurable with it (Step 8); therefore CL is incommensurable with FL [10.13]. But CL and FL are rectangles of the same height, namely CD, so CL is to FL as CM is to FM [6.1]. Therefore CM is incommensurable in length with FM [10.11].

**Step 11.** CM and MF are both rational (Steps 7 and 9), so the squares on them are rational areas, each commensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4]; hence the squares on CM, MF are commensurable with one another [10.12], that is, CM, MF are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Since they are incommensurable in length (Step 10), CM, MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore CF, the remainder when MF is subtracted from CM, is an apotome, with whole CM and annex MF [10.73].

**Step 12.** It remains to show that CF is a first apotome. Since the square on AG and the rectangle AG, GB have the common side AG, the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as AG is to GB [6.1]; likewise the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB as AG is to GB [6.1]. Therefore the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB [5.11]. Now CH is equal to the square on AG, NL to the rectangle AG, GB, and KL to the square on GB, and equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude [5.7]; therefore CH is to NL as NL is to KL. But CH is to NL as CK is to NM, and NL is to KL as NM is to KM [6.1]; therefore CK is to NM as NM is to KM [5.11], so that the rectangle CK, KM is equal to the square on NM [6.17].

**Step 13.** Since FM is bisected at N, the square on FM is equal to the squares on FN, NM together with twice the rectangle FN, NM [2.4], and since FN is equal to NM this is four times the square on NM. Hence the rectangle CK, KM, being equal to the square on NM, is the fourth part of the square on FM.

**Step 14.** Since the squares on AG, GB are commensurable with one another (Step 6), CH is commensurable with KL; and CH is to KL as CK is to KM [6.1]; therefore CK is commensurable in length with KM [10.11].

**Step 15.** Now CM and FM are two unequal straight lines, FM being a part of CM and therefore the less [CN5]. To the greater, CM, there has been applied the rectangle CK, KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, FM, and deficient by the square on KM, and it divides CM into the parts CK, KM, which are commensurable in length. Therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on FM by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CM [10.17].

**Step 16.** Thus CF is an apotome whose whole CM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD set out (Step 7), and the square on the whole CM is greater than the square on the annex MF by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CM (Step 15). Therefore CF is a first apotome [D10.3.1]. Hence the square on an apotome applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a first apotome. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on a first apotome of a medial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a second apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a first apotome of a medial straight line and CD a rational straight line, and to CD let there be applied the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB, producing CF as breadth [1.45]. We show that CF is a second apotome.

**Step 2.** Let BG be the annex to AB, so that AG is the whole and GB the annex. Since AB is a first apotome of a medial straight line, AG and GB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a rational rectangle AG·GB [10.74].

**Step 3.** To CD apply the rectangle CH equal to the square on AG, producing CK as breadth, and to KH apply the rectangle KL equal to the square on GB, producing KM as breadth [1.45]. Then the whole rectangle CL, contained by CD and CM, is equal to the sum of the squares on AG and GB.

**Step 4.** Since AG and GB are commensurable in square, the square on AG is commensurable with the square on GB [D10.1.2]. Hence their sum CL is commensurable with the square on AG [10.15]. But AG is medial, so the square on AG is a medial area [10.21]; therefore CL, being commensurable with a medial area, is itself medial [10.23, Porism].

**Step 5.** CL is thus a medial area applied to the rational straight line CD producing CM as breadth; therefore CM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 6.** Since the straight line AG is cut at B, the squares on AG and GB together are equal to twice the rectangle AG·GB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Now CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB, and CE is equal to the square on AB; subtracting equals from equals, the remainder FL (the rectangle contained by FE, which equals CD, and FM) is equal to twice the rectangle AG·GB [CN3].

**Step 7.** The rectangle AG·GB is rational, hence so is its double FL. FL is therefore a rational area applied to the rational straight line FE, equal to CD, producing FM as breadth; therefore FM is rational and commensurable in length with CD [10.20].

**Step 8.** FL, being rational, is commensurable with the square on CD [D10.1.4], while CL, being medial and hence irrational, is incommensurable with the square on CD [10.21, D10.1.4]. Since FL is commensurable with the square on CD and the square on CD is incommensurable with CL, FL is incommensurable with CL [10.13].

**Step 9.** The rectangles CL and FL have the same height CD, so as CL is to FL, so is CM to FM [6.1]. Since CL is incommensurable with FL, CM is incommensurable in length with FM [10.11].

**Step 10.** CM and FM are both rational straight lines, so each is commensurable at least in square with CD [D10.1.3]; hence the squares on CM and FM, being each commensurable with the square on CD, are commensurable with one another [10.12], while by Step 9 CM and FM are incommensurable in length. Thus CM and MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and CM, being the whole, is greater than its part MF [CN5]. Therefore CF, the remainder when MF is subtracted from CM, is an apotome [10.73], with whole CM and annex MF.

**Step 11.** To determine its order, bisect FM at N [1.10] and through N draw NO parallel to CD, meeting EL at O [1.31]. The parallelograms FO and NL stand on the equal bases FN, NM and lie in the same parallels FM, EL, so they are equal [1.36]; since together they make up FL, which is twice the rectangle AG·GB, each of FO and NL is equal to the rectangle AG·GB.

**Step 12.** By 6.1, the square on AG is to the rectangle AG·GB as AG is to GB, and the rectangle AG·GB is to the square on GB as AG is to GB; hence the square on AG is to the rectangle AG·GB as the rectangle AG·GB is to the square on GB [5.11], i.e. the rectangle AG·GB is a mean proportional between the squares on AG and GB. Since CH equals the square on AG, NL equals the rectangle AG·GB, and KL equals the square on GB, it follows that as CH is to NL, so is NL to KL.

**Step 13.** Again, since CH, NL have the same height, as CH is to NL so is CK to NM, and since NL, KL have the same height, as NL is to KL so is NM to KM [6.1]. Therefore as CK is to NM, so is NM to KM [5.11], and so the rectangle CK·KM is equal to the square on NM [6.17]. Since FM is bisected at N, the square on FM is four times the square on NM [2.4]; hence the rectangle CK·KM is equal to the fourth part of the square on FM.

**Step 14.** Since the square on AG is commensurable with the square on GB (Step 4), CH is commensurable with KL; and as CH is to KL, so is CK to KM [6.1]; therefore CK is commensurable in length with KM [10.11].

**Step 15.** Now CM and MF are two unequal straight lines, CM being the greater, and to CM there has been applied the parallelogram CK·KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less MF and deficient by the square figure on KM, and it divides CM at K into parts CK, KM which are commensurable in length. Therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on MF by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CM [10.17].

**Step 16.** Thus CF is an apotome (Step 10) whose annex MF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD (Step 7), and the square on the whole CM is greater than the square on the annex MF by the square on a straight line commensurable with CM (Step 15). Therefore CF is a second apotome [D10.3.2]. Hence the square on a first apotome of a medial straight line, applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a second apotome. QED.

result.statement: The square on a second apotome of a medial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a third apotome.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.99
**Statement:** The square on a second apotome of a medial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a third apotome.

Let AB be a second apotome of a medial straight line, let CD be a rational straight line, and to CD let there be applied the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB, producing CF as breadth (1.45). I say that CF is a third apotome.

**Step 1.** Let BG be the annex to AB. Then AG, GB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle (10.75).

**Step 2.** To CD apply the rectangle CH equal to the square on AG, producing CK as breadth, and the rectangle KL equal to the square on BG, producing KM as breadth (1.45). Then the whole CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB together (CN2), and its breadth is CM.

**Step 3.** Since AG, GB are commensurable in square, the squares on AG, GB are commensurable (D10.1.2); hence their sum CL is commensurable with the square on AG (10.15). The square on AG is a medial area, since AG is medial (10.21); therefore CL, being commensurable with a medial area, is medial (10.23, Porism).

**Step 4.** CL, a medial area, is applied to the rational straight line CD; therefore CM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD (10.22).

**Step 5.** Since the straight line AG is cut at B, the squares on AG, GB together are equal to twice the rectangle AG·GB together with the square on AB (2.7). But CE is equal to the square on AB and CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB. Therefore the remainder FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG·GB (CN3), and its breadth is FM.

**Step 6.** The rectangle AG·GB is medial (Step 1). Twice the rectangle AG·GB has to the rectangle AG·GB the ratio 2 : 1, which a number has to a number; therefore they are commensurable (10.6), and hence FL is medial (10.23, Porism). FL is applied to the rational straight line CD; therefore FM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD (10.22).

**Step 7.** Since AG, GB are commensurable in square only, AG is incommensurable in length with GB. The square on AG is to the rectangle AG·GB as AG is to GB (6.1); therefore the square on AG is incommensurable with the rectangle AG·GB (10.11). CL is commensurable with the square on AG (Step 3), so CL is incommensurable with the rectangle AG·GB (10.13); and FL is commensurable with the rectangle AG·GB (Step 6), so FL is incommensurable with CL (10.13).

**Step 8.** CL is to FL as CM is to FM, since they are rectangles of the same height CD (6.1); therefore CM is incommensurable in length with FM (10.11).

**Step 9.** CM and FM are each rational, so each is commensurable in square with CD (D10.1.3); hence the squares on CM and FM, being each commensurable with the square on CD, are commensurable with one another (10.12). Thus CM, FM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Since FM is a part of CM, CM is greater than FM (CN5). Therefore CF, the remainder when FM is subtracted from CM, is an apotome (10.73), CM being the whole and FM the annex.

**Step 10.** I say next that it is a third apotome. Neither CM nor FM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD (Steps 4 and 6).

**Step 11.** Since the squares on AG, GB are commensurable (Step 3), CH is commensurable with KL. CH is to KL as CK is to KM (6.1); therefore CK is commensurable in length with KM (10.11).

**Step 12.** Bisect FM at N (1.10), and through N draw NO parallel to CD (1.31). Then FO, NL are parallelograms on the equal bases FN, NM and in the same parallels, so FO is equal to NL (1.36); hence each is half of FL, that is, NL is equal to the rectangle AG·GB.

**Step 13.** The square on AG is to the rectangle AG·GB as AG is to GB, and the rectangle AG·GB is to the square on GB as AG is to GB (6.1); therefore the square on AG is to the rectangle AG·GB as the rectangle AG·GB is to the square on GB (5.11). That is, CH is to NL as NL is to KL.

**Step 14.** CH is to NL as CK is to NM, and NL is to KL as NM is to KM (6.1); therefore CK is to NM as NM is to KM (5.11). Hence the rectangle CK·KM is equal to the square on NM (6.17).

**Step 15.** Since FM is bisected at N, the square on FM is equal to the squares on FN, NM together with twice the rectangle FN·NM, that is, to four times the square on NM (2.4); therefore the rectangle CK·KM is equal to the fourth part of the square on FM.

**Step 16.** Thus, of the two unequal straight lines CM, FM, to the greater CM there has been applied the parallelogram CK·KM equal to the fourth part of the square on the less FM and deficient by the square on KM, and it divides CM into the parts CK, KM which are commensurable in length (Step 11). Therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on FM by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CM (10.17).

**Step 17.** Therefore CF is an apotome whose whole CM and annex FM are neither of them commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD, while the square on the whole CM exceeds the square on the annex FM by the square on a straight line commensurable with CM. Hence CF is a third apotome (D10.3.3).
