Therefore the square on a second apotome of a medial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a third apotome. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 10.75, 1.45, CN2, D10.1.2, 10.15, 10.21, 10.23, 10.22, 2.7, CN3, 10.6, 6.1, 10.11, 10.13, D10.1.3, 10.12, CN5, 10.73, 1.10, 1.31, 1.36, 5.11, 6.17, 2.4, 10.17, D10.3.3

result.statement: The square on a minor straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a fourth apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a minor straight line and CD a rational straight line. To CD let there be applied, in a right angle, the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB, producing CF as breadth [1.44]. I say that CF is a fourth apotome.

**Step 2.** Let BG be the annex to AB, so that AB is the remainder when GB is subtracted from AG. By the definition of a minor straight line, AG and GB are incommensurable in square, the squares on AG, GB added together are rational, and the rectangle contained by AG, GB is medial [10.76].

**Step 3.** To CD apply the rectangle CH equal to the square on AG, producing CK as breadth, and adjacent to it (on KH, which equals CD [1.34]) the rectangle KL equal to the square on GB, producing KM as breadth [1.44]. Then the whole CL equals the squares on AG, GB together [CN2], and CL is applied to CD producing CM as breadth.

**Step 4.** The squares on AG, GB together are rational (Step 2); therefore CL is a rational area. It is applied to the rational straight line CD; therefore its breadth CM is rational and commensurable in length with CD [10.20].

**Step 5.** Since AG is cut at B, the squares on AG, GB together equal twice the rectangle AG, GB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Now the whole CL equals the squares on AG, GB, and its part CE equals the square on AB; therefore the remainder FL equals twice the rectangle AG, GB [CN3]. Thus CE is less than CL, F lies between C and M, and FL is the rectangle contained by FE and FM.

**Step 6.** The rectangle AG, GB is medial (Step 2). Twice that rectangle is measured by it and so is commensurable with it [D10.1.1]; and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23]. Therefore FL is medial. Its side FE equals CD [1.34] and is therefore rational; and FL is applied to FE producing FM as breadth. Therefore FM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 7.** CM is commensurable in length with CD (Step 4), while FM is incommensurable in length with CD (Step 6); therefore CM is incommensurable in length with FM [10.13]. Both CM and FM are rational, so the square on each is commensurable with the square on CD [D10.1.3]; hence the squares on CM, FM are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Therefore CM, MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Also MF is less than CM, being a part of it [CN5]. Hence, MF being subtracted from CM, the remainder CF is an apotome, with whole CM and annex MF [10.73].

**Step 8.** I say next that CF is a fourth apotome. Since AG, GB are incommensurable in square, the squares on AG, GB are incommensurable [D10.1.2]; therefore CH, KL, which equal them, are incommensurable. But CH, KL stand under the same height CD, so CH is to KL as CK is to KM [6.1]; therefore CK is incommensurable in length with KM [10.11].

**Step 9.** Let FM be bisected at N [1.10], and through N let NO be drawn parallel to CD, meeting EL at O [1.31]. The parallelograms FO, NL stand on the equal bases FN, NM and lie in the same parallels FM, EL; therefore FO equals NL [1.36]. Hence NL is half of FL, that is, NL equals the rectangle AG, GB (Step 5). Moreover NO equals CD [1.34].

**Step 10.** The square on AG and the rectangle AG, GB stand under the same height AG, so the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as AG is to GB [6.1]; and the rectangle AG, GB and the square on GB stand under the same height GB, so the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB as AG is to GB [6.1]. Therefore the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB [5.11]; that is, CH is to NL as NL is to KL.

**Step 11.** CH and NL stand under the same height (CD equals NO), so CH is to NL as CK is to NM [6.1]; likewise NL is to KL as NM is to KM [6.1]. Therefore CK is to NM as NM is to KM [5.11]; hence the rectangle CK, KM equals the square on NM [6.17]. And since FM is double NM, the square on FM is four times the square on NM; therefore the rectangle CK, KM equals the fourth part of the square on FM.

**Step 12.** Thus CM, MF are two unequal straight lines, CM the greater; to the greater CM there has been applied the rectangle CK, KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less MF and deficient by the square on KM; and it divides CM into the parts CK, KM, which are incommensurable (Step 8). Therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on MF by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CM [10.18].

**Step 13.** CF is therefore an apotome whose whole CM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD set out (Step 4), and the square on the whole CM exceeds the square on the annex MF by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the whole (Step 12). Therefore CF is a fourth apotome [D10.3.4]. Hence the square on a minor straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a fourth apotome. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a fifth apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, let CD be a rational straight line, and to CD let there be applied the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB, producing CF as breadth. We show that CF is a fifth apotome.

**Step 2.** Let BG be the annex to AB, so that AB is the remainder when BG is subtracted from AG. Since AB produces with a rational area a medial whole, AG and GB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AG, GB is medial, and twice the rectangle AG, GB is rational [10.77].

**Step 3.** To CD let there be applied the rectangle CH equal to the square on AG, producing CK as breadth, and let there be applied KL equal to the square on GB, producing KM as breadth, so that CH and KL together form the rectangle CL contained by CD and CM [1.45]. Then the whole CL is equal to the sum of the squares on AG, GB, which is medial; so CL is a medial area.

**Step 4.** The medial area CL is applied to the rational straight line CD producing CM as breadth; therefore CM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 5.** Since AG is cut at B, the squares on AG, GB together are equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Now CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB, and CE, a part of CL, is equal to the square on AB; subtracting, the remainder FL, contained by CD and FM, is equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB [CN3], which is rational. Thus FL is a rational area applied to the rational straight line CD producing FM as breadth; therefore FM is rational and commensurable in length with CD [10.20].

**Step 6.** CM is incommensurable in length with CD while FM is commensurable in length with CD; therefore CM is incommensurable in length with FM [10.13]. Moreover CM and FM are both rational, so the square on each is commensurable with the square on CD [D10.1.3]; hence the squares on CM, FM are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Therefore CM, MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and CF, the remainder when MF is subtracted from CM, is an apotome [10.73], whose whole is CM and whose annex MF is commensurable in length with CD.

**Step 7.** Let FM be bisected at N [1.10], and through N let NO be drawn parallel to CD [1.31], cutting FL into the rectangles FO and NL. These stand on the equal bases FN, NM and lie in the same parallels, so FO is equal to NL [1.36]; together they make up FL, which is twice the rectangle AG, GB; hence NL is equal to the rectangle AG, GB.

**Step 8.** The square on AG and the rectangle AG, GB are parallelograms under the same height AG on the bases AG, GB, so the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as AG is to GB [6.1]; likewise the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB as AG is to GB [6.1]. Hence the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB [5.11]. Since CH, NL, KL are equal respectively to these three areas, CH is to NL as NL is to KL [5.7].

**Step 9.** CH, NL, KL are rectangles under the same height CD on the bases CK, NM, KM; so CH is to NL as CK is to NM, and NL is to KL as NM is to KM [6.1]. Therefore CK is to NM as NM is to KM [5.11], and the rectangle CK, KM is equal to the square on NM [6.17]. Since FM is double NM, the square on FM is four times the square on NM; so the rectangle CK, KM is the fourth part of the square on FM.

**Step 10.** AG, GB are incommensurable in square, so the square on AG is incommensurable with the square on GB [D10.1.2]; that is, CH is incommensurable with KL. But CH is to KL as CK is to KM [6.1]; therefore CK is incommensurable in length with KM [10.11].

**Step 11.** FM is a part of CM, so CM is the greater of the two unequal straight lines CM, FM [CN5]. To the greater, CM, there has been applied the parallelogram contained by CK, KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, FM, and deficient by the square on KM; and it divides CM at K into the parts CK, KM, which are incommensurable. Therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on FM by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CM [10.18].

**Step 12.** Thus CF is an apotome whose whole CM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD, whose annex MF is rational and commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD set out, and in which the square on the whole exceeds the square on the annex by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the whole. Therefore CF is a fifth apotome [D10.3.5]. Hence the square on the straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a fifth apotome. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a sixth apotome.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.102
**Statement:** The square on the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a sixth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, and let BG be the annex to it, so that AG is cut at B, AB is the remainder when GB is subtracted from AG, and AG, GB are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, twice the rectangle AG·GB medial, and the squares on AG, GB incommensurable with twice the rectangle AG·GB [10.78]. Let CD be a rational straight line. I say that the square on AB, applied to CD, produces as breadth a sixth apotome.

**Step 2.** To CD apply the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB, producing CF as breadth; to CD apply also the rectangle CK equal to the square on AG, producing CH as breadth, and adjoining it apply KL equal to the square on BG, producing HM as breadth, so that the whole rectangle CL has breadth CM [1.45]. Then CL is equal to the sum of the squares on AG, GB [CN2].

**Step 3.** Since the straight line AG is cut at B, the squares on AG, GB together are equal to twice the rectangle AG·GB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Therefore CL is equal to CE together with twice the rectangle AG·GB, so that CE is a part of CL, the point F lies on CM between C and M, and the remainder FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG·GB [CN3].

**Step 4.** The sum of the squares on AG, GB is medial; hence CL is a medial area, that is, an area equal to the square on a medial straight line, and it has been applied to the rational straight line CD. Therefore its breadth CM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 5.** Twice the rectangle AG·GB is medial; hence FL is a medial area, and it has been applied to the straight line FE, which is equal to CD [1.34] and is therefore rational. Therefore its breadth FM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 6.** The squares on AG, GB are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AG·GB; therefore CL is incommensurable with FL. But CL and FL are parallelograms under the same height, so CL : FL = CM : FM [6.1]; therefore CM is incommensurable in length with FM [10.11].

**Step 7.** Since CM and FM are each rational, each is commensurable with CD either in length or in square [D10.1.3], and in either case the square on CM and the square on FM are each commensurable with the square on CD [D10.1.2]; hence the square on CM is commensurable with the square on FM [10.12]. Thus CM, FM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Moreover FM is a part of CM, so CM is greater than FM [CN5]. Therefore CF, the remainder when FM is subtracted from CM, is an apotome [10.73], CM being its whole and FM its annex.

**Step 8.** Bisect FM at N [1.10], and through N draw NO parallel to CD [1.31], cutting FL into the rectangles FO and NL. Since FN is equal to NM and the rectangles FO, NL stand on these equal bases between the same parallels, FO is equal to NL [1.36]; hence NL is half of FL, that is, NL is equal to the rectangle AG·GB.

**Step 9.** Since the square on AG and the rectangle AG·GB are under the same height AG, AG : GB = square on AG : rectangle AG·GB [6.1]; and since the rectangle AG·GB and the square on GB are under the same height GB, AG : GB = rectangle AG·GB : square on GB [6.1]. Therefore square on AG : rectangle AG·GB = rectangle AG·GB : square on GB [5.11], that is, CK : NL = NL : KL. But CK : NL = CH : NM and NL : KL = NM : HM, since these rectangles are under the same height [6.1]; therefore CH : NM = NM : HM [5.11], so that the rectangle CH·HM is equal to the square on NM [6.17].

**Step 10.** Since FM is cut into the equal parts FN, NM, the square on FM is equal to the squares on FN, NM together with twice the rectangle FN·NM [2.4], that is, to four times the square on NM. Therefore the rectangle CH·HM, being equal to the square on NM, is the fourth part of the square on FM.

**Step 11.** Since AG, GB are incommensurable in square, the square on AG is incommensurable with the square on GB [D10.1.2], that is, CK is incommensurable with KL. But CK : KL = CH : HM, these rectangles being under the same height [6.1]; therefore CH is incommensurable in length with HM [10.11].

**Step 12.** Thus CM, FM are two unequal straight lines, CM being the greater, and to CM there has been applied the parallelogram CH·HM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less FM and deficient by the square on HM, and it divides CM into the parts CH, HM which are incommensurable in length. Therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on FM by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with CM [10.18].

**Step 13.** Therefore CF is an apotome whose whole CM and annex FM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, neither of which is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD set out (Steps 4 and 5), and the square on the whole CM is greater than the square on the annex FM by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CM (Step 12). Therefore CF is a sixth apotome [D10.3.6]. And CF is the breadth produced when CE, the square on AB, is applied to the rational straight line CD. Therefore the square on the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a sixth apotome. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 10.78, 1.45, CN2, 2.7, CN3, 10.22, 1.34, 6.1, 10.11, D10.1.3, D10.1.2, 10.12, CN5, 10.73, 1.10, 1.31, 1.36, 5.11, 6.17, 2.4, 10.18, D10.3.6

result.statement: A straight line commensurable in length with an apotome is an apotome and the same in order.
result.proof:
**Statement:** A straight line commensurable in length with an apotome is an apotome and the same in order.

**Step 1.** Let AB be an apotome, and let CD be a straight line commensurable in length with AB. Let G be the rational straight line set out, with reference to which the order of the apotome AB is assigned. Since AB is an apotome, let BE be the annex to it, so that E lies on AB produced beyond B, AE is the whole, and AE, EB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.73].

**Step 2.** Produce CD beyond D [P2], and on the produced line take DF such that, as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF [6.12]. Then F lies on CD produced beyond D, so that CF is made up of CD and DF, just as AE is made up of AB and BE.

**Step 3.** Since AB : CD = BE : DF, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents [5.12]; therefore (AB + BE) : (CD + DF) = AB : CD = BE : DF, that is, AE : CF = AB : CD = BE : DF.

**Step 4.** Now AB is commensurable in length with CD, and AB : CD = AE : CF; therefore AE is commensurable in length with CF [10.11]. Again AB : CD = BE : DF; therefore BE is commensurable in length with DF [10.11].

**Step 5.** Since CF is commensurable in length with AE, the square on CF has to the square on AE the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore the square on CF is commensurable with the square on AE [10.6]. Now AE is rational, that is, commensurable with G either in length or in square only [D10.1.3]; in the former case the square on AE is commensurable with the square on G by the same reasoning [10.9, 10.6], and in the latter case by definition [D10.1.2]. Hence the square on CF is commensurable with the square on G [10.12], so that CF is commensurable in square with G [D10.1.2] and is therefore rational [D10.1.3]. In exactly the same way, since DF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line EB, the square on DF is commensurable with the square on EB [10.9, 10.6], hence with the square on G [10.12], and DF is rational [D10.1.2, D10.1.3].

**Step 6.** The squares on CF, FD, being each commensurable with the square on G, are commensurable with one another [10.12]; thus CF, FD are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. But AE is incommensurable in length with EB (Step 1), and AE is commensurable with CF (Step 4); therefore CF is incommensurable in length with EB [10.13]. And EB is commensurable with DF (Step 4); therefore CF is incommensurable in length with DF [10.13]. Hence CF, FD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 7.** Therefore CD, which is the remainder when the rational straight line FD, commensurable with the whole in square only, is subtracted from the rational straight line CF, is an apotome [10.73], with whole CF and annex DF.

**Step 8.** Since AE : CF = BE : DF (Step 3), alternately AE : EB = CF : FD [5.16]. Now AE, EB being the whole and the annex of the apotome AB, the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on some straight line, which is either commensurable or incommensurable in length with AE.

**Step 9.** If the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on a straight line commensurable with AE, then, since AE : EB = CF : FD, the square on CF is also greater than the square on FD by the square on a straight line commensurable with CF [10.14]. And if the square on AE is greater than the square on EB by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE, then the square on CF is greater than the square on FD by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CF [10.14].

**Step 10.** Further, if AE is commensurable in length with G, then, since CF is commensurable in length with AE, CF is also commensurable in length with G [10.12]; if EB is commensurable in length with G, then likewise DF is commensurable in length with G [10.12]; and if neither AE nor EB is commensurable in length with G, then, since CF is commensurable with AE and DF with EB, neither CF nor DF is commensurable in length with G [10.13].

**Step 11.** Thus the whole CF and the annex DF of the apotome CD stand to G exactly as the whole AE and the annex EB of the apotome AB stand to G, both as regards the excess of the square on the whole over the square on the annex (Step 9) and as regards commensurability in length with G (Step 10). Therefore, if AB is a first apotome, so is CD [D10.3.1]; if a second, so is CD [D10.3.2]; if a third, so is CD [D10.3.3]; if a fourth, so is CD [D10.3.4]; if a fifth, so is CD [D10.3.5]; and if a sixth, so is CD [D10.3.6].

**Step 12.** Therefore CD is an apotome and the same in order with AB. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P2, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.3.1, D10.3.2, D10.3.3, D10.3.4, D10.3.5, D10.3.6, 5.12, 5.16, 6.12, 10.6, 10.9, 10.11, 10.12, 10.13, 10.14, 10.73

result.statement: A straight line commensurable with an apotome of a medial straight line is an apotome of a medial straight line and the same in order.
result.proof:
**Statement:** A straight line commensurable with an apotome of a medial straight line is an apotome of a medial straight line and the same in order.

Let AB be an apotome of a medial straight line, and let CD be commensurable in length with AB. I say that CD is also an apotome of a medial straight line and the same in order as AB.

**Step 1.** Since AB is an apotome of a medial straight line, it is either a first or a second apotome of a medial straight line. Let EB be the annex to it, so that the whole AE and the annex EB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only; and the rectangle AE·EB is rational if AB is a first apotome of a medial straight line [10.74], or medial if AB is a second apotome of a medial straight line [10.75]. Since AE, EB are commensurable in square only, the square on AE is commensurable with the square on EB, while AE is incommensurable in length with EB [D10.1.2].

**Step 2.** Let it be contrived that, as AB is to CD, so is EB to FD, F lying on CD produced, so that CF is the whole and FD the annex [6.12].

**Step 3.** Since AB : CD = EB : FD, and AB is commensurable with CD, therefore EB is commensurable in length with FD [10.11].

**Step 4.** Since AB : CD = EB : FD, alternately AB : EB = CD : FD [5.16]; hence componendo, AE : EB = CF : FD [5.18]; and alternately again, AE : CF = EB : FD [5.16].

**Step 5.** Since AE : CF = EB : FD, and EB is commensurable with FD, therefore AE is commensurable in length with CF [10.11].

**Step 6.** AE and EB are medial straight lines; CF is commensurable with AE and FD is commensurable with EB; therefore CF and FD are also medial straight lines [10.23].

**Step 7.** Since AE : EB = CF : FD, and AE is incommensurable in length with EB, therefore CF is incommensurable in length with FD [10.11]. Again, since AE : EB = CF : FD, the squares on them, being similar figures similarly described on proportional straight lines, are proportional: sq(AE) : sq(EB) = sq(CF) : sq(FD) [6.22]; and the square on AE is commensurable with the square on EB, so the square on CF is commensurable with the square on FD [10.11]. Therefore CF, FD are medial straight lines commensurable in square only [D10.1.2].

**Step 8.** The rectangles AE·EB and CF·EB stand under the same height EB, so rect(AE, EB) : rect(CF, EB) = AE : CF [6.1]; and AE is commensurable with CF; therefore rect(AE, EB) is commensurable with rect(CF, EB) [10.11]. Likewise the rectangles CF·EB and CF·FD stand under the same height CF, so rect(CF, EB) : rect(CF, FD) = EB : FD [6.1]; and EB is commensurable with FD; therefore rect(CF, EB) is commensurable with rect(CF, FD) [10.11]. Hence rect(AE, EB) is commensurable with rect(CF, FD) [10.12].

**Step 9.** If AB is a first apotome of a medial straight line, rect(AE, EB) is rational, that is, commensurable with the rational square; then rect(CF, FD), being commensurable with rect(AE, EB), is commensurable with the rational square [10.12] and is therefore rational [D10.1.4]. If AB is a second apotome of a medial straight line, rect(AE, EB) is medial; then rect(CF, FD), being an area commensurable with a medial area, is itself medial [10.23].

**Step 10.** Therefore CD is the remainder when from the medial straight line CF there is subtracted the medial straight line FD, which is commensurable with CF in square only and contains with CF a rectangle that is rational exactly when AB is a first apotome of a medial straight line, and medial exactly when AB is a second apotome of a medial straight line. In the former case CD is a first apotome of a medial straight line [10.74]; in the latter case CD is a second apotome of a medial straight line [10.75]. Therefore CD is an apotome of a medial straight line and the same in order as AB. Q.E.D.

*Path note.* "Commensurable" in the enunciation is taken as commensurable in length, since the proof requires EB commensurable with FD in length (Step 3). For the commensurability of the two rectangles (Step 8), the most direct route is two applications of 6.1 through the intermediate rectangle CF·EB combined with 10.11 and 10.12; this avoids passing through the proportion rect(AE,EB) : sq(EB) = rect(CF,FD) : sq(FD) and a separate argument that the squares on EB and FD are commensurable.

result.statement: A straight line commensurable with a minor straight line is minor.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a minor straight line, and let CD be a straight line commensurable in length with AB. I say that CD is minor.

**Step 2.** Since AB is minor, by 10.76 there is a straight line BE annexed to AB, so that B lies between A and E, AE is the whole, and AB is the remainder when EB is subtracted from AE, such that AE, EB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AE, EB is rational, and the rectangle contained by AE, EB is medial.

**Step 3.** By 6.12 let a fourth proportional be found to the three straight lines AB, CD, BE; produce CD beyond D (P2) and cut off DF equal to that fourth proportional (1.3). Then as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF; and since D lies between C and F, CF is the whole made up of CD and DF, so that CD is the remainder when FD is subtracted from CF.

**Step 4.** Since as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF, alternately (5.16) as AB is to BE, so is CD to DF. Componendo (5.18), as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD. Alternately again (5.16), as AE is to CF, so is EB to FD.

**Step 5.** Since as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF (Step 3), and as AE is to CF, so is BE to DF (Step 4), therefore by 5.11 as AB is to CD, so is AE to CF.

**Step 6.** AB is commensurable with CD by hypothesis. Since as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF, by 10.11 BE is commensurable with DF; and since as AB is to CD, so is AE to CF, by 10.11 AE is commensurable with CF. Since AE, CF are commensurable in length, the squares on them have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and are therefore commensurable (10.6); in the same way the square on EB is commensurable with the square on FD.

**Step 7.** Since as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD (Step 4), and the squares on these four straight lines are similar figures similarly described on them, by 6.22 as the square on AE is to the square on EB, so is the square on CF to the square on FD. But AE, EB are incommensurable in square, so the square on AE is incommensurable with the square on EB (D10.1.2). Therefore by 10.11 the square on CF is incommensurable with the square on FD; that is, CF, FD are incommensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 8.** Since as the square on AE is to the square on EB, so is the square on CF to the square on FD, componendo (5.18) as the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the square on EB, so is the sum of the squares on CF, FD to the square on FD; and alternately (5.16) as the sum of the squares on AE, EB is to the sum of the squares on CF, FD, so is the square on EB to the square on FD. But the square on EB is commensurable with the square on FD (Step 6); therefore by 10.11 the sum of the squares on AE, EB is commensurable with the sum of the squares on CF, FD. Now the sum of the squares on AE, EB is rational, that is, commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.4); hence by 10.12 the sum of the squares on CF, FD is also commensurable with that square, and is therefore rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 9.** The square on AE and the rectangle AE, EB are parallelograms under the same height AE, standing on the bases AE, EB respectively; therefore by 6.1 as the square on AE is to the rectangle AE, EB, so is AE to EB. Likewise, as the square on CF is to the rectangle CF, FD, so is CF to FD. But as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD (Step 4); therefore by 5.11 as the square on AE is to the rectangle AE, EB, so is the square on CF to the rectangle CF, FD; and alternately (5.16) as the square on AE is to the square on CF, so is the rectangle AE, EB to the rectangle CF, FD. But the square on AE is commensurable with the square on CF (Step 6); therefore by 10.11 the rectangle AE, EB is commensurable with the rectangle CF, FD. Now the rectangle AE, EB is medial, and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23, Porism); therefore the rectangle CF, FD is medial.

**Step 10.** Therefore CF, FD are two straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 7), which make the sum of the squares on them rational (Step 8) but the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 9); and CD is the remainder when FD is subtracted from CF (Step 3). Therefore by 10.76 CD is a minor straight line. Hence a straight line commensurable with a minor straight line is minor. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A straight line commensurable with that which produces with a rational area a medial whole is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
result.proof:
## Proposition 10.106
**Statement:** A straight line commensurable with that which produces with a rational area a medial whole is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let CD be a straight line commensurable in length with AB. I say that CD is also a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.

**Step 2.** Let BE be the annex to AB, so that AE is the whole straight line from which BE was subtracted to leave AB. Then, by the definition of a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, AE and EB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AE, EB is medial, and twice the rectangle AE, EB is rational [10.77].

**Step 3.** Let CD be produced to F so that DF is a fourth proportional to AB, CD, BE, that is, so that, as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF [6.12]. Then CF is a whole straight line from which DF is subtracted, and CD is the remainder.

**Step 4.** Since, as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF, therefore, componendo, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD [5.18].

**Step 5.** Since AB is commensurable with CD, and, as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF, therefore BE is commensurable with DF [10.11].

**Step 6.** Since BE, DF are commensurable in length, the square on BE has to the square on DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore the square on BE is commensurable with the square on DF [10.6].

**Step 7.** Since, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD, and the squares on these straight lines are similar figures similarly described on them, therefore, as the square on AE is to the square on EB, so is the square on CF to the square on FD [6.22].

**Step 8.** But AE, EB are incommensurable in square, that is, the square on AE is incommensurable with the square on EB [D10.1.2]. Therefore the square on CF is also incommensurable with the square on FD [10.11]; that is, CF, FD are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 9.** Since, as the square on AE is to the square on EB, so is the square on CF to the square on FD, therefore, componendo, as the squares on AE, EB are to the square on EB, so are the squares on CF, FD to the square on FD [5.18]; and, alternately, as the squares on AE, EB are to the squares on CF, FD, so is the square on EB to the square on FD [5.16].

**Step 10.** But the square on EB is commensurable with the square on FD (Step 6); therefore the sum of the squares on AE, EB is commensurable with the sum of the squares on CF, FD [10.11]. And the sum of the squares on AE, EB is medial; but an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]; therefore the sum of the squares on CF, FD is medial.

**Step 11.** Again, the rectangle AE, EB and the square on EB have the same height EB and stand on the bases AE, EB respectively; therefore, as AE is to EB, so is the rectangle AE, EB to the square on EB [6.1]. Likewise, as CF is to FD, so is the rectangle CF, FD to the square on FD [6.1]. But, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD; therefore, as the rectangle AE, EB is to the square on EB, so is the rectangle CF, FD to the square on FD [5.11]. Alternately, as the rectangle AE, EB is to the rectangle CF, FD, so is the square on EB to the square on FD [5.16].

**Step 12.** But the square on EB is commensurable with the square on FD; therefore the rectangle AE, EB is commensurable with the rectangle CF, FD [10.11]. And twice the rectangle AE, EB has to twice the rectangle CF, FD the same ratio as the rectangle AE, EB has to the rectangle CF, FD [5.15]; therefore twice the rectangle AE, EB is commensurable with twice the rectangle CF, FD [10.11].

**Step 13.** But twice the rectangle AE, EB is rational, that is, it is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]; therefore twice the rectangle CF, FD, being commensurable with twice the rectangle AE, EB, is also commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [10.12], and is therefore rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 14.** Therefore from the straight line CF there has been subtracted the straight line FD, which is incommensurable in square with CF, and which with CF makes the sum of the squares on them medial but twice the rectangle contained by them rational; therefore the remainder CD is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole [10.77].

Therefore a straight line commensurable with that which produces with a rational area a medial whole is itself a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 10.77, 6.12, 5.18, 10.11, 10.9, 10.6, 6.22, D10.1.2, 5.16, 10.23, 6.1, 5.11, 5.15, 10.12, D10.1.4

result.statement: A straight line commensurable with that which produces with a medial area a medial whole is itself also a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, and let CD be commensurable with AB. We must show that CD is also a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. Throughout, write AE² for the square on AE and AE·EB for the rectangle contained by AE, EB. Since AB is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, let BE be the annex to it, so that AB is the remainder when EB is subtracted from AE; then AE, EB are straight lines incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AE, EB is medial, twice the rectangle AE, EB is medial, and the squares on AE, EB are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AE, EB [10.78].

**Step 2.** To the three straight lines AB, CD, BE let a fourth proportional DF be found, so that as AB is to CD, so is BE to DF [6.12], and let DF be placed in a straight line with CD beyond D, so that CF is the whole made up of CD and DF.

**Step 3.** Since AB : CD = BE : DF, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents together to all the consequents together; therefore AE : CF = AB : CD [5.12]. And BE : DF = AB : CD by construction; since ratios which are the same with the same ratio are the same with one another, AE : CF = BE : DF [5.11].

**Step 4.** AB is commensurable with CD, and AB : CD = AE : CF (Step 3); therefore AE is commensurable with CF [10.11].

**Step 5.** Since AE : CF = BE : DF (Step 3), alternately AE : EB = CF : FD [5.16]. Squares are similar figures similarly described on their sides; therefore AE² : EB² = CF² : FD² [6.22]. But AE, EB are incommensurable in square, that is, AE² is incommensurable with EB² [D10.1.2]; therefore CF² is incommensurable with FD² [10.11], so that CF, FD are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 6.** Since AE is commensurable in length with CF (Step 4), the square on AE has to the square on CF the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore AE² is commensurable with CF² [10.6].

**Step 7.** Since AE : CF = EB : FD (Step 3), AE² : CF² = EB² : FD² [6.22]; therefore, as one antecedent is to one consequent, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents: (AE² + EB²) : (CF² + FD²) = AE² : CF² [5.12]. But AE² is commensurable with CF² (Step 6); therefore AE² + EB² is commensurable with CF² + FD² [10.11]. And AE² + EB² is medial (Step 1); an area commensurable with a medial area is medial; therefore CF² + FD² is medial [10.23].

**Step 8.** The square AE² and the rectangle AE·EB are under the same height AE, so AE² : AE·EB = AE : EB; likewise CF² : CF·FD = CF : FD [6.1]. But AE : EB = CF : FD (Step 5); therefore AE² : AE·EB = CF² : CF·FD [5.11], and alternately AE² : CF² = AE·EB : CF·FD [5.16]. Since AE² is commensurable with CF² (Step 6), AE·EB is commensurable with CF·FD [10.11]. Now equimultiples have the same ratio as the magnitudes themselves, so 2·AE·EB : 2·CF·FD = AE·EB : CF·FD [5.15]; therefore 2·AE·EB is commensurable with 2·CF·FD [10.11]. And 2·AE·EB is medial (Step 1); therefore 2·CF·FD is medial [10.23].

**Step 9.** AE² + EB² is incommensurable with 2·AE·EB (Step 1), and CF² + FD² is commensurable with AE² + EB² (Step 7); therefore CF² + FD² is incommensurable with 2·AE·EB [10.13]. Again, 2·CF·FD is commensurable with 2·AE·EB (Step 8), and 2·AE·EB is incommensurable with CF² + FD²; therefore 2·CF·FD is incommensurable with CF² + FD² [10.13].

**Step 10.** Therefore CF, FD are straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 5) which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 7), twice the rectangle contained by them medial (Step 8), and the squares on them incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them (Step 9); and CD is the remainder when FD is subtracted from CF. Therefore CD is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole [10.78]. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If from a rational area a medial area be subtracted, the âsideâ of the remaining area becomes one of two irrational straight lines, either an apotome or a minor straight line.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If from a rational area a medial area be subtracted, the "side" of the remaining area becomes one of two irrational straight lines, either an apotome or a minor straight line.

**Step 1.** Let BC be a rational area, let the medial area BD be subtracted from it, and let EC be the remainder, so that BD together with EC makes up BC. Set out a rational straight line FG. To FG apply, at right angles, a rectangle GH equal to BC, its breadth being FH; the application of a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure to a given straight line in a given angle is effected by 1.44 applied triangle by triangle in the manner of 1.45 [1.44, 1.45]. Since BD is a part of BC, BD is less than BC [CN5]. To FG apply likewise a rectangle GK equal to BD, its breadth being FK [1.44, 1.45]. Then GK is less than GH; and since both rectangles stand on the common side FG, FK is less than FH (otherwise GK would not be less than GH), so K falls on FH between F and H. Let KH be the remaining part of FH, and let LH denote the rectangle contained by KL (equal to FG) and KH, which is what remains of GH when GK is taken away.

**Step 2.** Since GH is equal to BC and GK is equal to BD, the remainder LH is equal to the remainder EC [CN3]. The "side" of an area is the straight line on which is described a square equal to that area [D10.1.4]; a square equal to LH is therefore also equal to EC [CN1]. Hence the side of EC is the side of LH, and it suffices to determine the side of LH.

**Step 3.** GH is a rational area, being equal to the rational area BC, and it is applied to the rational straight line FG. Therefore its breadth FH is rational and commensurable in length with FG [10.20].

**Step 4.** GK is a medial area, being equal to the medial area BD; that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21], and it is applied to the rational straight line FG. Therefore its breadth FK is rational and incommensurable in length with FG [10.22].

**Step 5.** FH is commensurable in length with FG (Step 3), and FG is incommensurable in length with FK (Step 4). Therefore FH is incommensurable in length with FK [10.13].

**Step 6.** FH and FK are both rational straight lines (Steps 3 and 4), so each is commensurable in square with the rational straight line FG [D10.1.3]; that is, the square on FH and the square on FK are each commensurable with the square on FG [D10.1.2]. Therefore the square on FH is commensurable with the square on FK [10.12], so that FH and FK are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Together with Step 5, FH and FK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 7.** KH is what remains when the rational straight line FK, commensurable in square only with the whole FH, is subtracted from the rational straight line FH. Therefore KH is an apotome [10.73], FH being the whole and FK the annex.

**Step 8.** Since FH is greater than FK, the square on FH is greater than the square on FK by the square on some straight line; and this straight line is either commensurable in length with FH or incommensurable in length with FH. Consider the two cases.

**Step 9.** First, let the square on FH be greater than the square on FK by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FH. The whole FH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line FG set out (Step 3). Therefore the apotome KH is a first apotome [D10.3.1].

**Step 10.** The rectangle LH is contained by the rational straight line KL (equal to FG) and the first apotome KH. Therefore the side of LH is an apotome [10.91]. By Step 2, the side of EC is an apotome.

**Step 11.** Secondly, let the square on FH be greater than the square on FK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FH. The whole FH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line FG set out (Step 3). Therefore the apotome KH is a fourth apotome [D10.3.4].

**Step 12.** The rectangle LH is contained by the rational straight line KL (equal to FG) and the fourth apotome KH. Therefore the side of LH is a minor straight line [10.94]. By Step 2, the side of EC is minor.

**Step 13.** The two cases of Step 8 exhaust the possibilities. Therefore, if from a rational area a medial area be subtracted, the side of the remaining area is either an apotome or a minor straight line; and each of these is irrational [10.73, 10.94]. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 1.44, 1.45, CN1, CN3, CN5, D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4, D10.3.1, D10.3.4, 10.12, 10.13, 10.20, 10.21, 10.22, 10.73, 10.91, 10.94

result.statement: If from a medial area a rational area be subtracted, there arise two other irrational straight lines, either a first apotome of a medial straight line or a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let BC be a medial area, that is, an area equal to the square on a medial straight line, and let the rational area BD be subtracted from it, so that BD is a part of BC and the remainder is the area EC (BC = BD + EC). It is to be shown that the "side" of EC — the straight line on which is described a square equal to EC [D10.1.4] — is either a first apotome of a medial straight line or a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and that in either case it is irrational.

**Step 2.** Let a rational straight line FG be set out. To FG let there be applied, in a right angle at F, the rectangle GH equal to BC, having FG, FH as its sides; and, on the same side of FG and in the same right angle at F, the rectangle GK equal to BD, having FG, FK as its sides [1.44, 1.45].

**Step 3.** Since BD is a part of BC, BD is less than BC [CN5]; therefore the rectangle GK is less than the rectangle GH. As both rectangles stand on the same side FG in the same right angle at F, FK is less than FH; for otherwise the rectangle GK would coincide with or contain the rectangle GH and so would not be less than it [CN5]. Hence K lies between F and H, and the side of GK opposite to FG divides the rectangle GH into the rectangle GK and the rectangle KH contained by FG, KH.

**Step 4.** Therefore the rectangle KH is the remainder when GK is subtracted from GH, and since GH = BC and GK = BD, the rectangle KH is equal to the remainder EC [CN3]. Thus EC is equal to the rectangle contained by the rational straight line FG and the straight line KH.

**Step 5.** Since BC is equal to the square on a medial straight line, and the rectangle GH equal to it has been applied to the rational straight line FG, the breadth FH is rational and incommensurable in length with FG [10.22].

**Step 6.** Since BD is a rational area, and the rectangle GK equal to it has been applied to the rational straight line FG, the breadth FK is rational and commensurable in length with FG [10.20].

**Step 7.** FK is commensurable in length with FG, while FG is incommensurable in length with FH; therefore FK is incommensurable in length with FH [10.13].

**Step 8.** FH and FK are both rational, so each of them is commensurable in square with FG [D10.1.3]; that is, the square on FH and the square on FK are each commensurable with the square on FG [D10.1.2]. Therefore the square on FH is commensurable with the square on FK [10.12], so that FH, FK are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Together with Step 7, FH and FK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** Now KH is the remainder when FK is subtracted from the greater FH (Step 3), and FK is a rational straight line commensurable with the whole FH in square only; therefore KH is an apotome [10.73], with whole FH and annex FK. Moreover its annex FK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, FG (Step 6).

**Step 10.** The square on FH is greater than the square on FK by the square on some straight line, and this straight line is either commensurable or incommensurable in length with FH [D10.1.1]. Two cases arise.

**Step 11.** Case (i): let the square on FH be greater than the square on FK by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FH. Since the annex FK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line FG set out, the apotome KH is a second apotome [D10.3.2]. Then EC, being equal to the rectangle contained by FG, KH (Step 4), is an area contained by a rational straight line and a second apotome; therefore the side of EC is a first apotome of a medial straight line [10.92], which is irrational [10.74].

**Step 12.** Case (ii): let the square on FH be greater than the square on FK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FH. Since the annex FK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line FG set out, the apotome KH is a fifth apotome [D10.3.5]. Then EC is an area contained by a rational straight line and a fifth apotome; therefore the side of EC is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole [10.95], which is irrational [10.77].

**Step 13.** Therefore, if from a medial area a rational area be subtracted, the side of the remaining area is one of two irrational straight lines, namely either a first apotome of a medial straight line or a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If from a medial area there be subtracted a medial area incommensurable with the whole, the two remaining irrational straight lines arise, either a second apotome of a medial straight line or a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let BC be a medial area, and from it let there be subtracted the medial area BD, incommensurable with the whole BC; let EC be the remainder, so that BC is BD together with EC. It is to be proved that the "side" of EC (the straight line whose square is equal to EC) is one of two irrational straight lines, either a second apotome of a medial straight line or a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line FG. To FG apply, in a right angle, the rectangle GH equal to BC, producing FH as breadth [1.45]; and, cutting it off from GH along FG, apply likewise the rectangle GK equal to BD, producing FK as breadth [1.45]. Since BD is a part of BC, BD is less than BC [CN5]; hence GK is less than GH, so that FK is less than FH and K lies on FH between F and H.

**Step 3.** The remainder of GH after GK is taken away is the rectangle contained by FG, KH. Since GH is equal to BC, GK is equal to BD, and the remainder of BC after BD is EC, the rectangle contained by FG, KH is equal to EC [CN3].

**Step 4.** Since BC is a medial area, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line; and GH, which is equal to BC, is applied to the rational straight line FG. Therefore the breadth FH is rational and incommensurable in length with FG [10.22]. In the same way, since BD is a medial area and GK, equal to BD, is applied to FG, the breadth FK is rational and incommensurable in length with FG [10.22].

**Step 5.** FH, being rational, is commensurable with FG either in length and in square, or in square only [D10.1.3]; and since it is incommensurable in length with FG, FH is commensurable with FG in square only. Likewise FK is commensurable with FG in square only. Therefore FH and FK, being each commensurable in square with the same straight line FG, are commensurable in square with one another [10.12].

**Step 6.** The rectangles GH, GK are under the same height FG; therefore GH is to GK as FH is to FK [6.1]. But GH is equal to BC and GK to BD, and BC is incommensurable with BD; hence GH is incommensurable with GK, and therefore FH is incommensurable in length with FK [10.11].

**Step 7.** Thus FH and FK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 4 to 6), and FK is subtracted from FH. Therefore the remainder KH is an apotome [10.73], FH being the whole and FK the annex. Moreover, neither the whole FH nor the annex FK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line FG set out (Step 4).

**Step 8.** Since FH is greater than FK, the square on FH is greater than the square on FK, and the excess is the square on a straight line which is either commensurable in length with FH or incommensurable in length with FH. There are therefore two cases.

**Step 9.** First case: let the square on FH be greater than the square on FK by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FH. Then, since neither FH nor FK is commensurable in length with FG, KH is a third apotome [D10.3.3]. The rectangle contained by FG, KH is therefore contained by a rational straight line and a third apotome, so the "side" of it is the irrational straight line called a second apotome of a medial straight line [10.93]. But this rectangle is equal to EC (Step 3); therefore the "side" of EC is a second apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 10.** Second case: let the square on FH be greater than the square on FK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FH. Then, since neither FH nor FK is commensurable in length with FG, KH is a sixth apotome [D10.3.6]. The rectangle contained by FG, KH is therefore contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, so the "side" of it is the irrational straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole [10.96]. But this rectangle is equal to EC (Step 3); therefore the "side" of EC is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

**Step 11.** Therefore, if from a medial area there be subtracted a medial area incommensurable with the whole, the "side" of the remaining area is one of the two remaining irrational straight lines, either a second apotome of a medial straight line or a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. Q.E.D.

Note on path: for the application of a rectangle equal to a given area to the straight line FG, 1.45 is cited (its construction applies, in a given angle, a parallelogram equal to any rectilineal figure to a given straight line); 1.44 alone would cover only a triangle.

result.statement: The apotome is not the same with the binomial straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be an apotome, and suppose, if possible, that AB is also a binomial straight line. Set out a rational straight line DC (D10.1.3), and to DC apply, in a right angle, the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB (1.45), producing DE as breadth.

**Step 2.** Since AB is an apotome and its square has been applied to the rational straight line DC, the breadth DE is a first apotome (10.97). Let EF be the annex to DE, so that F lies on DE produced beyond E, DF is the whole, and DE is the remainder when FE is subtracted from DF. By 10.73, DF and FE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; and, since DE is a first apotome, the whole DF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DC set out (D10.3.1).

**Step 3.** Again, since AB is by hypothesis a binomial and its square has been applied to the rational straight line DC, the breadth DE is a first binomial (10.60). Let DE be divided into its terms at G, DG being the greater term. By 10.36, DG and GE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; and, since DE is a first binomial, the greater term DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DC set out (D10.2.1).

**Step 4.** Since DF and DG are each commensurable in length with DC, DF is commensurable in length with DG (10.12).

**Step 5.** G lies between D and E, and F lies on DE produced beyond E; hence the points lie in the order D, G, E, F, so that DF is made up of DG and GF, and GF is made up of GE and EF. Since the whole DF is commensurable with the part DG, the parts DG and GF are commensurable (10.15); and therefore the whole DF is also commensurable in length with GF (10.15).

**Step 6.** Since GF is commensurable in length with DF, and DF is commensurable in length with DC, GF is commensurable in length with DC (10.12); therefore GF is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 7.** Since DF and FE are commensurable in square only, DF is incommensurable in length with FE. But GF is commensurable with DF; therefore GF is incommensurable in length with FE (10.13).

**Step 8.** Since GF and DF are commensurable in length, the squares on GF and DF have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and are therefore commensurable (10.6). But the square on DF is commensurable with the square on FE, since DF and FE are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). Hence the square on GF is commensurable with the square on FE (10.12), that is, GF and FE are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). Combining this with Step 7, GF and FE are commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** Therefore GF and FE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and FE, being a part of GF, is less than GF (CN5). Hence the remainder GE, obtained by subtracting FE from GF, is an apotome, and is therefore irrational (10.73).

**Step 10.** But GE, being a term of the binomial DE, is rational (Step 3). Thus GE would be both commensurable and incommensurable with the rational straight line DC set out, which is impossible (D10.1.3). Therefore the supposition is false, and the apotome is not the same with the binomial straight line. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on a rational straight line applied to the binomial straight line produces as breadth an apotome the terms of which are commensurable with the terms of the binomial and moreover in the same ratio; and further the apotome so arising will have the same order as the binomial straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line and let BC be a binomial straight line divided into its terms at D, DC being the greater term. Since BC is binomial, its terms CD, DB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; hence CD > DB, the square on CD is commensurable with the square on DB [D10.1.2], and CD is incommensurable in length with DB. Let the square on A, applied to BC, produce EF as breadth, so that the rectangle BC, EF is equal to the square on A. It must be shown that EF is an apotome whose terms are commensurable in length with CD, DB respectively and in the same ratio as CD to DB, and that EF has the same order as BC.

**Step 2.** Apply to the straight line BD a rectangle equal to the square on A [1.45], and let G be its breadth, so that the rectangle BD, G is equal to the square on A. Then the rectangle BC, EF is equal to the rectangle BD, G [CN1]. Since the rectangle contained by the extremes BC, EF is equal to the rectangle contained by the means BD, G, the four straight lines are proportional: CB is to BD as G is to EF [6.16].

**Step 3.** Alternately, CB is to G as BD is to EF [5.16]; and CB is greater than BD [CN5]; therefore G is greater than EF [5.14]. Produce EF beyond F [P2] and cut off from the produced line EH equal to G [1.3]. Since EH = G > EF, the point F lies between E and H, so that HF is the excess of HE over EF. Since G = EH, G is to EF as HE is to EF [5.7]; therefore CB is to BD as HE is to EF [5.11].

**Step 4.** CB is composed of CD and DB, and HE is composed of HF and FE; so the proportion CB : BD = HE : EF is a proportion componendo, and separando CD is to DB as HF is to FE [5.17]. Alternately, CD is to HF as DB is to FE [5.16]; and CD is greater than DB, therefore HF is greater than FE [5.14].

**Step 5.** From FH cut off FL equal to FE [1.3], so that LH is the excess of HF over FE. Take X, a third proportional to LH and FE [6.11], so that LH is to FE as FE is to X. Produce FE beyond E [P2] and cut off EK equal to X [1.3]. Then K, E, F, H lie in this order on one straight line, and FK = FE + EK, HK = HE + EK, HK = HF + FK. Since LH : FE = FE : EK, componendo (LH + FE) : FE = (FE + EK) : EK [5.18]; that is, HF is to FE as FK is to KE.

**Step 6.** In the proportion HF : FE = FK : KE the antecedents are HF, FK and the consequents are FE, KE; therefore the sum of the antecedents, HF + FK = HK, is to the sum of the consequents, FE + KE = FK, as FK is to KE [5.12]: HK is to KF as FK is to KE. Moreover FK : KE = HF : FE = CD : DB (Steps 4 and 5) [5.11], so also HK : KF = CD : DB [5.11]. Thus the three straight lines HK, KF, KE are in continued proportion, and HK : KF = KF : KE = CD : DB.

**Step 7.** Since CD : DB = HK : KF, the squares on CD, DB, being similar figures similarly described on them, are proportional to the squares on HK, KF: the square on CD is to the square on DB as the square on HK is to the square on KF [6.22]. But the square on CD is commensurable with the square on DB (Step 1); therefore the square on HK is commensurable with the square on KF [10.11].

**Step 8.** Since HK, KF, KE are three proportional straight lines, as the first HK is to the third KE, so is the square on HK to the square on KF, the similar figure similarly described on the second [6.19, Porism]. But the square on HK is commensurable with the square on KF; therefore HK is commensurable in length with KE [10.11].

**Step 9.** HK is the sum of HE and EK, and the whole HK is commensurable with the part EK; therefore HE is commensurable in length with EK [10.15].

**Step 10.** Since G = EH, the rectangle BD, G is the rectangle BD, EH, and it is equal to the square on A (Step 2). Because A is rational, the square on A is a rational area [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]; hence the rectangle EH, BD is rational. This rational area is applied to the rational straight line BD and produces EH as breadth; therefore EH is rational and commensurable in length with BD [10.20]. EK is commensurable with EH (Step 9) and EH with BD; therefore EK is commensurable in length with BD [10.12]; and EK, being commensurable with the rational straight line EH, is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 11.** Since CD : DB = FK : KE (Step 6), the square on CD is to the square on DB as the square on FK is to the square on KE [6.22]. The square on CD is commensurable with the square on DB; therefore the square on FK is commensurable with the square on KE [10.11]. And CD is incommensurable in length with DB; therefore FK is incommensurable in length with KE [10.11]. Now KE is rational, so the square on KE is a rational area [D10.1.4]; the square on FK, being commensurable with the square on KE, is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [10.12] and is therefore rational [D10.1.4]; hence FK is commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.2] and is rational [D10.1.3]. Therefore FK, KE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 12.** FK = FE + EK, so FK is greater than KE [CN5], and FE is the remainder when KE is subtracted from FK. Thus from the rational straight line FK there has been subtracted the rational straight line KE, commensurable with FK in square only; therefore FE is an apotome [10.73], its whole being FK and its annex KE.

**Step 13.** From CD : DB = FK : KE, alternately CD is to FK as DB is to KE [5.16]. DB is commensurable in length with KE (Step 10); therefore CD is commensurable in length with FK [10.11]. Thus the terms FK, KE of the apotome EF are commensurable in length with the terms CD, DB of the binomial BC respectively, and FK : KE = CD : DB, so they are in the same ratio.

**Step 14.** Let the rational straight line set out, with reference to which the binomial BC receives its order, be called R. Since CD is commensurable with FK and DB with KE: if CD is commensurable in length with R then FK is commensurable in length with R, and if FK is commensurable with R then CD is commensurable with R [10.12]; likewise DB is commensurable in length with R if and only if KE is [10.12]. Consequently FK is commensurable in length with R exactly when CD is; KE exactly when DB is; and neither of FK, KE exactly when neither of CD, DB is.

**Step 15.** CD, DB, FK, KE are four proportional straight lines. Hence, if the square on CD is greater than the square on DB by the square on a straight line commensurable with CD, the square on FK is greater than the square on KE by the square on a straight line commensurable with FK; and if the square on CD is greater than the square on DB by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CD, the square on FK is greater than the square on KE by the square on a straight line incommensurable with FK [10.14].

**Step 16.** Six cases arise for the binomial BC, and in each the apotome EF, with whole FK and annex KE, falls under the corresponding definition. (i) If BC is a first binomial [D10.2.1], the square on CD exceeds the square on DB by the square on a line commensurable with CD and CD is commensurable with R; then by Steps 14 and 15 the square on FK exceeds the square on KE by the square on a line commensurable with FK and the whole FK is commensurable with R, so EF is a first apotome [D10.3.1]. (ii) If BC is a second binomial [D10.2.2], the same excess condition holds and DB is commensurable with R; then KE, the annex, is commensurable with R, so EF is a second apotome [D10.3.2]. (iii) If BC is a third binomial [D10.2.3], the same excess condition holds and neither CD nor DB is commensurable with R; then neither FK nor KE is commensurable with R, so EF is a third apotome [D10.3.3]. (iv) If BC is a fourth binomial [D10.2.4], the square on CD exceeds the square on DB by the square on a line incommensurable with CD and CD is commensurable with R; then the square on FK exceeds the square on KE by the square on a line incommensurable with FK and FK is commensurable with R, so EF is a fourth apotome [D10.3.4]. (v) If BC is a fifth binomial [D10.2.5], the same incommensurable excess condition holds and DB is commensurable with R; then KE is commensurable with R, so EF is a fifth apotome [D10.3.5]. (vi) If BC is a sixth binomial [D10.2.6], the same incommensurable excess condition holds and neither term is commensurable with R; then neither FK nor KE is commensurable with R, so EF is a sixth apotome [D10.3.6].

**Step 17.** Therefore the square on the rational straight line A, applied to the binomial BC, produces as breadth EF, which is an apotome whose terms FK, KE are commensurable with the terms CD, DB of the binomial and in the same ratio, and which is of the same order as the binomial BC. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The square on a rational straight line, if applied to an apotome, produces as, breadth the binomial straight line the terms of which are commensurable with the terms of the apotome and in the same ratio; and further the binomial so arising has the same order as the apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line and BD an apotome, and let the rectangle contained by BD, KH be equal to the square on A, so that the square on A applied to BD produces KH as breadth. Let ρ be the rational straight line set out, with reference to which BD is an apotome of one of the six orders. I say that KH is a binomial straight line whose terms are commensurable with the terms of BD and in the same ratio, and that KH is of the same order as BD.

**Step 2.** Let DC be the annex to the apotome BD, so that BC is the whole and CD the annex, D lying between B and C. By 10.73, BC and CD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Since CD is a part of BC, CD is less than BC [CN5].

**Step 3.** Produce BC beyond C [P2] and cut off CM equal to CD [1.3]. Then the straight line DM is bisected at C, and BD is added to it in a straight line. Therefore, by 2.6, the rectangle contained by BM, BD together with the square on CD is equal to the square on CB.

**Step 4.** Since BC, CD are commensurable in square, the square on BC is commensurable with the square on CD [D10.1.2]. By Step 3 the square on BC is made up of the rectangle BM, BD and the square on CD, and this whole is commensurable with one of its parts, the square on CD; therefore the rectangle BM, BD is commensurable with the square on CD [10.15]. But CD is rational, so the square on CD is rational, that is, commensurable with the square on ρ [D10.1.4]; hence the rectangle BM, BD is also commensurable with the square on ρ [10.12], that is, the rectangle BM, BD is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** A is rational, so the square on A is rational [D10.1.4]; and the rectangle BD, KH is equal to the square on A, so the rectangle BD, KH is rational. The rectangles BD, KH and BD, BM are therefore both commensurable with the square on ρ, and hence commensurable with one another [10.12].

**Step 6.** The rectangles BD, KH and BD, BM are under the same height BD; therefore the rectangle BD, KH is to the rectangle BD, BM as KH is to BM [6.1]. The first is commensurable with the second (Step 5); therefore KH is commensurable in length with BM [10.11].

**Step 7.** Cut KH at F similarly to BM, which is cut at C [6.10], so that KF : FH = BC : CM, that is, KF : FH = BC : CD. Alternately, KF : BC = FH : CD [5.16]; hence, as one antecedent is to its consequent, so is the sum of the antecedents to the sum of the consequents: KH : BM = KF : BC = FH : CD [5.12]. Since KH is commensurable with BM, KF is commensurable in length with BC, and FH is commensurable in length with CD [10.11].

**Step 8.** KF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line BC, and FH with the rational straight line CD; therefore KF and FH are rational [D10.1.3]. Since BC : CD = KF : FH and BC is incommensurable in length with CD, KF is incommensurable in length with FH [10.11]. Since the four straight lines BC, CD, KF, FH are proportional, the squares on them are proportional: the square on BC is to the square on CD as the square on KF is to the square on FH [6.22]; and the square on BC is commensurable with the square on CD (Step 4), so the square on KF is commensurable with the square on FH [10.11], that is, KF and FH are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Thus KF, FH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and KH, which is made up of them, is a binomial straight line whose terms are KF and FH [10.36].

**Step 9.** The terms KF, FH of KH are commensurable with the terms BC, CD of the apotome respectively, and KF : FH = BC : CD (Step 7). Moreover, since BC : CD = KF : FH, alternately BC : KF = CD : FH [5.16]; and BC is greater than CD (Step 2), so KF is greater than FH [5.14]. Thus KF, the greater term of KH, answers to the whole BC of the apotome, and FH, the lesser term, to the annex CD.

**Step 10.** Since BC : CD = KF : FH, by 10.14: if the square on BC is greater than the square on CD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with BC, then the square on KF is greater than the square on FH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with KF; and if the square on BC is greater than the square on CD by the square on a straight line incommensurable with BC, then the square on KF is greater than the square on FH by the square on a straight line incommensurable with KF.

**Step 11.** Since KF is commensurable in length with BC and FH with CD: if BC is commensurable in length with ρ, so is KF [10.12]; if CD is commensurable in length with ρ, so is FH [10.12]; if BC is incommensurable in length with ρ, so is KF [10.13]; and if CD is incommensurable in length with ρ, so is FH [10.13].

**Step 12.** Combining Steps 10 and 11: if BD is a first apotome [D10.3.1], the square on KF exceeds the square on FH by the square on a straight line commensurable with KF and the greater term KF is commensurable in length with ρ, so KH is a first binomial [D10.2.1]; if BD is a second apotome [D10.3.2], the lesser term FH is commensurable in length with ρ, so KH is a second binomial [D10.2.2]; if BD is a third apotome [D10.3.3], neither term is commensurable in length with ρ, so KH is a third binomial [D10.2.3]. Likewise, when the square on BC exceeds the square on CD by the square on a straight line incommensurable with BC, the square on KF exceeds the square on FH by the square on a straight line incommensurable with KF, and BD being a fourth, fifth or sixth apotome [D10.3.4, D10.3.5, D10.3.6] makes KH a fourth, fifth or sixth binomial respectively [D10.2.4, D10.2.5, D10.2.6].

**Step 13.** Therefore the square on the rational straight line A, applied to the apotome BD, produces as breadth the binomial straight line KH, whose terms KF, FH are commensurable with the terms BC, CD of the apotome and in the same ratio; and KH has the same order as the apotome BD. Q.E.D.

Path note: an alternative route applies the square on A also to the whole BC, obtains a breadth commensurable with BC, and then reaches the terms of KH through a convertendo proportion and a continued-proportion construction; the route through 2.6, which shows at once that KH is commensurable with BC + CD, is shorter and was chosen.

result.statement: If an area be contained by an apotome and the binomial straight line the terms of which are commensurable with the terms of the apotome and in the same ratio, the âsideâ of the area is rational.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** (Setting out.) Let AB be an apotome, AF its whole and FB its annex, so that AF and FB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, FB is less than AF, and AB is the remainder when FB is subtracted from AF [10.73]. Let CD be a binomial straight line, CE its greater term and ED its lesser term. By hypothesis the terms of the binomial are commensurable with the terms of the apotome and in the same ratio: CE is commensurable with AF, ED is commensurable with FB, and AF : FB = CE : ED. Let the rectangle contained by AB, CD be equal to the square on G, so that G is the "side" of the area. We must show that G is rational.

**Step 2.** (Construction.) Set out a rational straight line H. Divide the square on H by a diameter into two triangles and apply each in turn to the straight line CD in a right angle [1.44]; the two parallelograms so applied lie side by side on CD and together make up a rectangle contained by CD and a breadth KL, equal to the square on H. Thus the square on the rational straight line H has been applied to the binomial CD and produces KL as breadth.

**Step 3.** By 10.112, the square on a rational straight line applied to a binomial straight line produces as breadth an apotome whose terms are commensurable with the terms of the binomial and in the same ratio. Hence KL is an apotome; let KM be its whole and ML its annex (so ML is less than KM [10.73]). Then KM is commensurable with CE, ML is commensurable with ED, and CE : ED = KM : ML.

**Step 4.** Since AF : FB = CE : ED (Step 1) and CE : ED = KM : ML (Step 3), ratios which are the same with the same ratio are the same with one another; therefore AF : FB = KM : ML [5.11].

**Step 5.** Taking the proportion alternately, AF : KM = FB : ML [5.16].

**Step 6.** Here FB is a part subtracted from the whole AF, and ML is a part subtracted from the whole KM (Steps 1 and 3), and, as whole AF is to whole KM, so is the part FB to the part ML (Step 5). Therefore the remainder is to the remainder as whole is to whole: AB : KL = AF : KM [5.19].

**Step 7.** AF is commensurable with CE (Step 1) and CE is commensurable with KM (Step 3); magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another, so AF is commensurable with KM [10.12].

**Step 8.** In the proportion AB : KL = AF : KM (Step 6) the third term AF is commensurable with the fourth term KM (Step 7); therefore the first term AB is commensurable with the second term KL [10.11].

**Step 9.** The rectangle CD, AB and the rectangle CD, KL are parallelograms under the same height CD, so they are to one another as their bases: rect(CD, AB) : rect(CD, KL) = AB : KL [6.1]. Since AB is commensurable with KL (Step 8), the rectangle CD, AB is commensurable with the rectangle CD, KL [10.11].

**Step 10.** But the rectangle CD, KL is equal to the square on H (Step 2); therefore the rectangle CD, AB is commensurable with the square on H. And the square on G is equal to the rectangle CD, AB (Step 1); therefore the square on G is commensurable with the square on H.

**Step 11.** H is a rational straight line, so the square on H is a rational area [D10.1.4]. The square on G is commensurable with the square on H (Step 10), and the square on H is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line; hence the square on G is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [10.12], and so the square on G is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 12.** Since the square on G is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line, G is commensurable in square with that straight line [D10.1.2]; therefore G is rational [D10.1.3]. And G is the "side" of the rectangle contained by the apotome AB and the binomial CD. Therefore, if an area be contained by an apotome and the binomial straight line the terms of which are commensurable with the terms of the apotome and in the same ratio, the "side" of the area is rational. Q.E.D.

result.statement: From a medial straight line there arise irrational straight lines infinite in number, and none of them is the same as any of the preceding.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a medial straight line, and let a rational straight line B be set out [D10.1.3]. Form the rectangle contained by B and A, and let C be the side of a square equal to the rectangle B·A [2.14]. Thus the square on C, applied to the rational straight line B, produces as breadth the straight line A.

**Step 2.** The rectangle B·A is irrational. For it is applied to the rational straight line B and produces as breadth A. If it were a rational area, A would be rational and commensurable in length with B [10.20]. But A is medial, and a medial straight line is irrational [10.21]; a straight line cannot be both rational and irrational [D10.1.3]. Hence the rectangle B·A is not rational, that is, it is incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out, and so it is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 3.** Since the square on C is equal to the irrational area B·A, the straight line C is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 4.** (Lemma.) A medial straight line is neither rational, nor a binomial straight line, nor an apotome. Let M be medial, and let the square on M be applied to B, producing a certain breadth. (i) M is not rational, since M is irrational [10.21, D10.1.3]. (ii) If M were a binomial straight line, the breadth would be a first binomial [10.60], which is a binomial straight line [D10.2.1] and therefore irrational [10.36]; but since M is medial, that same breadth is rational [10.22]; and a straight line cannot be both rational and irrational [D10.1.3]. (iii) If M were an apotome, the breadth would be a first apotome [10.97], which is an apotome [D10.3.1] and therefore irrational [10.73]; but since M is medial, the breadth is rational [10.22]; which is impossible [D10.1.3].

**Step 5.** C is not the same as any of the thirteen irrational straight lines obtained before, namely the medial, the six formed by addition, and the six formed by subtraction. For the square on C, applied to the rational straight line B, produces as breadth A, which is medial [Step 1].
(a) If C were medial, the breadth A would be rational [10.22]; but A is not rational [Step 4 (i)].
(b) If C were a binomial, a first bimedial, a second bimedial, a major, a side of a rational plus a medial area, or a side of the sum of two medial areas, the breadth A would be respectively a first, second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth binomial [10.60, 10.61, 10.62, 10.63, 10.64, 10.65], and hence in every case a binomial straight line [D10.2.1, D10.2.2, D10.2.3, D10.2.4, D10.2.5, D10.2.6]; but A, being medial, is not a binomial [Step 4 (ii)].
(c) If C were an apotome, a first apotome of a medial, a second apotome of a medial, a minor, a straight line producing with a rational area a medial whole, or a straight line producing with a medial area a medial whole, the breadth A would be respectively a first, second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth apotome [10.97, 10.98, 10.99, 10.100, 10.101, 10.102], and hence in every case an apotome [D10.3.1, D10.3.2, D10.3.3, D10.3.4, D10.3.5, D10.3.6]; but A, being medial, is not an apotome [Step 4 (iii)].
Therefore C is an irrational straight line [Step 3] which is not the same as any of the preceding; in particular C is not rational, not medial, not a binomial, and not an apotome.

**Step 6.** Again, let D be the side of a square equal to the rectangle B·C [2.14]. The rectangle B·C is applied to the rational straight line B and produces as breadth C; if it were rational, C would be rational [10.20], whereas C is irrational [Step 3, D10.1.3]. Hence the rectangle B·C is irrational [D10.1.4], and therefore D is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** D is not the same as any of the preceding, namely the thirteen irrational straight lines and C. For the square on D, applied to B, produces as breadth C.
(a) If D were medial, C would be rational [10.22]; but C is irrational [Step 3].
(b) If D were any one of the six irrational straight lines formed by addition, C would be a binomial of one of the six orders [10.60, 10.61, 10.62, 10.63, 10.64, 10.65], hence a binomial straight line [D10.2.1, D10.2.2, D10.2.3, D10.2.4, D10.2.5, D10.2.6]; but C is not a binomial [Step 5].
(c) If D were any one of the six irrational straight lines formed by subtraction, C would be an apotome of one of the six orders [10.97, 10.98, 10.99, 10.100, 10.101, 10.102], hence an apotome [D10.3.1, D10.3.2, D10.3.3, D10.3.4, D10.3.5, D10.3.6]; but C is not an apotome [Step 5].
(d) D is not the same as C: for the square on C, applied to B, produces as breadth a medial straight line, whereas the square on D, applied to B, produces as breadth C, which is not medial [Step 5].
Therefore D is an irrational straight line not the same as any of the preceding; in particular D is not rational, not medial, not a binomial, not an apotome, and not the same as C.

**Step 8.** The process continues without end. Suppose that after A the straight lines C, D, ..., K, L have been obtained in this manner, each being the side of a square equal to the rectangle contained by B and the straight line before it, and that L is irrational and not the same as any of the preceding (the thirteen irrational straight lines and C, D, ..., K); so L is neither rational, nor medial, nor a binomial, nor an apotome, nor the same as any of C, ..., K. Let N be the side of a square equal to the rectangle B·L [2.14]. The rectangle B·L is applied to B and produces as breadth L; it is not rational, for otherwise L would be rational [10.20], which it is not [D10.1.3]; hence the rectangle B·L is irrational [D10.1.4], and N is irrational [D10.1.4]. Further, the square on N, applied to B, produces as breadth L. N is not medial, for then L would be rational [10.22]; N is not any of the six irrational straight lines formed by addition, for then L would be a binomial of some order [10.60, 10.61, 10.62, 10.63, 10.64, 10.65] and so a binomial straight line [D10.2.1, D10.2.2, D10.2.3, D10.2.4, D10.2.5, D10.2.6]; N is not any of the six formed by subtraction, for then L would be an apotome of some order [10.97, 10.98, 10.99, 10.100, 10.101, 10.102] and so an apotome [D10.3.1, D10.3.2, D10.3.3, D10.3.4, D10.3.5, D10.3.6]; and N is not the same as any of C, D, ..., L, because the square on each of these, applied to B, produces as breadth the straight line before it (A, C, ..., K respectively), whereas the square on N, applied to B, produces L, which is not the same as A (L not being medial) nor as any of C, ..., K. Thus N is irrational and not the same as any of the preceding, and N satisfies the same conditions as L; so the construction may be repeated indefinitely, each new straight line being irrational and different from all before it.

**Step 9.** Therefore from the medial straight line A there arise irrational straight lines C, D, ..., N, ... infinite in number, and none of them is the same as any of the preceding. Q.E.D.
